TH' OWD COT AW WER BORN IN, " Teddy O'Neale.") .Ikw've landed once moor i'th' owd country this mornin', Where aw lived i' mi childhood, so careless an' free; aw've just bin to look at th' owd cot aw wer born in— Id stands under t' shade o' yon giant ooak tree. They'n med terble changes sin last aw'd a peep in, When poverty drooav us to th dark, smooky teawn— They'n blocked up th' owd garrets eawr lads use' to sleep in, Brunt up o' th' hand looms, an' pood th' weyvin' shop deawn.

ud th' pooarch where ml granny oft coom wV her knittin' Is just like id waur i' them breet summer heawrs; th' owd rustic cheer as mi dad use' to sit in Stands under th' gred plum tree, i'th' midst o' some ileawrs. There's cbilder at play, an' there's merry bells ringin' O'er yon little brook, as rolls gaily to th' sea; There's Ettle brids hoppin', an' buildin', an' single', An' one f yon bush sings a sweet song to me--

For id chirps like a lad w' a heart true an' steady, 'At's waited an' warked for this warm sunny day, When i'th' dear native spot he's a bonny hooam ready For a lass 'at's bin pininfi'th' teawn far away. Ay, sweet little brid ! tha sings gaily this mornin', Bud nod a tit gayer than Jenny an' rite, For we're just beawn to live i'th' owd cot aw wet born in, An' sing under th" branches. like thy mate an' thee! Higher Walton, Oct. 18,1887. GEORGE HULL.

not niake it a free library-because the 'loss of revenue from the subscription would leave them with a deficit, and thus make them worse off than they were at present. They had a good deal of talk and discussion, and he be- lieved it was Mr. Robert Davies who suggested that a penny per book should be charged, and it struck him (Mr. l‘lonks) as being a happy thought. They. stuck to that idea as one of the solutions of the difficulty, and after discussing it very fully they came to the conclusion that after all it was perhaps the best solution of the difficulty. One condition that they contended for was that all the subscribers, whether they paid ,a penny per volume, is. ed. a quarter, or ss. or a guinea a year should be treated in precisely the same way. They held out for that, and he must say that the representatives of the Museum Committee conceded it gracefully. The whole thing, therefore, was in that form, and he sup- posed that the Town Council would be recommended to adopt a suggestion that the subscriptiens re- main precisely as they are, but that t., books be lent at a penny per volume, on condi- tion that those who borrowed them complied with the usual safeguard at: free public libraries by bringing a guarantee form on iborrowing the book. IMr. Monks then mentioned that a book that could be obtained for the penny might be of one, two, or three voluinds. There was another condition that all residents outside the municipal boundary should pay double fees. One matter which he (Mr. Monks) fell in with most cordially, and Which was a fact new to him was that the Museum. Com- mittee could by law take in hand the establishment and working of science and art classes. He thought this was a very proper work for the Museum Committee, and if the arrangement that was suggested with regard to the library was carried out it would certainly-not lessen the income of the committee, but rather increase it, and he hoped it would enable the committee to take in hand at once the science lectures and perhaps extend it to a tech- nical school, but he did not know whether that would be

quite within the scope of their powera. If the Museum Committee had adopted the suggestion of the sub-com- mittee it would now rest with the Town Council to sanc- tion the proposal or riot, and if they did it would rest with the Museum Committee that would be elected on the 9th November to carry out the new arrangement in the best way they could. (Hear, hear.) Dr. GoimAix. asked how the proposed arrangement would affect people who resided outside the borough, but who were interested in the borough. The CHAIRMAN : Have you any property in the borough for which you are rated? , Dr. GORNALL : Yes. The CHAIRMAN said that in that case Dr. Gornall, he expected, would be in the same position as any other ratepayer. There were a large number of cleiks and others who were not directly ratepayers, and he knew that the Museum Committee did not wish to exclude them from the benefit of the arrangement. Dr. Gastrula asked if it were not very doubtful whether the Museum Committee were conferring any benefit on the people of Warrington by the new arrange- ment. The CHAIRMAN said that was a matter of opinion; some people would say they were and some would say they were not. In his opinion the new arrangement would be a great benefit. Dr. GORNALL : I don't see it. The Rev. S. WILKINSON thought their thanks were due to the chairman and Mr. Morris for going to meet the Museum Committee and for the \ trouble they had taken, and their thanks were also due to the Museum Commit- tee for the very courteous manner in which they had met the arguments which had been addressed/to them on be- half of the inhabitants of Warrington. He thought the whole thing now resolved itself into a matter of pounds, shillings, and pence: With regard to the proposal of the committee that subscribers of a pound shouldhave no ; more advantage than subscribers of ss. or id. per book, ; rather contrary to their experience of human nature. It seemed to him that if a man paid a pound he would ex- pect to get more for it than the man got who paid a smaller sum. Dr. Pr ornall asked—and there was a great deal in it—would this new arrangement really Confer any benefit upon the inhabitants of Warrington. Some people were very quick readers, and if they paid a penny for each book they read they might have very little advan- tage. The CHAIRMAN said the argument had been that the subscription of ss. a year or is. ed. a quarter was a bar to many people using the library, and, taking that state- ment as correct, an endeavour was being Made to make it so that any one who was really anxious to read should have as little to pay as possible. • The Rev. S. WILKINSON said that Mr. Walker and others went in for the freeing of the library as a matter of principle. The CHAIRMAN said the Museum Committee would agree with Mr. Walker, and would make the library free to-morrow if their income could be made to meet their expenditure. There was nb question of• principle involved. Mr. WALKER said that as far as he was concerned, he would not have bent his back to that work for the last eighteen months if he had thought it was going to end in what he would term little better than a fiasco. (Hear, hear.) For his part he had a strong sense of the injus- tice of a charge at all, and he should advise that they accept the small boon that was offered, but continue to demand that the library in Warrington should be made a Free Lending Library. (Applause.) The CHAIRMAN said he should look at that thing as a practical question. Did they thitik that the requirement of a penny per book would debar any youth or man from going, down to the library and taking a book? The word injustice was used, but there was nothing granted to anyone in Warrington that was not equally offered to working-men. He did not see that there was any injus- tice. Mr. WALKER said that if John Smith came from Widnes, where he had been in the habit of getting books free, to Warrington, where after paying his rates, he could not get a book without paying a subscription, would he not think he was subjected to an injustice? The CHAIRMAN said he could not see where the injus- tice was. If John Smith was debarred, because he was a working-man. from having books on the samdterms as anybody else, then there would be an injustice. There ' was no one in Warrington who could come to the library and take out a book without paying a subscription of 5s a year or Is fid a quarter, and John Smith could have books on the same terms. There was no injustice; it was a question of finance. Mr. WALKER asked if there was no injustice when there was a breach of the law ? The CHAIRMAN said he did not hesitate to say that the Library Committee in what they were doing occupied a perfectly legal position. Mr. WALKER said it was a pity the Library Committee did not state their ease. He knew that one member of the Library Committee, who is a lawyer, did not believe that the position in which the committee stood was sound in law. Mr. SUTCLIFFE asked in what position they would be if a ratepayer determined to take a test case before the courts. The CHAIRMAN said that if the Museum Com- mittee defended their own position the ratepayers would have to pay the cost of the defence. It would be an in- dividual ratepayer against the collective ratepayers. Mr. WALKER said that made them feel the wrong all the more. When asked, the Museum Committee would not show.the section of the Act whielf, defined their position, but practically said to those who were moving for a free library that they must fight if they, wanted one. v did not think that • -s ilia r•,-ition of

div.p: Carittits.

• If you desire the permanent happiness of your children, teach them obedience and self-restraint. Excess of ceremony shows want of breeding. That . civility is best which excludes all superfluous formality.. It is only when our path leads down into some dark gorge of trial where no sunbeams fall that we learn the worth of the lamps of heavenly promise. Their beams shone dimly as we walked in the sunshine of human joy and strong-earthly hope; but now, in the darkness, they 'flash out in brilliancy, and change night into day. While self-distrust is always draining and enervating the powers, self-respect is always using and strengthen- ing them. It neither whines nor boasts. With true simplicity of heart it recognises -whatever is good and -valuable, and gathers ever new courage to push onward to further endeavours in the hope of reaping yet richer harvests. That a man's house is his -castle is an old and very much battered tradition supposed to be common law.- But the due and full understanding of the precept is not common. It is not always from foes or disturbances without that the castle needs defence; the inner furnieh; ing and comfort also require to be diligently looked after. When this is done, for " castle "we substitute the better and pleasanter ward "home." And the home should be in the best and highest sense the "castle" for man, woman, and child. THE BUTTERFLY AND rem Pee.—On a splendid autumn day, when all the flower-beds were ablaze with purple, and orange, and crimson, and gold, a modest brown bee and a gorgeous butterfly found themselves together on the same cluster of scarlet geranium. "Dear me, how you do slave, neighbour!" said the butterfly. " Here have you been working away ever so long on this one flower, whilst I have rayed over a dozen beds in the same time. And then, hew people admire me, and stare at me, and run after me!" "Yes; and sometimes catch you," said the bee; "and kill you." The butterfly was a little taken aback; but he was a jaunty fellow, and soon recovered himself. "Well, I'm off," he said. "You can stay and plod here all day on one stupid flower if you choose. Give me constant change." All that is very fine," said the bee. " But those who gad about so much seldom do any good work. Besides, as you say, you only stop a moment on eaeh flower ; whereas I never leave it till I have sucked all the honey out of it. So I -work, and yet fly about all the same." "Yes, yes !" answered the butterfly. "But all Your toil only causes you to be killed for the sake of your honey. I die after an idle life, and you after a busy one. But we both die, so where is the difference ?" "'We must all die," said the bee; "but there is this great difference. You die, and no one regrets or remembers you. But when I die the work that I have done has not only maintained me during my life, but will benefit others after my death." —Little Folks, for October. KAFIRS AND SOAlL—Kafirs are always eagerly glad and thankful for a little fat or oil, and as our boys were no exception, I soon found out it was a grand bribe to offer as an encouragement to washing. You see, with no covering under the fierce sun, the skin, unless lubricated with grease, dries and blisters, and especially the feet, which get full of cracks, into which the dry dust pene- trates, adding to the irritation, and, unless they are washed and greased, become very sore. Indeed, there is a great prejudice against washing without afterwards using fat as an after-polish. Of course splashing a little cold water over the body does not remove years of dirt and grease; so I used, in order to promote cleanliness, to provide soap, and, if they used it, serve out portions of dripping or sour butter afterwards. They liked dripping best, as they said it did not leave any smell. Fancy a Kafir minding a smell! My house-boys generally had a wash all over every day; but the farm hands, except for dashing a little water over their legs or washing their feet—that is to say, scrubbing them on or with a piece of sandstone at sundown—never washed! The following Is the authorised way of cleaning the head :—lt being found impossible to extract them from the woolly tangle in which they have their habitation each one, on being found, is bundled up in a tiny ball Of clay, where it dies from lack of nourishment. In a few days it is dead, and the clay is broken off. When first I saw a head thus ornamented, in my ignorance I fancied it must be some sort of clay of a saponaceous nature, perhaps, known to the natives, and I thought how nice and clever of them to use it. But I was soon brought back to earth, and disillusioned on the subject. Excuse this revelation on matters not generally mentioned to ears polite; but it is only showing up the manners and customs of our black brethren, arid will perhaps prevent people falling into the same mistake as I did. DISCOVKRIES AT POMPEII.—Recent excavations at the ruins of Pompeii have brought to light a set of surgical instruments, many of which resemble instruments in use - at the present time. Four beautiful silver urns of fair size have been found, also four smaller vessels, eight open vases, four cups ornamented with leaves and figures of animals, and a very beautiful statue of Jupiter seated on a throne. Besides these silver objects, several gold ornaments, such as rings, earrings, Am., have been dis- covered. A Naples correspondent writes :—I have just had a private view of the silver objects lately found at Pompeii, which are now in the museum here, but not yet publicly exhibited, being kept in a case in one of the deposit rooms. 'They have evidently all belonged to the same table service. The most interesting object is a small figure in silver of Jupiter, which together with its tiny square pedestal, is not more than three inches high. The figure, seated on a high-backed throne, is most delicately chiselled, and, in spite of corrosion,the features are tolerably distinct. The head resembles that of the Olympian Jove. The left arm is missing, but from the position of the socket, it must have been raised on high, and probably held a sceptre, the end of which rested on: the ground. The mantle is folded over the left shoulder, and falls in graceful drapery across the knees. The right hand rests on the right knee, and holds the lightnings. Of the sandalled feet, the right rests on the pedestal, while the left is slightly raised as if it had had a footstool beneath it, now missing. The - whole was most likely an ornament of some central piece belonging to the service. There are four deep silver wine Cups on slender pedestals, perfectly plain, and generally as bright as if the housewife had yesterday taken them from her cupboard. Also several small plates or saucers, with finely chiselled rims, bearing a pattern of foliage, flowers, swans, and panthers in a running design. A small silver sieve would seem to indicate that wine was warmed with some herbs or other ingredients, and poured through it into the cups, 2.S it is of just the fitting size. There is also a little silver bottle with narrow neck and holes in the bottom, as if for sprinking spice. Some smaller and larger spoons, egg cups of different sizes and quite plain, and a flat, round bronze dish, which has been lined with silver, now almost all destroyed and separated in flakes from the bronze, are the remaining objects of this interesting service of silver plate. There are no initials or signs to denote either the goldsmith who executed or the owner who possessed it. The ob- jects have not yet been studied or explained by the savants of the Museum, nor can I tell you to what period they are supposed to belong.
sARAff BERNHARDT'S IMMENSE RECEIPTS AND _PATTI'S PERIL. . _

Sarah Bernhardt's re-ceip;,-for-Ker late tour in South -Arr.r;,-,,are the largestever taken by any dramatic ar- tiste. But the reckless Sarah scarcely ever has a franc to spaie ! Patti has alSo achieved great success, and a very large amount of money, in Mexico and South America, but came very near being the victim of a dynamiter, who attempted to throw an explosive bomb at her while ,-she was singing at the Grand Opera House in San Fran- cisco California. She was called again and again in front of the curtain when, as she was finally retiring, a ' man in the gallery suddenly rose, picked up a bomb from under the seat, and raising it in the air, was about to throw it, when' it exploded in his hand, shattering his • arm and face, and intlicting other injuries. Had the man not placed himself under the protection of a policeman, who met him as he was rushing down stairs, he would have hem torn in pieces by the infuriated people. Patti ..displayed great coolnesg. and presence of mind, and succeeded in restoring quiet by singing "Home, Sweet Home." Poor Patti! It is a wonder she was not killed by the ' nervous shock, or that she did not faint, or that her hair did not turn grey through fright. Think of Patti with grey hair! A beautiful head of hair is the crowning glory af woman, and its loss is her greatest misfortune—a mis- fortune which may be prevented by the use A that fa- mous hair restorer and dressing, known as Mrs. S. A. Allen's World's Hair Restorer, which will prevent bald- mess, and restore grey hair to its natural color, strength, and gyms. It can be had at any chemist's or perfumer's Asap in the civilized world.

tions of life were very much against him, and that he thought he had better go somewhere else to find if those conditions were a little easier. It was possible to make England a happy land. There were a lot of burning questions that wanted bringing to the front, and those who sudied politics ever so little would know what ques- tion he was referring to. These questions should be brought to the front as speedily as possible and em- ployers and workmen should alike put their shoulders to the wheel. He was strongly of opinion that if the I question affecting the land were dealt with it would help them out of their diffculties. (Hear, hear.) That ques- tion if dealt with would give England a long commer- ci 1 career, Hut if it were not dealt with he was afraid the crisis through which they were passing would be made such good use of by other countries that they should have a long struggle to maintain their position. (Hear, hear.) In conclusion he again thanked the I subscribers for their kind expressions and for their sub- stantial help. (Loud applause).
"Auld lang sine" was next sung by the company, after which the interesting proceedings terminated.

Mr. Whitham has also been presented with a gold pen and pencil case by the members of the Prince of Wales Lodge of Oddfellows, of which he is a member, and in which he has gone through the offices of the lodge and district to the satisfaction of the lodge and with credit to himself. The golden case, which had been supplied by Mr. Carter, jeweller, Bridge-street, was engraved with words setting forth that it had been presented as a mark of esteem and regard to P.P:G.M. Henry Whitham by the members of the Prince of Wales Lodge. Mr. Whitham and family left the Central Station, War- rington, for Liverpool by a tfain leaving a little .before nine o'clock on Thursday morning. They were accom- panied by Mr. S. Hope and Mr. Page, who, like Mr. Whitham, are skilled wiredrawers, and have also received an engagement with a large firm of manufactmtrs in San Francisco. At the station a tato number of the friends of the emigrants had %O bled to bid them farewell, and they left the station Amidst a chorus of well wishes. They were accompanied to Liverpool by a number of rela- tives and more intimate friends, and these did not part with them till late in the afternoon, when the vessel which was to convey them to New York was about to leave the river. The steamer by which they sail is the "Egypt," of the National Line. From New York, which port they are expected to reach in about nine days, they will travel overland to their destination, San Francisco.

div.head: AN IRISH TENANT FARMER ON COERCION. •
div.p: AN IRISH TENANT FARMER ON COERCION. •

I The following is a characteristic- extract from a ; letter written by a tenant farmer, in county Tipper- ary, Ireland, under date the 12th inst., to a well- known resident in Newton-le-Willows. After com- menting upon personal matters, the letter proceeds: —I suppose the English press do not give a very full re- port of events in Ireland. Such a fault could be easily , remedied by reading Irish papers, the "Freeman's Jour- nal," or "The Weekly Freeman," in particular. As a 1 rule they give the two sides of the picture, and it is very easy to judge which is the correct side. Another advan- tage to be gained from reading them is a full report is always given in their columns. "United Ireland,' "The Nation," and "Weekly News" are thoroughly Irish and very truthful, but the " Express" and the "Irish I Times" are red hot Conservative prints. Their chief I character is they are splendid liars and bitter enemies of the Irish people. I regret lam not able to give you an extended view of the current events in this country, however, I will do my best. In the first place the Coer- cion act has done a terrible lot of mischief, and there was not the slightest reason for the passing of it. It simply caused crime as it brings into collision the armed ; forces of the Crown with the people. The chief aim of its promoters is to bolster up the landlords and to help them to evict their unfortunate tenants. The struggle ' between the tenantry and landlordism is very bitter and fierce. The landlords are using every cruelty that the I devil can suggest or human ingenuity can carry oilt to I reduce to slavery the people of Irelana ; they are backed up by the Government in everything, no matter how cruel or heartless. The people, however, are well able ' for them, and with the help of God the people will win— they have justice and right on their side ; they are backed ' up by the democracy of England and by the people of the civilised world. The path to victory is pointed out to them by their own chosen leader and by the greatest of living Englishmen. The fatal affray at Mitchelstown is another nail driven into the• coffin of the Government and of landlordism. It was a cowardly proceeding for I armed men to fire from behind iron shut- ters upon an unarmed crowd —it was cold blooded murder. The blood of the victims will rise up before God and bring down His just wrath upon their murderers. The police are convicted before the world on their own evidence. Well, let them do their best, their days are numbered; their reign is over. You 1 may think this to be a picture drawn from my imagina- tion, and the fact of my being an Irish tenant may lead i you to that opinion. .But lam telling Gospel truth. Not I until the great Judgment Day, when we will all appear before our Maker, will the wrongs inflicted on the Irish r people by the landlords be fully known. The people of 1 Ireland will outlive the landlords: they will soon own the land they till ; they have cast off 1 the shackles of serfs, and will assert their rights; and when bloody Balfour and Co. will have sunk into 1 oblivion, the Irish people will live in peace and joy in I their own land in the light of freedom and prosperity.
TOOTH WARTC H. BY THE ORIGINAL SAMMY BUTTERCI7P.

It's comin' cowd weather neaw, an' thoose uts getten ony grinders uts a bit hollow ul sooin begin o' scrooin their meawths up to keep th' cowd woinds eawt. Ther wur a chap co'd Jack-o'-Matty's. a fustin cutter„ut wur awfully tormented wi' one, an' it cost him a lot o' trubble to get shut on't. Aw co'd at Jack's heawse one fleet to smook mi bacco wi' him, an' th' owd fella ud getten his yead lapt up as iv he'd bin feightin wi somebudy an' getten knockt o'er th' rooape. He could see +GA aw wur wonderin. what wur up wi' him, so he oppend his een bike two brunt hoyles th' blanket, shaked his yead, an' then peighnted to his meawth. _ _ _

"He's getten th' toothwartch," his woife sed," an he's as cranim'd as an owd foo." " Theau should get it pood eawt," aw sed, an after a deol o' perswadin aw geet him to goo wi' mi to a druggist. When we geet to th' shop, Jack gen th' dur a gradely good punse, he wur i etch pain. A chap oppend th' dur an' took us in a little reawm wheer ther wur two wimmin an' a mon waitin' to be operated on.

Th' druggist ud lust getten th' pliers i' th' Chap's meawth to draw him a tooth, an when he gen it a gradely good twitch th' pliers slipt off. Th' fella jumpt up an fotcht th' druggist a kick ut sent him wi' his back agean a greyt lookin'-glass, an' then he seet off reawnd:th' reawm after us; but, as ther happend to be a table i' th' middle, we run reawnd it an' monaged to dodge him. Th' wimmm begun o' skroikin bike mad. It Wur as bad as bein' i' Bedlam. Th' druggist lee uppoth floor, th' wimmin wur sheawtin "Murder!" an' Jack wur swearin' bike a trooper. At last me an' Jack monaged to °poen th' dur an run eawt, an' Jack !wet off whoam at full speed, an' me after him, but he wur awhoam lung afoar me, an' he'd gone to bed. Aw co'd at Jack's th' nest after, but he wur no better, an owd Tommy Crumpit wur sittin theer campin him. Neaw owd Tommy wur a vegetarian, an didno beleov foak havin their teeth pood eawt •he sed as heaw it Injured their health an spoilt their bewty. "Fr ever it spoils his bewty," Jack's woife sed, " ther'll be a bonny neyse i'th hqyle; because it took sich a lung while to finish him off." But owd Tommy perawaded him to goo to a quack doctor, an ax for a bottle o' capsicum, an Jack went an geet , one. When Jack geet back, Tommy told him to put a drop e capsicum on his finger, oppen his meawth asoide o'th foyar, an rub th' capsicum dgean his wartehin tooth. Jack did as he wur towd, an as luck ud have it, his woife had a rowsin foyer, so Jack planted his shins toart th' bars, an temm'd some capsicum on his finger, then he oppend his meawth welly as woide as a barn dur; but estid o'th capsicum gooin toart th' tooth, it went deavvn his throoat, an then ther wur a gradely'fiareup, for it brunt bike vitril. Jack jumpt up an fotcht th' fender a punse, then he seet off upstayrs sheawtin, " Aw'm brunin !" He fotcht th' reawm dur deawn wi his foot, stuck his fist throo t' reawm window, then went deawnstayrs agean full bat, but aw gen him a sling tin full o' wayter just fis he geet to th' bottom, an deawn he went uppoth floor. We monaged to bring him reawnd after a deol o' trubble, an geet him to bed. Aw co'd agean th' neet after, an he wernt a bit better. "By gum 1" aw sed, " Theau's had some trubble wi that fang; let's goo an get a doctor to't." Aw took him to th' doctor, but aw stopt eawt- snide while he geet operated on. It wernt mony minits afoar aw yerd a bit e frabbin gooin on, an then ther wur a skroike, just for o t' weld bike that buzzer at th' Vulcan Feawndry. Ther wur another slip! Then aw pept throo t' keyhoyle an seed Tack runnin after th' doctor wi his knife oppen, sweearin till he wur black i'th face. Aw bowted in an pacified Jack a bit. Th' doctor towd him as heaw it wur nobbut a bit uv a slip, an Jack axt him what a gradely full slip wur bike iv that wur nobbut a bit o' one. Ileawever, th' doctor clapt his pliers on agean, gen another twitch an bonded th' tooth, and when aw seed it aw med sure as bum th' back part ov his yead ud come eawt. It wur a whopper, an no mistake. •It wur Oh' same shape and welly hauve as big as a aleheawse stoo.

CHAPTER V.
A WEDDING PRESENT.

More than two years had passed since the trial of Martin Derrick, when the quiet, even tenor of life at Row-Tor Farm was suddenly interrupted by a loud, cheerful, but discordant note. Susan, the youngest sister,. had descended upon her brother's home, seem- ing as much out of place there as a brass band playing dance music would be on a tca of Dartmoor. Hervarious attractions had led to the first overtures of friendship being made to Martin,since he had stood in the dock at Exeter, James Stambridge, mine captain—who had made money- in the clays now, perhaps, gone for ever, when money was to be made in Devonshire mines—a sober, middle-aged man, a highly respected member of the congregation who Worshipped at the little white-washed Wesleyan chapel at St. Stephen's—had fallen in love with Susan, and had offered to marry her. And for Susan's sake he Was willing to be civil to her sister Anne, whom secretly he sneered at as a strong-minded old maid; for Susan's sake be would even try to be friends with her unsociable and ungodly brother, who spoke to nobody at market except the cattle- dealers who bought his beasts, who shunned village. concerts and tea-meetings, and never attended a "place of worship" on Sundays. For a few weeks the old farmhouse on the border of the moor was transformed. Susan's gay laughter rang through the silent rooms, her light footsteps pattered up and down the staircase, the homely parlour was littered with her finery. All day long she sewed, and tried on hats and bonnets and gowns and looked' at herself in the glass, and gowns, with Miss Taylor, the village dressmaker, whom she had summoned to help her prepare • her trousseau. In the evenings Captain Stam- bridge would—as he expressed it—' drop in and have a cup of tea," and sit smiling, at his proielaed bride and utter fatuous compliments, and then Anne Would retreat to the kitchen to wash the china tea-things, and Martin would flee to his cheerless smoking-room to read,leaving the engaged couple in ' undisturbed possession of the parlour. One Wednesday evening in that month of Novem- ber, Martin returned home from Tavistock, and en- . tered the parlour, where every chair and table in the room was strewed with gowns in more Or less ad- vanced stages of manufacture, while Susan stood before the fire, 'trying on a hat and ogling herself in the old-fashioned glass over the mantel-shelf. He went up to her and took a roll of hank notes out of a large leather purse— , " Here, Susan," said he abruptly, "I sold those bullocks to-day, so here's the price •of them for a wedding present. Buy what you like with it," and he went out of the room again, before she had hardly • recovered from her surprise enough to thank him. For, as she said to her lover afterwards—" Who would have thought of grampy old Martin coming out so handsome? Well, I am glad that money hasn't gone in buying books, any way." That evening Martin, having no better refuge, for the fire in his little den refused to burn, came into the kitchen and seated himself in a hard, straight- backed wooden chair by the wide hearth. With his elbows on his knees, his hands supporting his head, his eyes fixed on the tire, he appeared plunged into profound despondency. Anne glanced at him as she put away the tea things. Her sympathy with her .brother, her. natural insight told her much that was in his thoughts. Part of his frequent depression of spirits arose from the circumstances lie had chosen for himself. The solitary life he loved so well, the life of wandering on the moors, of study and of silent thought,sometimes weighed him down with a sense of the awfulness of nature and of human destiny—with all those mysteries of life and death, of sin, sorrow, and loss, which the dwellers amidst the constant society of their kind find it so easy to forget. Presently, when the servant girl had left the room he said to Anne, " I. shall be glad when this busi- ness of Susan's is over. and done with. Seems to me all this wedding finery and feasting is out of keeping with this house." "I can't bear to see you giving up your armchair by the parlour fire; as you do night after night, Martin."

"Oh, as for that, I am more comfortable where I am. „Stambridge is a man I can hardly bear to be in the same room with. Bat if Susan likes him, that's the main point; I suppose she does, Anne. I don't understand girls," "She likes him as much as it's in her nature to like anybody, and men generally don't care to be loved in a very strong sort of way, it seems to me. Plenty of flattery and a luke-warm liking is whatthey look for from the girls they are going to marry." , "I have sometimes thought," replied Martin, looking at his sister with rather a sad smile, "I have sometimes thought that you might have mar- ried, if it had not been for me." , "Don't talk nonsense, Martin"; and then having shut the door of her china cupboard, she seated herself by the fire with her knitting. "Just think of all the men You know, and say if there is onel would marry, or that would marry me? You may be sure that when a woman is happy and contented in her own company, and wants above all things peace, and freedom from worry and interfer- ence, then that womari was born to be an old maid. No, no, my dear Martin, I have got the kind of life I like best, so don't you trouble yourself about me."

Martin looked at Anne, with her fair face, her clear truthful eyes, and thought of her calm temper, her faithfulness to duty, her never-fail- ing sympathy, all that made her like an atmos- phere of restfulness in his home. "Anne, you are like Wisdom," he had once said to her. "All her ways are pleasantness, and all her paths are peace." "Well, a. little patience," he replied to-night, "and all this vanity and vexation of love and marriage will be done with for ever, and you and I, Anne, old maid and old bachelor, will have the house to ourselves again. Thank heaven, by this day fortnight we shall be left in peace." On the following day, Captain Stambridge drove his betrothed in his dog-cart to Tavistock, where Susan wished to expend part of Martin's presentin buying ornamental articles for her future home. The lovers had spent several hours in each other's company, and nothing had happened to ruffle their mutual satisfaction; nor had they even quarrelled over choosing a best china tea-service. Differences of taste often lead to as bitter disagree- ments as theological controversy; and as the Arian heresy was to Athanasius, so are aniline dyes to a true aasthete. But Susan and Stambridge were equally destitute of real refinement and cultivation; although the late lady's-maid had a smattering of London fashion, which enabled her a little to overawe her provincial lover when it was a matter of deciding between a cheap and sticky-looking black and gold cabinet, and a clumsy walnut wood, marble-topped chiffonier of an earlier date. The lovers were driving homewards, when about two miles from Row-Tor Farm the horse lost a shoe. They had not long passed a blacksmith's forge, and Stambridge, grumbling a little at the delay, said they must turn back. "Help me down, then," said Susan, "I am cold and tired." Tired of her lover's company, she might have added. "I'll walk on to Mrs. Hanham's, only a quarter of a mile, and stop there until you come. She'll give me a cup of tea, you may be sure— yeti know Mrs. Hanhani and her kettle ? " and Susan laughed meaningly. "What is the joke 2" asked Stambridge. - "Oh, don't you know? it's a regular gaying in these parts—so Miss Taylor told me—Mrs. Hanham'a kettle. She'sla regular stingy old screw, and when a friend drops in of an afternoon, and the kettle is on the fire, she asks them to have a cup of tea, just for politeness sake—but, says she, if you're in a hurry It's no good to pay heea to that kettle, he will sing for an hour or two on a stretch before he'll boil; and so you see they go away again without the cup of tea after all."

Some half-hour or more afterwards Stambridge drove up to the little whitewashed, slate-roofed cottage, wherein dwelt Mrs. Hanham and her music- loving kettle, and where he expected to find Susan. To his surprise, the thrifty mistress of the house in- formed him that she had not seen Susan that day. In perplexity Stambridge drove slowly onward. I can't have missed her anyhow," he thought. "I have come straight along the road, and she would not have turned off into either of the lanes I have passed, as they would 'lead her out of her way." He drove some distance at . a walking pace!! looking to right and left of him; the substantial form of Susan seemed to have melted into air. Presently, his bewilderment gave place to a sense of injured dignity. ,

"She is playing hide-and-seek or some such game with me. It may be all very well this side of the wedding-day, but I shan't put up with being made _ a fool of, and kept dawdling about when I wen i t- - my tea, when she s once my wife." ig used in all public oeremonies as an acceptable offering 4° their deity—the Sun God. The leaves of this marvellous Shrub, when ready for nitarket, are transported on mules up the steep mountain sides, across the icy and desolate plateaux, 414 through the passes of the Bolivian Andes mountains, many (4 them 13,000 and 14,000 feet above the level of the sea, and !hen downwards on the other side of the mountains into Peru tor shipment from the port of Callao (Lima.) LORD HARTINGTON AT NOTTINGHAM.

Lord Hartington and other ibading Liberal Unionists who were to take part in the meeting at Nottingham on Monday, arrived in that town on Saturday. Lord Hartington proceeded at once to Bestvaood Lodge, the seat of the Duke of St Albans, whose guest he has been during his stay in the neighbourhood. In the evening the Duke-and 'Duchess entertained a large part at dinner, amongst those present, in addition to Lord Hartington, being Lord and Lady Helper, Mr. Finley, Q.C., M.P., Professor Leckey, Mr. Buszard, Q.C., Mr. Albert Grey, Mr. F. J. S. Foljambe, Mr. Webb, of Newstead Abbey, and M. W. W. Bag,nall. After Dinner there was a reception, for which invitations had been issued to a large number of local Liberal Unionists. The guests were received by the Duchess of St. Albans. and introduced to Lord Har- tington. When the company had assembled in the drawing-room, the Hake of St Albans addressed a few words of welcome to Lord Hartington, and those who had come to meet him. Lord HARTINGTON, 'who was very cordially received, In reply expressed his indebtedness to the Duke and Duchess of St. Albans for having given him the oppor- tunity of meeting such a large number of fellow Liberals who were in accord with him on the Irish question. He refer-edto the extreme effort it must have required on their part, as on his own, to separate themselves from old and valued political friends, and to the pain which was consequent upon that separation. He was, how- ever, more than gratified to find so many genuine and earnest Liberals prepared in that which they believed to be a time of danger to the best interests of their country to manfully put patriotism before party. If it were true, as had been said, that they represented the classes and not the masses, though he by no means admitted that to be the case, they had at any rate great influence upon those with whom they were associated, and he hoped that that influence would be earnestly used, and that they might effectually triumph in the important struggle in which they were employed. (Cheers.) On Monday evening, Lord Haetington addressed a Crowded meeting, held under the auspices of the Liberal Thaioniet Association, in the Mechanics' Hall. The as- sembly numbered about 3,500, and was very enthusiastic. The chair was taken by the Duke of St. Albans who was supported by the Marquis of Hartington' Laid Belper, Mr. Finlay, M.P., Mr. T. W. Russell, M.P., Sir john Lub- bock, na.r., Professor Lecky, and Mr. Albert Grey. Lord Hartington said li he rexpected at the Federation meeting last ek to have heard something definite from Mr. Gladstone as to his present Frish pohcy ; but they had learnt nothing except that Mr. Gladstonewould not walk into a trap with his eyes open. As to the pro- gramme sketched at the Federation meeting, it was not one of the immediate future, and it was equally clear that the promises as to disestablishment were only made to gather increased support for-Home Rule. It was a simple, undisguised, and naked bribe. It was impossible that questions which had been raised at the Federation could be settled whilst the Irish difficulty lasted, and he utterly repudiated the picture Mr. Gladstone had pain-

FOREIGN NEWS.
FRANCR-THE PATRIOTIC LEAGUE.- ARREST OF FOREIGNERS.

PARIS, MONDAY NIGYIT.-M, Deroulede has resumed his old position at the head of the Patriotic League, which now has 30,000 members. He is enthusiastic about Russia and her Czar, and has, he says, been autho- rised to declare that Alexander and his advisers have no animus against any French Republican. They perfectly understand that it is nothing to them what statesman is brought into power. What chiefly interests them is the French Army and after it the Navy. M. Deroulede, as a patriot, deplores the action taken by General Perron against General Boulanger, and thinks he is one of those men around whom a nation gathers as around a standard. Judgment has been delivered by the. Correctional Tri- bunal at Nantua in the case of the two foreigners O'Dann and Wollitz, who were arrested at Bellegarde for having returned to France in spite of the sentence of expulsion passed upon them last March. O'Dann was sentenced to three months' and Wollitz to one month's imprison- ment.

div.head: CAFFAREL SCANDAL.
div.p: THE CAFFAREL SCANDAL.

PARTS, TUESDAY.—!n the Chamber of Deputies to-day, M. Cqnes moved the nomination of a Court of Inquiry into the Caffarel case and the charges against 11d. Wilson. M. Rouvier opposed the demand, but the Chamber never- theless agreed to urgency. THE BULGARIAN QUESTION.—WHOLE- SALE ARRESTS.

SIICHAREST, SATURDAY.—The Bulgarian Emigrants, an association of ruffians in the employ of Russia, are leaving Roumania in considerable numbers for Semis.. It is, therefore, surmised that a coup of some kind is in- tended in that country. Si. PRTEII.4III7RO, SATURDAY.—The semi-official JOU?' Aoit de St. Petersburg, in an article to-day on the Bulgarian question, says:—" The resolut ions which may be adopted by the new Bulgarian Assembly will only be another in- termediary stage of the Bulgarian question. They will constitute no settlement The sham national represen- tation, which was obtained by trickery and violence, will be incapable of creating anything stable. The Bulgarian question, therefore, has not advanced one step, and the blood which has been shed cannot cement a union be- tween the nation and the Government." .

- VIENNA, MONDAY Mown—lntelligence has just been received here of wholesale arrests of conspirators at Sistova, Mikopolis, and Tirnova. It is stated that 70 arrests in all have been effected. Detats regarding the cause of this action have not yet been received. TkLE STANLEY EXPEDITION.—MORE MEN SENT FOR

According to private advices which have been received from Stanley Pool, and dated last month, it appears that Mr. H. M. Stanley has already penetrated the great African Continent further than he has ever been before, or indeed further than any white man has ever reached. The previous despatch had mentioned the spot up the Aruwimi River which the expedition had reached, and the present letter says that a further march of 150 miles up the river had been made. Mr. Stanley had sent back the little steamer Florida to Stanley Pool for more stores and also more men. This would indicate that the in- domitable explorer expected some opposition, though the despatch mentions that the natives in the districts traversed appeared to be very friendly. In order to be prepared against any surprise, Mr. Stanley had pitched two entrenched camps at his new halting-place, but the natives showed no disposition to molest him. On the contrary, they seemed to welcome the party into their country. The health of Mr. Stanley and the whole of the expedition was imported to be very good, and the men seemed to be in excellent spirits. It was believed that Stanley would not make any mere forward move- ment until the return of the Florida with the stores and men sent for.

div.head: SUEZ CANAL AND THE NEW' HEBRIDES.
div.p: THE SUEZ CANAL AND THE NEW' HEBRIDES.

PARIS, SUNDAY NIGHT.—The protocol of the Suez Canal Convention has at length been put into shape, and the conditions have been virtually arranged. I give these in the rose-coloured form adopted here, coupled as it is with the announcement of a French diplomatic success. It is clearly understood that the Suez Canal is neutralised out and out, and that this extends to a strip of territory on each blink. Under no circumstances, therefore, could the Canal be blockaded, even in case of war, and with Turkey as belligerent. The ports of access, the establish- ments of the Suez Canal Company, and the Fresh Water Canal to Cairo are included in the neutralisation. An International Commission composed of the Cpnsuls- General of the Powers interested will determine the further scope of the treaty as it may affect territory fortifications or gatherings of troops. This Commis- sion will have power to call upon the Egyptian, and In case (4 need upon European, troops to enforce its de- cision. The last clause of the arrangement, if it does not solve, at least turns the difficulty which existed be- tween French and English diplomacy on the subject of Egypt, and as France has declared herself satisfied there is no more to be said for the present The New Hebrides arrangement is also to be signed to-morrow. France consents to the withdrawal of her troops, a common agreement having been made which sufficiently guaran- tees the safety of French or British subjects in case of need. The miniature protectorate of France over Itaiatea and the oiher islands of the Windward group close to Tahiti which was renewed provisionally by England every six months, is now definitively acknowledged altogether. M. Flourens must be congratulated on the dignified and painstaking way in,which he.has destroyed a misunderstanding which gave a handle to exaggera- tion, and which was doubly harassing at a moment when more than one Power in Europe is inclined to see an enemy behind every hedge. PARIS, MONDAY Mawr.— The, effect on the French people with the arrangement which brings about so happy a settlement of the Suez Canal and New Hebrides questions has been immediate. The present feeling towards England is one of such sincere friendliness and goodwill as the most sanguine could not have antici- pated last week.

Pintsinunata, Mom:—.-The Rev. Charles A. Perry, a young English divine preached in Plymouth Church, Brooklyn, yesterday, and made a favourable impression. It is believed that be will succeed Mr. Henry Ward Beecher. •

PRILADIMPRIA, MONDAY. —A battery of six steam boilers in the Lawrence Ironworks at Ironton, Ohio, exploded today, killing four men and injuring 20 others. TERRIBLE LOSS OF LIFE AT SEA:: 285 PERSONS DROWNED. 44V•ti4 _ .

A " Times " second edition contains a San Francisco despatch, via Philadelphia, dated October 26, which says the steamship Gaelic arrived this morning from Hong Kong and Yokohama, bringing advices that on Septem- ber 15 the Chinese transport Waylee was lost in the Pes- cadores, and 280 Chinese and five Europeans were drowned. The British barque Oxforciwas stranded on the Balan coast on September 19; but no lives were lost. It is also reported that the steamer Anton encountered a typhoon, during which the second officer and 24 Chinese were washed overboard and'drowned. A typhoon is re- ported from various places in the China Sea, and nearly all the vessels arriving fro in Hong Kong report having suffered.

div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 29, 1887.

As to the administration of law and order in Ire- land, whilst such language was used by an ex-Prime Minister the arm of the Government was weakened; but in the end they must win in their endeavours against an unwritten code of the National League. The plan of campaign he stigmatised as unmitigated robbery, and said it was carried out with violence against the police and with brutal malignity. No doubt the Government had received checks in attempting to restore order, but they had a right to expect some support from Liberals, whereas Mr. Gladstone seemed to condemn the police be- fore they had been heard, and almost to pass sentence upon them himself. He did not say there might not be cases where violent agitation and even rebellion was necessary in the interests of the people, but in the case of Ireland there was no cause or reason for violence in the determination that she should be ruled by England. The loyal population, however, must not be deserted or betrayed.

div.head: CURRENT POLITICS.
div.p: CURRENT POLITICS.

Mrs. Cowen, President of the Nottingham Women's Liberal Association, has Deceived the following letter from Mr. Gladstone, to whom she had forwarded a copy of the resolution passed at a meeting of the Women's Liberal Federation held at Nottingham last week "Dear Mrs. Cowen,—l have received with much pleasure the resolution you so kindly transmit, and I trust we may safely exchange congratulations on the brightened prospects of the cause so intimately allied with the well- beina of the BritiskEmnira."

I -.111-1...../J-1; iii-O-RLY AT HALIFAX.—Mr. John Morley, speaking at Halifax on Tuesday evening, said Lord Hart- ington's speech at Nottingham was not the first in which he had pooh-poohed the Liberal Federation. He did the same thing when the franchise was sought for the agri- cultural labourers, but he was then swept off his feet, as he would be again, for Mr. Gladstone's influence was stronger than ever. The question for the constituencies was not the question of poor, trumpery party recrimina- tions. Lord Hartington had said that things were done in Ireland in 1885 analogous to those which the Gladsto- nian Liberals now condemned. The administration of 1885 had nothing to do with the question. What con- cerned us now was the restoration of health to the body politic. He saw a hopeful sign in the interchange of speeches in the two countries by English and Irish mem- I bers of Parliament. I Mn. CHAMBERLAIN AT ISLINGTON.—Mr. .1. Chamberlain on Tuesday night addressed a meeting at West Isling- ton of the friends and supporters of Mr. R. Chamber- lain, M.P. The right. hon gentleman said attempts had been made by the Irish in America to discredit what he might do on the fisheries question, but he believed that they would fail, as they always had done, to create fra- tricidal strife between a kindred people. Me denied that he intended any insult to the Canadians in his speech at Coleraine, when he said that if preferential duties were allowed on American goods, to the exclusion of goods from England, the slender tie between Canada and Eng- land might be severed. He accused Mr. Gladstone .of using language inciting to crime in Ireland, which Mr. Gladstone had himself denounced in the case of Mr. Par- nell • and he was certain that the English and Scottish people would never sanction a second Parliament in Dublin, and deprive the Ulster Loyalists of their birth tight of freedom. One outcome of the Gladstone-Par- nalite alliance was the disgraceful demonstrations in London, which he believed would operate against the interest of real working-men during the coming winter. I MR. GLADSTONE AT RIPON.—GII Tuesday morning Mr. Gladstone left Sudbury Hall, where he has been the guest of Lord Vernon, to visit the Marquis of Ripon at Studley Royal. Miring the early part of the journey the right hon. gentleman resisted the persistent efforts to obtain speeches from him ; but atLeeds hewas persuaded to reply to two addresses. Upon reaching Ripon Mr. Gladstone received addresses at the Town Hall from various Liberal Associations. Speaking about Ireland, the right hon. gentleman said the first principle of Libe- ralism was that no society could be even in a tolerable condition unless the laws were honoured and loved by the people. The laws with which the Government had principally concerned itself were not honoured nor loved by the people, and they were administered in a spirit more like that in i which n his early days the laws of the West Indian colonies were administered by rthe planters. The Executive Government and their agents were the men who had been setting the example of breaking the law. They were associated in what he did not scruple I to say he looked upon as a just and sacred cause which was rapidly vindicating itself as being not only the watchword of a party, but the necessary condition to the peace and happiness and consolidation of the Empire. LIBERAL DEMONSTRATION AT EDINBURGH. A great Liberal demonstration was held on Tuesday in Edin- burgh, at which the principal speakers were the Earl of Rosebery and Earl Spencer. The Corn Exchange, in which the meeting was held, was seated for 4,500 per- sons, but fully 5,000 people were present. Lord Rose- bery said that when so many others connected with these historic times had seen it to be their duty to stand by, and hold aloof from them, in their present contest for liberty and good government, they could not help coun- ting it a pride that they had with them still the head of the historic house of Spencer, willing, now and always, to lend his aid to the cause of the people.— Lord Spencer, who was accorded an enthusiastic recep- tion, gaid the Liberal party believed they had a remedy for the present state of thmgs, a policy which would , strengthen the Union which would prevent separation, I a policy which would put down in Ireland anarchy and illegality by the hand of an Irish Government, supported by the goodwill and the voices of the Irish nation. He ; devoutly hoped that they and their great leader would live to see the attainment of their noble work, the conciliation of the Irish people. On the motion of Mr. McEwan, M.P., seconded by Sir Wilfred Lawson a vote of thanks was accorded Lord Spencer for his address and services in the Liberal cause. LORD RANDOLPH CHURCHILL ON IRELAND AND FAIR TRADE.

In response to an invitation from the South-East Dur- ham Conservative Association, Lord Randolph Churchill addressed a great meeting in the Exchange Hall. Stock- ton, on /Monday. Mr. Thos. Wrightson presided, and was supported by Mr. Milvain, M.P., Mr. R. S. Donkin, DA.P., and many local Conservatives. An enthusiastic reception was given to Lord and Lady Randolph Churchill as they were conducted to the platform. After a few remarks from the Chairml, Lord R. Cnunenn.t., at the ou et, referred to the colli- sion between the people and the police at Woodford, which he said he was not surptised at when he reflected uponthe advice Mr. Gladstone had given to the Irish people. Mr. Wilfrid Blunt, who had been arrested, was is personal friend of his, and he had been made a mere tool of by artful and designing persons. He was a man of im- mense knowledge of Eastern affairs and customs, but he knew as much about Ireland as he did about the man in the moon. He hoped the Government would not be hard upon Mr. Wilfrid Blunt, for he was certain he did, not know that a rough-and-tumble conflict with the police was likely to occur, or he would not have taken his wife with him. The fact was that the people had seen the Government made such a "cockshy" of, that they had no idea of what an Executive was capable of if it chose to act sternly and promptly. There might be more of these struggles, but law-abiding people need not have the slightest fear as to how it would all end. He felt convinced that the National League and all the forces' of disorder in Ireland tvould be very nearly completely got under by the time Par- liament met next year. He pointed to America, where perfect freedom was supposed to prevail. There public order was looked upon as the highest of all objects, and if any American statesman had made such a speech in regard to the police as Mr. Glad- stone made to the Kidderminster deputation he would probably have been driven out of ' American public life. Referring to the condition of British trade and Mr. Henry Chaplin's comments upon his remarks last week on the subjectof Protection, Lord Randolph asked, What was Fair Trade? He said he had never been able to get a definition of it. If there were a strong national demand for a recurrence to a system of Protection which should involve a duty on food that would have the effect of making food higher in price to the people, he saw nothing to prevent the Tory party yielding to such a national demand. At any rate, if he saw such a national demand he should not think it his duty to offer a stub- born, prejudiced resistance to it; but, he asked, where was the national demand, where were the great mass meetings held in favour of a duty on corn? He had never seen one, and before he moved a step in that direction he must see an overwhelming national demand for such a policy. He was no fanatical disciple of the Cobden school, but the music of the Fair-traders was so discord- ant and screeching that he could not be charmed by it. No doubt at present British trade was hampered by the fortifications raised against it in foreign countries, but in spite of these fortifications an enormous amount of British manufactures got into those foreign countries, this being permitted because of the enormous advan- tages which foreigners experienced in having a free market in England. If we were to clap on high protec- tive duties and destroy this market to them, foreign countries would retaliate by keeping out that margin of British exports which now flowed over their protective barriers, and he did not know that we would be better off. Then, if we adopted protection, we should have in justice to allow India to do so too. What would Lanca- shire say if her cottons were kept out of India It would be very difficult also to refuse to Ireland a protective duty for Irish industries. If all this was to be allowed what would become of our commercial unity? These were questions which the fair traders ought to answer, and they ought not to get angry with people of their own party who differed with them, but not unfriendly. To the Tory party had been confided interests of a momen- tous character. The monarchy, the hereditary Second Chamber, the rights of property, order, and law, had all been confided to the guardianship of the Tory party, and no man in position and responsibility would risk the whole of those interests on what might be the turn of a card or the cast of a die.

div.head: GENERAL NEWS.
div.p: GENERAL NEWS.

A telegram from Toronto announces the death of the lion. Lewis Wallbridge, Chief Justice of Manitoba. The workmen employed at the Landore Iron and Steel works, numbering upwards of 2,090 hands, returned to work on Friday on the masters' terms.
The London Hospital Sunday Fund this year has amounted in all to £40,466, being the largest sum col- lected since the initiation of the movement.

A valuable agricultural and sporting property, near Sittingbourne, comprising nearly 340 acres, has been sold for £4,600, about half the price given for it a few years ago. The brush manufactory of H. Rose, Verulam-road, St. Albans;was destroyed by fire, on Saturday, damage to the amount of £6,000 being done. Nearly 300 work. people have been thrown out of employment.

The Sugar Bounties Conference will assemble at the Foreign Office about the end of December or the beginning of January next. As the meeting of representatives of foreign Powers takes place in England a prominent member of the British Government will act as president.

DEATH OF SIR HENRY W. GORDON.-Sir Henry W. Gordon, brother of the late General Gordon, died some- what suddenly on Saturday evening at Little Oat Hall, Flayward's Heath, where he had been residing for about three weeks. The deceased gentleman was taken ill only on Friday. A fine specimen of the sea-devil, or angler fish (Lophiug Piscatorius) was caught off Christchurch Ledge last week by a local fishermen, with an ordinary whiting line. The fish, which weighed 501 b., was sft. long, 3ft. 61n. wide, with an immense mouth. This is the first fish of the kind ever seen there. _

_ THE HEREFORD MURDER.—Two men, named John Coates and George Evans, were arrested at Tredegar on Saturday, on suspicion of being concerned in the murder of Mr. Ballard, at Hereford, on Thursday. On Evans two £lO notes were found, which he amounted for by stating that he received them on the death of his father

_ The house in which Dr. Samuel Johnson was born, at Lichfield, has been sold by public auction. The bidding commenced at £5OO, and rose to £BOO, at which sum the property was knocked down to Mr. J. H. Johnson, of Southport, who was stated to have bought the premises to save them from the MO of the spoiler. - - - - - - - -

FITNER.AL or LORD Da TABLET.—The funeral of Lord de Tabley took place on Saturday, at Great Budworth. A portion of the service was held in the private chapel at the Old Hall, and the body was interred in the family burial place at Great Budworth. The coffin was covered with floral tributes. There was a large attendance of Freemasons, the late lord having for 21 years been Grand Master of the Cheshire Province.

The death is announced of Baron Berman de Stern, the head of the firm of Stern Brothers, merchants, of Angel-court, London, The deceased gentleman, who was much respected, was in his 72nd year, and is stated to have amassed a fortune .of upwards of £3,000,000 sterling. The baron was a director of the Bank of Rou- mania, the Imperial Bank (Limited), and the London and San Francisco Bank (Limited).

Henry Taylor, described as a superintendent of public baths, gave himself up to the metropolitan police for having embezzled money belonging to the:Commissioners of the Paddington Baths and Wash-houses. Although the sum charged against the accused was comparatively small, his total defalcations were said to amount to over £l,OOO. He was brought up at the Marylebone Police. court and remanded on substantial bail. A meeting a the creditors of Messrs. Bowman Bros., stock and share brokers, Manchester. was held at Man- chaster on Monday. The liabilities were stated at £79,290, and the assets £ll2O. The causes of failure were attributed to liabilities of a speculative kind incurred far clients, speculations on the Stock Exchange, and bad debts. The debtors were adjudicated bankrupts, and a trustee and committee of inspection were appointed. At a meeting of the governors of the Owens College. Manchester, it was stated that the college had received during the past twelve months more than £32,000 in bequests or gifts. Of this, £21,000, from the estate of the late Sir J. Whitworth, will be devoted primarily to establishing a laboratory in the engineering department; and £lO,OOO left by the late Abel Heywood, to providing instruction for women and girls.

The result of the private inquiry; held at Ramsgate, into the alleged outrage by the Gravelines fishing boat on the Shoreham boat Primrose, is that the commander of the Avon misunderstood the Fisheries Convention, the damage to the Primrose being only slight, and that he should have taken the French boat into a French port, instead of to Ramsgate. The Gravelines skipper was informed that he could proceed to sea at once. ' At Wigan Borough Sessions, on Monday, the Mayor (Aid. Park) made feeling reference to the death of Mr. W. Pickard, J.P., who, as miners' agent, displayed good common sense and general fairness, and was respected by both masters and men. The colliers had lost a good and-true friend, for he was upright, straightforward. and 'honourable; and Wigan had lost a very useful citizen, whom they could ill spare. Other magistrates present expressed similar sehtiments. MR. O'DONNELL'S ACTION AGAINST "THE Tiaras."—Mr. William Graham, of the Midland Circuit, has been in- structed by the solicitors of The Times to draw the state- ment of defence in the action brought by Mr. F. H. O'Donnell against the proprietor and printer of The Times in connection with the articles on " Parnellism and Crime." Sir Henry James, Q.C., M.P., and Mr. Lumley Smith. Q.C., have been retained with Mr. Graham to con- duct the case on behalf of the defendants. HEAVY SENTENCE ON A RECEIVER OF STOLEN GOLD.—At Birmingham Quarter Sessions, on Saturday, the Recorder, Mr. Dugdale, M.P., sentenced George Griffith to five years' penal servitude, for feloniously receiving 2oz. of gold scrap, which a youth, named Ravenscroft, had stolen from his employers. It was shown that the accused had requested the lad to find some "stuff" on two occasions. Ravenscroft stole gold and took it to him, and the Recorder, said it was necessary to pass in Birmingham a severe sentence for such an offence. ANOTHER TRADE 1)181.17.7TE AT BOLTON.—Before the pro- tracted strike in the eimineering trade at Bolton is con- cluded another dispute has occurred in the same town, this time in the local bleaching trade. The piece hands at Messrs. Blair and Suraner's Mill Hill Bleachworks have given a fortnight's notice to terminate their engagements unless the firm concede an advance in wages. The: number affected is about 110. The hands contend that they are not able to earn sufficient on the prices paid for certain wqrk, but the firm on the other hand assert that they pay the full rates for the particular finish referred to. It is not as yet known whether the bleaching trade generally will be affected, the men taking this as a test I effort, or whether Mill Hill is the only establishment where an advance is sought.

EXTRAORDINARY CHAROR AGAINAT A BARONET.-.A case of a very senst tional nature, provided an arrest is effected, will shortly occupy the attention of one of the London West End Police Courts. A baronet, middle- aged and well known in society and at the clubs, is al- leged to have decoyed from her parents a young lady, L 3 years of age. Several weeks ago, on a sworn informa- tion embodying the facts, a magistrate's warrant was granted wider the provisions of the Criminal Law Amendment Act, for the arrest of the baronet, who had, however left the country. A week since an extradition warrant was privately applied for, and obtained. This has been entrusted to a Scotland Yard officer of large experience, who, it is stated, has proceeded to the Con- tinent in the hope of being able to execute it. The cir- cumstances of the alleged offence are of an extraordinary nature. The young lady is the daughter of a professional man, and it is said that for some considerable time be- fore any discovery was made she clandestinely met the baronet in the neighbourhaod of Bromptou; that he used to drive her about in his brougfhani ; and that finally he took her to a house in Pimlico. Great efforts have been made to hush up the matter, but a warrant once granted cannot be withdrawn without the consent of the Court. This is not at all likely to be obtained. SALARIES OF POOR LAW OFFICIALS IN LANC.ASHIRE.- A return just issued shows the excessive proportion of the officers' salaries, rations, remunerations, and superan- mations, to the amount expended in the maintenance of paupers. The returns are from the latest reliable infor- mation in the hands of the Local Government Board, viz., for the parochial year ended in 1886. In that year the maintenance of paupers in England and Wales cost £1,837,6244 and the out-relief £2,490,025, while the salaries, &c., of officers, Sre., amounted to £1,332,017. In addition to this a very large sum was paid in salaries, poundages, and superannuation allowances of parochial officers not distinguished from other items. As showing how rapidly the administration expenses increase, the salaries, &c., of officers, in 1874, amounted to £909,231. Since that date the number of paupers has decreased from 827,466 to 796,036; but the cost of officers has in- creased by about 50 per cent., the amount now paid being £1,332,017. In the Preston Union the maintenance cost £6,296, and the out-relief £2,576; the salaries. &c., of officers amounted to £3,614. Liverpool, in £29,179, out £13,387, salaries £16,939; Toxteth Park, in £5,195, out £5,157, salries £3,614; %Vest Derby, in £23,727, out £22,895, salaries £11,951; Prescot„ in £6,335, out £7,421, salaries £3,279; Ormskirk, in £3,010, out £3,788, salaries £1,780; Wigan, in £2,912, out £11,372, salaries £2,939 Warrington, in £4,340, out £4,033, salaries £3,101; .Leigh, in £1,657, out £3,875, salaries £1,635; Bolton, in £6,891, out £9,676, salaries £4,223; Bury, in £3,971, out £8,828, salaries £3,080; Barton-upon-Irwell, in ' £2,361, out £3,762, salaries £1,751; Chorlton, in £17,281, out £12,138, salaries £9,453; Salford, in £14,758, out £8,721, salaries £8,980; Manchester, in £28,738, out £4,637, salaries £16,686; Prestwich, in £4,095, out £3,185, salaries £2,261; Ashton- under.Lyne, in £6,064, out £5,447, salaries £3,084; Old- ham, in £6,981, out £5,583, salaries £3,367; Rochdale, in £5,039, out £8.551, salaries £2,957; Haslingden, in £3,036, out £4,958, salaries £1,918; Burnley, in £3,774, out £11,084; salaries £2,684; Clitheroe, in £1,173, out £1,947, salaries £1,072; Blackburn, in £6,505, out £6,824, salaries £2,970; Chorlev, in £1,791, out £2,689, salaries £1,390; Fylde, in £l,Ol, out £1,970, salaries £1,008; Garstang, in £240, out £770, salaries £453: Lancaster, In £1,165, out £1,582, salaries £045; Lunesdale, in £214, out £379, salaries £442; Ulverston, in £2,425, out £3,59}, salaries £1,315; Barrow-in-Furness, in £1,765, out £3,071, salaries £742. It will be seen from the above that the paupers in the county of Lancashire cost for in- maintenance £201,969, and out relief £181,195, while the officers cost 4119,611.
