div.head: IRELAND.
div.p: IRELAND.

A destructive fire broke out on Monday in the ex- tensive felt manufactory of Me. Tear and Co., Belfast. The damage is estimated at many thousands sterling. A report comes from Kilrush of a League meeting being held near that town on Sunday afternoon, notwithstand- ing energetic measures on the part of the constabulary to prevent it The police were outmanceuvred in the completest manner, and the meeting, being undisturbed by them, passed ain peace. Mr. Cox, M.P., was present The will of the late Mr. Justice Lawson has been proved by his eldest son, and his friend Mr. Justice Murphy-, two of the executors, the assets being sworn at £30,673, of which he leaves £3,000 to each of his children --three daughters and three sons—leaving the house and lands of Clontart co. Dublin, to his widow, and appoint- ing her residuary legatee and devisee. Intelligence was received in Belfast on Monday that the Lord-Lieutenant, accompanied by Lady Londonderry, will visit the North of Ireland early next month. While the visit will be of a private character, it is understood that his Excellency will take the opportunity of consult- ing with his county Down tenantry regarding their claims for a reduction of rents.

An attempt was made about 11 o'clock on Sunday night to blow up the house of County Inspector Rodger, situate in the main street of Cavan, by placing a quan- tity of gunpowder, rammed in the iron box of a cart wheel, on the sill of the parlour window. The explosion shattered the window and damaged the shutters, while windows on the opposite side of the street were broken. No cause can be assigned for the outrage, as the district Is peaceable. Twenty-one prisoners, arrested on Sunday in connec- tion with the Ballykerogue eviction, were taken from New Ross bridewell on Monday. It being early, not more than 200 people assembled to witness their depar- ture for Wexford prison, but there were present several representatives of the National League, and the local brass band played at the railway station. On their way thither each prisoner was between two policemen, with a rearguard of about 100 constables. Mr. E. J. Walsh, proprietor of the Wexford People, was on Monday committed to prison for a month by two resi- dent magistrates, at Wicklow, for having published an , article calculated to incite people to take part in a pro- claimed nr,eting. The charge was brought under the Crimes Act —On Tuesday, the case against Mr. Walsh, for having published a report of a meeting of a suppressed branch of the National League, was heard, and he was sentenced to two months' imprisonment, with hard labour; but a reserved case to the Exchequer Court was granted, and bail accepted. Four other summonses against the defendant were withdrawn'

div.head: PROCLAIMED MEETING AT CORK.
div.p: THE PROCLAIMED MEETING AT CORK.

Whilst the police and military were guarding the Courthouse at Cork, on Tuesday. the meeting of citizens which they were ordered to suppress was held In the Chamber of Commerce. The Mayor presided, and there were present Messrs. Dillon, M. Healy, Cox, Lane, Flynn, and Hooper, members of Parliament. A resolution was adopted protesting against the Recorder of Cork adju- dicating on the trial of the appeal of Messrs. O'Brien and Mandeville, on the ground that these gentlemen cold not expect a fair trial from the Recorder, after his extraordinary and prejudiced declaration on the 17th inst.; protesting against the tyrannical and um constitutional acts of the Irish Executive in proctaftning the peaceable city of Cork under the Crimes Act; and warmly denouncing the high-handed and clearly illegal manner in which they had forcibly seized and held the City Court House. which was the property of the citizens.
The proceedings were over when the police and mili- tary arrived to stop them, and soon after the streets had their usual aspect. -
EVICTION SCENE NEAR NEW ROSS.

A desperate resistance was offered on Saturday to the eviction at Ballykerogue, eight miles from New hose, on '[...the estate of Colonel Tottenham. The tenants on this ~estat a haying adopted the "Plan of Campaign" the most wealthy occupier among them was proceeded against. The work of taking possession was commenced on Satur- day by the sheriff, accompanied by a number of police. The house was strongly fortified, and when the emer- gency men attempted to force an entrance they were blinded by boiling water and tar. At four o'clock the emergency men gave up the task, and a guard of police was put round the house for the night, to prevent those inside from communicating with the crowd outside. Mr. Dunstercille, who was in charge of the police, ordered a number of people, including Roman Catholic clergy, out of the yard; and asked those inside the house to surren• der. They firmly refused to do this, and the house was subsequently forced open by armed police, who arrested 23 inmates. They were charged and remanded for a I week.
ARREST OF MR. WILFRID BLUNT.-EXCITING SCENES.-POLICE COURT PROCEEDLNGS.

Placards were posted in the neighbourhood of Wood- ford announcing that an indignation meeting would be held on Sunday, under the auspices of the English Horne Rule Union, "to protest against the heartless and cruel evictions carried out during the week on the estate of Lord Clanricarde." Mr. Wilfrid Blunt was announced to preside, and it was stated that several English members of Parliament would attend. The authorities were determined to prevent the meeting being held, and a large force of constabulary was drafted into the town during Saturday night, as well as a detach- ment of Scotch Fusiliers from Loughrea on Sunday morn- ing. The constabulary were busily engaged posting a pmclamation to the effect that the object and effect of the meeting would be intimidation and interference With and resistance to the Administration of Ireland, and that. as the meeting would cause alarm and terror, and pro- time tkbreacl.o th,it. pease, it would be suppressed and diSperseN. mosi•6a-faitio, was dated 22nd October, and signed Arthur Jas. Balfour.

, From an early, hour in the morning bodies of notice occupied the streets, the military being kept in reserve In a building hi a side street A few minutes before two o'clock a small procession, consisting of Mr. Wilfrid Blunt and Lady Wilfrid Blunt, Mr. James Rowlands, M.P., and Mrs. Rowlands; Mr. Sheehy M.P. with several leading local Nationalists, proceeded to the plat- form, which was erected in a field at the back of the main street. A force of police, under the command of Mr. Byrne, divisional magistrate, was already on the spot As soon as the speaker proceeded to get on the platform, Mr. Byrne advanced and said te. Mr. Blunt," I wish to inform you that this meeting is proclaimed, and cannot permit it to be held. It is my duty to tell you that." Mr. Blunt replied, "It is my- duty to hold the meeting." Mr. Townsend, RM., then said, "Suppress this meetinff," and the police at once proceegled to clear the platform. Mr. Blunt struggled with several police- men and the Divisional Magistrate, who seized him, and was twice taken from the platform. Mr. Blunt then shouted to the police, "Are you such cowards that you dare not arrest me." A District Inspector re- plied, '1 arrest you," and immediately Mr. Blunt was marched off.

During the fight at the platform a stone struck a police- man on the helmet and dazed him for a moment. The police then charged, and several desperate hand-to-hand conflicts ensued. A company of Scotch Fusiliers, who had appeared on the scene during the struggleiwith the occupants of the platform were hurried up towards the exit from the field, and so soon as the police bad passed out with their prisoner and Lady Blunt, the soldiers barred this entrance. Another arrest was made shortly after Mr. Blunt had been lodged in the lock-up, Mr. Roach, Door law guardian, being taken into custody, charged with assaulting the police. During the clearing of the town a policeman, named Connor, for falling to do his duty, was at once placed under arrest. At five o'clock Mr. Blunt was brought before two resident magistrates, Messrs. Paul and Townsend, and charged under the Crimes Act with wilfully and un- lawfully resisting Mr. John Byrne, district magistrate, and Sergeant Thomas Walton, in the execution of their duty. Sergeant Thomas Walton deposed that Mr. Blunt attempted to address the proclaimed meeting at Wood- ford. He resisted Mr. Byrne, and Mr. Byrne said "Put this man down," and witness seized him by the side collar, but Mr. Blunt shook off his hold. Witness then with some others, took hold of him behind and put him off the platform. Mr. Paul: Do you wish to ask the witness any ques- tions? Mr. Blunt: No. District-inspector Murphy, in reply to Mr. Paul, said that what he asked for was a remand until the petty sessions next day. Mr. James Rowlands, M.P., said he wished to ask if Mr. Blunt should be released on bail. Mr. Paul: You have no locus siandi here? Mr. Rowlands: Not as an English citizen? Mr. Paul: No. Mr. Blunt must apply. District-inspector Murphy I will oppose bail. Mr. Paul: On what grounds? Mr. Murphy: Owing to the excitement there is here at present. The case will be heard at the petty sessions In the morning, so there will be no inconvenience. Mr. Paul (to Mr. Blunt): Will you give an understand- hig that no meeting will be held here to4night if you have bail? Mr. Blunt: No; I consider that the proclamation which, it is said, was issued on sworn information was false, lying, and perjured information; on that ground I refuse.

Mr. Blunt was removed in custody. Mr. Reach was also remanded. ,Mr. Wilfrid Blunt and Mr. Roche arrived at Woodford from Loughrea on Monday, escorted by about ten cars full of police. They were met outside the town by Mr. Jas. Rowlands, M.P., Mr. Sheehy, M.P., and a number of people, accompanied by a brass band. On entering the town Mr. Blunt was loudly cheered by a largo crowd in the street leading to the Court House, 'which was guarded by large bodies of police, some armed with batons, and others with rifles, and also by a com- pany of Fusiliers. Mr. Blunt has received a large num- ber of telegrams from different parts of England, con- gratulating him on his action. Mr. Blunt applied to the resident magistrate for an adjournment for a fortnight, but the Crown officials op- posed, end asked that the adjournment should be only until Tuesday. This the Bench acceded to, and Mr. Blunt and Mr. Roche were released on bail. They were tol- -1

- SENTENCE OF MR. BLUNT. At the resumed proceedings in connection -with the prosecution of Mr. Wilfrid Blunt at Woodford, county Galway, on Thursday, the 'case for the Crown closed, and Mr. Harrington then applied for the decision of the magistrates as to whether the proclamation was a pro- clamation under the Crimes Act. Their Worships decided that it was, and Mr. Harrington then applied for the dis- missal of the case on the ground that a copy ' of the For Children suffering from Whooping Cough, Bronchitis, and "Dublin Gazette " containing the Proclamation had not and Cough—relieves them instantly. The magistrates pointed out that defendant was liable to ' be prosecuted under section 2 of the Act, whether the meeting had been proclaimed or not, on a charge of re- sisting police in discharge of their duty. They con- sidered that the hands of the authorities had been strengthened by the issuing of the proclamation and ruled against Mr. Harrington. Mr. Harrington pro- ceeded to argue that the Bench should state a ease, but the Bence declined at that stage to do so, and shortly afterwards the court was cleared and the magistrates proceeded to consider their decision. On resuming they stated that they should sentence Mr. Blunt to two months' imprisonment:

div.head: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at the Workhouse on Wednesday morning. There were present the Rev. G. F. Roberts (chairman), Messrs. Darbyshire, Greening, W. Houghton, Jolley, Voisey, J. Houghton, Clarice, Ratcliffe, Wright, Blackhurst. Harrison, Grange, Humphreys, and Hibbert ; J. C. Sutton (clerk), and S. Sutton (assis- tant clerk.)
PADOATE SCHOOLS COMMITTEE THE DEVELOPMENT OP TALENT.

This committee's minutes stated that the Superinten- dent had reported that a gift of a piano to the schools had been received from Mr. Hy. Thornton, and it was resolved that the best thanks of the committee be accor- ded to Mr. Thornton for his gift. Dr. Canneil had re- ported that the health of the children was generally satisfactory, and the Chaplain reported that the girls' school had passed a satisfactory examination. An ap- plication for an increase of salary by the Superinten- dent was referred to the Board for consideration.—The CHAIRMAN moved, and Mr. RATCLIFFE seconded, the adoption of the minutes.—Mr. Deasrsaraa asked if it was to be understood that the children would be learned music, or was the piano for special occasions.—The CHAIRMAN said it was for special occasions, when enter- tainments were given by the Band of Hope and -others. Mr. JOLLEY : It must not go forth to the public that the children are receiving a musical education, because I object to that. (Laughter.)—The Ca AIRMAN : I think that scarcely re- quires contradiction.—Mr. VOIffEY did not think they could object to anything that was given. It might be that there would be a child at the schools of special musical talent, and if the piano assisted it to develope that talent everybody would be glad. (Hear, hear.)—The CLERK said he had been told of a boy who was brought up in a workhouse who was natv as a professional man receiving £9OO a year, and they did not know what little trifles might have helped to develope that boy's special talents. (Hear, hear.)—The minutes were then confirmed.

div.head: SCHOOL FEES.
div.p: SCHOOL FEES.

The School Fees Committee reported that fees had been allowed in 68 cases, 18 of which were new and 50 old cases.—Mr. BLACKHIIIIST, in moving the adoption of the minutes, said that, considering the time of the year, it was very satisfactory hat there were so few applica- tions for fees. Ile thought it spoke very well for the prospects of the winter. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. .Touzy seconded the adoption of the minutes, which was agreed to.

div.head: AttticATMPO xontAsE ó1 sALAnit§.
div.p: AttticATMPO xontAsE ó1 sALAnit§.

--.—.-- ---___. The Xewton Relief Committee, to whom the applica- tion of Mr. Houghton, collector, Newton, for an increase of salary had been referred, reported that they had con- sidered the application, and had come to the conclusion that they could not recommend an increase.—This report was adopted unanimously.—An application for an in- crease of salary was read from Mr. Mines, superinten- dent of Padgate schools, who pointed out that he had been 19 years in the service of the Board, and also re- ferred to the excellent reports that had been made as to the condition and management of the schools.—Mr. BLACHHURST, while speaking in complimentary terms of i the manner n which Mr. Mines performed his duties, thought that this was not the time to raise salaries. He referred to the heavy rates that had to be paid, and to 'the fact that although population and house property increased the assessment value decreased owing to the reduction in the assessments. He moved that they did not make any %crease at Any rate f..ir this year.—This proposition was however, not seconded, and several members expressed the opinion that Mr. Mines was en- titled to an increase on his present salary of £95 a year. —Ultimately it was agreed on the motion of the CHAIR- MAN, seconded by Mr. GREENING. that an increase of £lO per annum should be granted.

ODARDIANS- AND THEIR OFFICERS. Communications were submitted from the Darlington and Merthyr Tydvil Boards of Guardians asking the Board to Join in memorialising that additional powers lof dealing with their officers be granted to Boards of Guardians. The Darlington Board of Guardians was desirous that powers should be granted to Boards of Guardians to reduce the salaries of their officers if they thought fit without the sanction of the Local Govern- ment Board, while the Merthyr Tydvil Guardians ex- pressed themselves in favour of powers being granted both to reduce the salaries of and to discharge officers. Some discussion took place on the communication from the Darlington Board of Guardians. In the course of it the CHAIRMAN remarked that this was a question of the decentralisation of powers. He thought that if they had the power to increase salaries they ought to have the power to decrease them if they thought proper to do so. Why should the power to do that be central- ised elsewhere with a body that could not enter into the full merits of the case ?—The CLERK said he might point out that when an officer was appointed there was an honourable understanding that the appointment would last during his good behaviour, and the officer knew that when his appointment had been confirmed by the Local Government Board that engagement would remain unless he was removable on account of bad behaviour. Mr. VOISEF spoke against the signing of the memorial. He thought it would be unfair to the officers if they had to hold their offices at the goodwill of the Guardians for the time being.--ME. DARBESHIRS was in favour of signing the memorial, and said he would be the last to think that Boards of Guardians would take any undue advantage of their officers. Decentralisation would, he thought, be of advantage in many ways both to Boards of Guardians and Local Boards, and those who found the money ought to have a voice in the spending of it. He proposed, therefore, that they sign the memorial.—Mr. HARRISON seconded this proposal. He did not think that they who found the money ought to be mere auto- matons in the hands of the Local Government Board. They ought to know more of their own requirements than people in London could do, and they had most in-, terest in directing their expenditure aright without any jobbery whatever.—Mr. GREENING pointed out that the Town Council had the powers over their officers re- ferred to.—The CHAIRMAN And do you know of any instance in which their salaries have been reduced t—Mr. GREENING said he did not know of any instance.—Mr. JOLLEY having also spoken in favour of signing the me- morial, Mr. Darbyshire's proposition was agreed to. , i The relief cases were then proceeded with.

COAGULINE.—Cement for Broken Articles, 6d. and is. ; pest- age, 2d. Sold everywhere. Kay Bros., M., Stockport—Advt. At the Central Criminal Court, on Thursday, Joseph Carlin was sentenced to ten years' penal servitude for at- tempting to murder Esther Bird, a servant girl, at St. John's Wood. The Duchess of Connaught, with her three children, left London on Thursday morning for India. The Prince of Wales and the Duke of Cambridge were at the station to see her off. div.head: TA TUDOR WILLIAMS, L.D.S. MEDICAL HALL, ABERDARE, WALES.
div.p: TA TUDOR WILLIAMS, L.D.S. MEDICAL HALL, ABERDARE, WALES.
THE GEOLOGICAL HISTORY OF
THE EARTH.

The second of the series of lectures on "The Ancient Geography and Geological History of Britain" was delivered on Monday evening, in the Co-operative Hall, Warrington, by Professor Boyd Dawkins. There was a large audience.—ln the course of his very interesting lecture, Professor Dawxmis said, with regard to the temperature of the • earth, that their universal experience was that the deeper they went down into the earth the hotter did its temperature become. That observation as to the in- crease of temperature from the surface downwards was confirmed by deep sinking's. They had it confirmed by the existence of thermal springs. The spring of hot water at Buxton derived its heat from passing through great depths in order to reach the surface, and all other, springs of the same nature owed their beat to the same. cause. Volcanoes also proved that the interior of the earth is very much hotter than the outer parts. They were justified in taking it as a feet that for every 65 feet they went down beneath the surface there was a rise of one degree of heat. A temprature of 98 degrees or Mood heat was reachedat a depth of 1120 yards, and. that was the limit fixed by the coal commissioners for the workable amotmt of coal. At ahigher temperature than that it was assumed by the Government Commissioners that coal could not be worked. At a depth of 34 miles they should find a temperature of ,2788 degrees, and they would see from that that they were led to conclude that the surface of the earth On which they 'lived and moved is a very thin film supported by, an enormously hot sub- stratum of some sort or another. At a depth of 34 miles everything they knew on the surface of the earth would arrive at atemeprature which would undoubtedly cause it to assume a fluid if not a gaseous form. . Were they then to assume that the outer part of the earth is merely a thin film 34 miles in thickness, floating upon hot fluid,? They had, however, another clement corning in. They knew that pressure increased enormously as they went deeper and deeper into the earth, and it was just conceivable that the pressure at 34 miles depth might be so great as to prevent those highly heated substances from becoming fluid. They would see then that they could not make out whether the interior of the earth was fluid or solid, and he was not able to give their' any evidence, but they were certain of the fact that the earth is enor- mously heated in its interior parts. And they knew that if the pressure be relaxed ever so little they might have a portion of that enormously heated material deep down in the earth suddenly passing from the solid to the fluid state. The results of Sir William Thompson's investipc • , tions into the physical constitution of the globe was that the whole of the earth taking it as one mass is certainly as solid as an equal sphere of steel or of glass wouldbe. I That, however, did not tell them whether there might not lbegreat spacesm theinteriorpartsof the earth, which are perfectly fluid. The materials of the earth are arranged according to their density or relative weight. At the present time the earth is losing heat minute by minute, and year by year, and, in fact, might be said to be cool- ing just as a hot brick cools. Bearing this in mind they could see that the farther back they went the hotter the earth would be, and there must have been some one time when the earth was sufficiently hot to allow of its being molten at the surface. This molten condition of the earth was a condition which would satisfactorily explain the fact that the heaviest materials are to be found in the interior parts of the earth, and that from the interior to the exterior the lighter layers are found outside and the heavier layers inside. The lecturer then alluded to the outer planets as throwing light on the early condition of the earth, and mentioned that the moon was now in a state which the earth would probably arrive at when it had lost its heat. They might, he went on to say, conceive of the earth and the other planets one by one being ab- sorbed into the mass of the sun, and then his fiery atmos- phere would gradually become cooler and cooler, and his mass become more and more condensed. It was per- fectly conceivable that all those elements of the sun which. are now prevented from combining together would form various materials which we find on the surface of the earth. In other words the sun would pass into a cooling globe, useful for life and capable of habitation, even as the earth is at the present time. But then the sun him- self is revolving around an infinitely remote centre, and therefore they had opened to their minds in unlimited space an unlimited vision of change—a passing from an enormously heated condition to a cold condition. They must look upon the present condition of the earth as a cooling globe to be a state which is being passed through which has been passed through, or which will bd passed through by everything they could see in this universe. (Hear, hear, and applause).

THE BOLTON STEHLE : Taints oF SarriziamYr ACCEPTED. —On Thursday morning the representatives of the men on strike in the Bolton engineering trade had an inter- view with the employers, and the latter practically ac- cepted the men's proposal for settlement of the dispute. The masters, however, made certain stipulations, and these were to be laid before a mass meeting of the men. The terms of settlement include the formation of a Board of Conciliation to take evidence on wages in other towns. The men's joint committee believe the terms will be ac- cepted, and the strike, which has now la'sted 25 weeks, will end. KAY'S COMPOIIND.—Aethrna and Bronchitis are immediately relieved by it. 'lowed by the crowd down the street cheering, but a party ,of police followed, and no attempt was made to hold a meeting or to make speeches. The crowd ultimately dispersed quietly. Mr. Blunt says he was treated with consideration while in prison, but he complains that the magistrates showed bias and predetermination in refusing the adjournment for a fortnight. On Tuesday the hearing of the summons took place, Messrs. J. J. Dillon and Mc.Sheehy being the presiding magistrates. Mr. T. Harrington, M.P., arrived at Woodford to defend both Mr. Blunt and Mr. John Roche, and was met out- side the town by a band and a large crowd of people. The entrance to the court was again guarded by a strong force of police, but there were not so many people in the town as on Monday. At the opening of the proceedings Mr. Harrington ob- jected to the jurisdiction of the Court on the ground that the Crimes Act provided that the magistrates should be specially appointed to try the case, and that one of them should be a person of whom the Lord Lieu- tenant had satisfied himself that he possessed sufficient legal knowledge to try the case. The Bench overruled the objection. Mr. Harrington then applied for a summons against Mr. Byrne for assault; and the magistrates postponed their decision on the point. . .

Mr. Ronan, Crowni prosecutor, in opening the case, said it was only important in this, that English politicians visiting Ireland must be taught that if they defied the law, they would be treated by the law exactly in the manner as if they were ordinary inhabitants of the country. About the facts of the case there was prac- ticably no dispute. If they came to the conclusion that Mr. Blunt was guilty, he hoped it would have a salutary effect, and teach his associates that they must obey the law. He hoped that the magistrates would enter such a judgment as would teach people that if they broke the law they must take the consequences. Evidence was given that Mr. Blunt was warned that the meeting had been proclaimed, and that he declared that he should persist in holding it, and several witnesses were examined to prove the actual resistance he offered when the police commenced to clear the platform.

LORD HARTINGTON has been working himself up into something ince a .temper. He addressed a meeting of Liberal Unionists and Conservatives at

Nottingham on Monday, and proceeded to quarrel with everything Mr. :GLADSTONE said last week in the same town. He.cannot forgive the leader of the Liberal party for wielding an influence over his followers Which, he said, is unparalleled in our history. His lordship calls it des- potism; but Liberals give it another name; they call it the power of attraction--a power

Which men like Lord HAETINGTON cannot undei- • stand, ,and cannot therefore exercise. It is not his fatilt, perhaps, that he repels rather that attracts the multitufie ;' but, if he is wise, he will cease to gibe at Mr. .GLArksoNx for being more highly endowed than himself. Lord HARTINGTON • Will never, be a leader,of men, because he cannot determine whither he mould go. He reproaches

• the Liberal party for bang " pledged to the 'repeal of the Union ; " but he knows, or ought to know, this is absolutely untrue. The act of Union is an Act of Parliament ',which, like any other Act, may be altered, and it 'would be quite son- etitutional to propose its repeaL Whether it would be wise to do so -is another thing; but, as a matter of fact, the Liberal party have never

thought of taking such a 'course. The talk about being pledged to the repeal of the Union is a weak invention of the enemy. lord HARTINGTON is nearer the truth when he says "the Home, Rule plan which the Federation representing the. Rome litule party is prepared to support is: 'founded on the principle of the bill of last year." It is, just because "the principle
_ 'of the bill of last year" is adhered to, and that, ttoo, without being tied down to details that Mr. 'OrAnsToma occupies a position 'which is unassail-
able. •Let the Unionists of all shades and no shade turn abootas they will, they anal:loomed to defeat,
41110 y ' because they have no prindiple to guide' them. Why,should Mr. GLansrovz turn his back

on the principle of Home Rule It would be political suicide to do so, for it is as-well to remem- ber—hOPiever sluggish Lord HARTINOTON may have all along been—that his chief henchman, Mr. JOSUE( CHAMBERLAIN, committed 'himself to the Prinelple of the bill when it was under discussion lhe ;House of !Commons. It is true Mr.. ,Onssi- nsamaszi has retrograded, but Mr. GLADSSONE is anettheekind of man; he either holds his ground or
goes :forward—he is not a backslider.
Before

girding so fiercely at his old friends, it would be ;veil if Lord HAILTINGTON would let it be known now he stands with his new. Does he really like their ways? expressed his doubts pretty early as to the wisdom of attempting to suppress the Xational League. Have his doubts been con-. ?irrned, or have they-been removed by the miser- able muddle which the Ministry have made of the

govermsient .of Ireland? There was a time, too, When be said that if 'Home Rule were to be granted, such a Land Purchase Bill as that brought by lir, GALADSTONE was absolutely neenssary. bees he still think so, and, if so, how does he make this' fall in with Mr. CHAMBERLAIN'S denunciation

of the scheme under any and every circumstance ? It Would be interesting to know how far he approves Of Mr. CHAMBERTAIN'S land purchase scheme, .-Vhich, by the by, has been so unceremoniously ra- diated by that other Unionist leader, Colonel,' 7.. .41TtnEitsoN. It is a pity that his lordship, when e has so much fault to find with what the berals propose to do, does not tell us what he . ould do himself. He is indignant with Mr, !o,l.c...nsToxn for holding out the bribe, as he calls it, Q't disesta.blishment in Wales and Scotland. It is 11°.btibe, of course, when Mr. CNAMBERLAIN talks :(4sestablishmeat, or when Lord ,RANDOLPH 4V,RVIIILL urges that the time has come to make ..,(:r ee ;Education a plank in the platform of the ti Oionitt party. His particular friends—and what ilk Pairl—may steal a horse, but Mr. GLADSTONE 011itt,nsr; so much as look over a hedga. With re- to; the Church,it is suggestive that Lord HAR- otorr-proceeds to say that he does "not take ' Iligh.eligious view upon this question ;" that to asyit is not a matter with him of religion, k. of pcso, purely and simply. He is ready to . '4ck the-State prop from under the Church at what ' • conceives to be the right time, buthe does net like idea of the leader of the Liberal party having V,_aud in the .job. Indeed, he tries to sho7 that '. • GrAnsroxn ought to have nothing to do with o',Seeing that some fifteen years ago he held the /3111. 441,_t0n that it was impossible to separate the T.4on of disestablislament in Wale from the 4114‘'5t10n of disestablishment inEngland. But a leZedd Inhoy things have happened in fifteen years; qa ', it 'ie to the glory of Mr. Gransrroxx that he Is:it/Pays learning—that be is ever moving onward tii 111Thara. Fifty years ago, Mr. GLADSTONE was ttifa e tilling hope of the unbending Tories; now he Ith: Liberal of Liberals, the greatest statesman of IL age--" the noblest Roman of them all." And ord .. „ ht,t u'ultritiorox, what is he He was a Liberal, the world asks—what is he now? _ Of Til° Warringtoll Library Committee, and many e tIl thillic members of the Town Council, seem to et4sio that they have made an extraordinary con- -11 to the public: demand to luwe a Free Len-

ding library in resolving that henceforth there shall be a charge of one penny per book lent out to those who are not subscribers of ss. per year, or la ficl. per quarter. They either cazmot, or will not, see that the objection is to the principle of any charge being made at all. If the charge is il- legal and we have over and over again shown that it is—it is as much a robbery to insist on id. per book as upon ss. per year ; a fraud, is a fraud whether it involves a penny or a pound. Theplea that the Committee cannot do without these charges has been shown to be worthless on finan- cial grounds; and it is certainly one that ought not to be listened to on moral grounds. What would be thought of an offender who had im- properly received "money in a trust committed to his sere, if he pleaded, on being brought before -the magistrates, that he couldn't live without the money he had wrongfully obtained? Would he not be told by the magistrates that that was no business of theirs; that it was their duty to en- force the law, and that he must cease to break the law, whatever the consequences to himself? In the case of the Warrington Library, we have mag- istrates making themselves a party to a 'Reach of the law, and the spectacle is one which,presents itself to us as the reverse of edifying. It is true that. Alderman DAVIES made an attempt to defend, from a legal point of view, the imposition of a charge; but his case tumbles to pieces the , moment it is touched. In the first place he is wrong as to what he conceives to be the facts. Referring to the Public Libraries- Act of 1865, Alderman DAVIES says :--" This particular Act of Parliament was passed to deal with public and not lending libraries, libraries such as the British Museum, the Bodlean Library, and others of that character." If Aldermim Derans wishes it to be thought that the Actiloes not apply to Warrington Library, and to all the public lending libraries by which we are surrounded, we have to say that he is labouring under a gross misapprehension, and has strangely, though we do not say wilfully, mis- -101 the members of the Town Council. The Libraries Act of 1865 applies not onlyto the War- rington Library, but to every Library in England which is supported out of the penny rate. Under it—as was stated in the resolution passed at the Town's Meeting—are established Free Lending Libraries 'not only in Wigan, St. Helens, Runcorn, Widnes, and other surrounding towns, but in over 100 other towns in'the country. Really, when an , elementary fact of this ',kind is unknown, or ignored, by a leading member of the Library Com- mittee, the public need not be surprised at the way in which the whole question has been dealt with' by that Committee. Proceeding to deal with the reply of the ArrOß-. NEY-GENERAL to the question put in the-House of Commons, Alderman DAVIES says the law officer of the Crown "did Rot say it was ultra vires to make any charge at all." He did not, it is true, use that particular form of words, but what he said in- evitably involved the conclusion that what the Committee is doing ,is ultra vire& 'Fortun- ately he used plain English; and the ratepayers can settle for themselves what is the plain mean- ing of his words. Further, the question put to the ATTORWEY..GENERAL was not as 'Alderman IDAvrEs tells us—" What powers does the Library Act of 1855 give ? " It was nothing so absurdly general in its character. It specifically related to the authority for, requiring subscriptions, and the answer was .equally specific. But we reprpd' uce the question and the answer in order that there may he no further, misconception. Mr. BRADLAUGH said—"l beg to ask whether, under 'the Public Libraries Act, 1855, the Warrington "Library and Museum Committee are justifiedlin 'requiring and receiving subscriptions from persons borrowing books from the Warrington Free Li- brary,,which is supported froaxt the rates; and whether the committee are legally justified in ao-: carding.privilege pto subscribers in respect of the: loan df books from the Free Library which are not &worded to [ratepayers who do not pay [special sub- scsiptions." The answer of the ATTORNEY-GENE- RAL to that [question`was—" There is no authority under the Public Libraries Act of 1855 for making any distinction between persons who subscribe and persons who do not." There is no mistake here as to the town ; there is no mistake as to the Act: there is no mistake as to the answer; and there is no mistake as to the fact that question and answer prove that Alderman DAVIES and the Library Committee are entirely in the wrong. If the Library Committee think that the ArIiOBNEY. GENERAL is mistaken—that the Act does give power to make a charge—why do they not quote the section upon which they rely? They have been challenged a score of times to do this, and we challenge them again for the twenty-first time.

Touching another point, Alderman DAVIES says: —" Clause 21 of the Act gave power to the Corpo- ration, through their Committee, to conduct the library in any way they thought best. In the in- terests of Warrington it was thought desirable that books should be lent, and that had been done." It sounds a trifle odd to hear it stated in one breath that the Committee, exercising their powers, had lent books, and in the next breath to be told that " there was no authority to lend at all." This is very much like an attempt to accom- plish the impossible feat of going up two different streets at the same time. However, we do not quarrel with the Committee for lending books; it is for making a charge when they do lend them. As to the 21st Section, it does not leave the Committee to do as they like; and it cer- tainly gives no authority to demand subscriptions. The section is as follows The general management, regulation, and control of such libraries and museums, schools for science and art, shall be, as to any borough, vested in and ex- ercised by the Council, and as to any district in and by the Board, and as to any parish or parishes in and by the Commissioners. or such Committee es such Council or Board may from time to time appoint, the members whereof need not be members of the Council or Board or be Combissioners, who may from time to time purchase and provide the neces- sary fuel, lighting, and other similar matter, books, newspapers, maps, and specimens of art and science. for the use of the library or museum, or school, and cause the same to be bound or repaired when neces- sary, and appoint salaried officers and servants, and dismiss the same, and make rules and regulations for the safety and use of the libraries and museums, and schools, and for the admission of the public. It will be seen that the regulations that can be made are for the "safety and use of the Libraries and Museums and Schools;" and with regard to ;the books, this means, as the ATTORNEY-GENERAL put it, that it would "be competent for the Com- mittee to require a reasonable deposit to ensure their safe return." But a deposit is one thing, and a subscription is quite another, although the Com- mittee are acting as if there was no difference be- tween the two. At the same time they make a mockery of the opinion of the ATTORNEY-GENERAL by making a "distinction between persons who subscribe and persons who do not." In moving the adoption of the minutes of the .Library Committee, Alderman WEBSTER said—" It had been urged over again that every ratepayer in the borough had a legal right to have books lent to him to comply with the provisions of the Act of

THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 29, 1887.

WIDNES COUNTY COURT.—His Honour Judge Thomp- son held a sitting of this court yesterday. The Cause list comprised 26 judgment summonses and 185 plaints. Pooh RATE FOR CLIFTON.—The Runcorn magistrates on Monday sanctioned the laying of a poor rate of Ls in the £ for the township of Clifton. The rate is estimated to realise £2lO Bs. 6d. RUNCORN CHURCH liisrrrum—Under the auspices of this-society the Rev. W. Bryant, 8.A., B.Sc., on Thursday evening delivered an interesting lecture on some of the phisical properties of water in the National Schools. CONCERT AT WIDNES.—Last night a successful concert in aid of the funds of the new Welsh Wesleyan Chapel was held in Lacey - street Schoolroom. The room wa 3 well filled with an appreciative audience, and Mr. D. H. Jones, of :Runcorn, occupied the chair. The vocalists were all of good reputation, and a most enjoy- able evening was spent. CONCERT AT Drrrox HALL.—On Thursday evening the German choir of St. Michael's, Ditton Hall, gave a con- cert in aid of the schools in connection with the church. There was a large attendance. The Rev. C. Wiederman, Rector, presided, and an introductory address was given by the Rev. Father ROSW111:. The music was of a high order, and the audience loudly expressed their ap- proval. ASSAULT ON A WOMAN AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, Ann Caldwell, an elderly woman, summoned William Hartles, a young man, for assaulting her on the 24th inst. The defendant, it appeared, ac- cused the complainant of " scandalizing ' him, and meeting her on the day mentioned, he struck her three times. She had both her eyes blacked, and her arm was so injured that she had to carry it in a sling. A fine of 10A, and costs es 6d, was imposed. RESIGNATION OF THE 11. FATHER TENNELLY. OUT • readers will learn with regret that the Rev. Father Fen- nelly has, owing to ill-health, resigned his position as parish priest at Runcorn. There are several cases of fever at •Sankey l3ridges, but, being outside the borough boundary, they are left as it were to their own sweet will. The local authority ought to bestir themselves and make arrangements for sending such cases to the Wzrrington Fever Hospital. They surely do not want to propagate disease.

Mr. Chamberlain has got to 4riking wild, as they do in the prize ring when they are getting the worst of it. Even the "Times," which now treats him as asort'of pet, remarks that he " presses himself with concentrated bitterness." Well, well, it is.the only material left him ant 'of which to build up his National Party. But it is poor stuff at the best.

Everybody knzws how generous Sir Gilbert Greenall can be at times. Warrington, happy. Warrington, has just been privileged with an in- stance of his munificence. As his grounds swexin with ,pheasants, he was recently applied to, on be- half Id the Park Committee, to present a pair for the aviary in the park. He didn't gibe the pheasants; but he gave—the name of a dealer who mils pheasants. Now wasn't that good of him? Wasn't it like him?

Councillor Platt hit the right nail on the head in calling attention, en Tuesday, to the fact that the Warrington Literary and Philosophical So- ciety paid a nominal rent to the Library Commit- tee when they should pay a real rent. The way in which they have for years been sponging upon the ratepayers has been pointed out previously, but now that the matter has come before the Town Council, there is good treason to hope that the wrong will be remedied.

Alderman Webster pleaded that the Library Committee desired to make the iastitution as pnb- Hely useful:as possible; tut the best way to do that would ,be to economise the penny in the pound, charge a fair rent to all who make use of the rooms for meeting purpoBe3, and apply the money in making the Library free. Pauperising rich Philosophers at the expense of poor Ratepayers is " abuseful "_rather than useful.

Some farmers who know not what they do are ~aryilig out for Protection. They seem to think I that it is within the power of Parliament to effect alremedy for low ces. Parlisznent would, if it meddled in the matter, make bah worse, as it has always done. If the larmers want to dip into the I public purse, let them ask for a graut, say so much per acre. This will be straightforward and intel- ligible, and the answer will be "no? If farmers wish to mend matters permanently, they must help the Radicals to effect a Indical reform ,of the land laws.

It is interesting to watoh the attitude of Lord Randolph Churchill' towards Protection. He scarcely disguises the fact that he has a profound contempt for the nostrum of the Pair Traders, and yet, by way of keeping a bait before their eyes he intimates that if the demand for Protectim: be- come national, he will listen to it Everybody has heard of the donkey whose rider kept it going by holding a wisp of hay before it. Lord Randolph evidently thinks he can ride the ass Protection in the same way.

At Liverpool, a candidate for municipal honours has been thrown out because, while his name is Henry Cartwright Gillmore, he was on the register as "Henry Charles" Gilimore. At Birmingham, a Mr. Haddon was on the register as Hatton; but the Mayor in this case "leaned to virtue's side," and ruled that the objection was a bad one. Is it not absurd that the path of a candidate should be blocked because of a printers' error? The voters' lists are made for men, and not men for the lists.

There is something pettyfogging, if not mean, about the way in which objection is always taken to the nomination of candidates who happen to be outsiders. If a nomination paper is so bad as to be misleading, it should of course be rejected; but why should a candidate run the risk of being thrown out because of the spelling of. a word? The law ought to require that the Town Clerk, or his clerk, shall fill up the nomination paper of any burgess who is being proposed as a candidate, the only condition being that the requisite material shall be brought to his hand.

There seems to have been some very hard swear- ing in connection with the proclamation which was issued against the Woodford meeting. The placards for the meeting were issued between one and two o'clock on Saturday afternoon, and, although Woodford is seven hours' journey from Dublin, the proclamation was "despatched from Dublin by the half-past seven train that very evening." How was it done? Have they got to swearing infor- mations by telegraph, or is this another 43viclenee of the way in which those who should maintain the law are breaking the law?

Acnow AGAINST WIDNES LOCAL BOARD. Yesterday, at Widnes County Court, George Hunt, bricksetter, Sr.c., of Ditton, sued the Widnes Local Board for £4 14s 3d for work done. Mr. Rideal, of Warringtoh, was for the plaintiff, and Mr. J. W. Knowles represented the Local Board. It appeared that the plaintiff had done some plastering work at Stock's Well pumping station, and the amount claimed was for "extras."—Mr. Knowles called Mr. Carr, the gas and water engineer, who said the contract of 5d per yard included all that the plaintiff had done. His Honour gave judgment for the . Local Board with costs. MANCHESTER EXHIBITION;—It Will be noticed from the advertisement that the exhibition will finally close on the 10th November. SUDDEN DEATH AT Chorr.—A sudden death, under very sad circumstances, has been reported to the county police, and by.them to the Coroner. It appears that a man named Joseph Lythgoe, who belongs to Manchester, was on a visit to friends at Croft, and, it is alleged, be hafi been drinking heavily. Soon after oleven o'clock on Tuesday night he went out of the house, and as he did not , return as soon as it was .expected he would do, his friends went.out and found him in the road in a very excited state. They were endeavouring to get him back to the house when he slipped, fell, I and immediately expired. I OBSTRUCTING NAVIGATION AT RUNCORN.—At Runcorn ' Petty Sessions, on Monday, before Mr. Henry Reynolds and Mr. G. L. Davies, John .Twigg and Henry Twigg, boatmen, were charged with having, on the sth October, obstructed the passage of vessels into or out of the Fran- cis Dock, of the Bridgewater Navigation undertaking of the Manchester Ship Canal Companp. Both defendants pleaded not guilty.—John Twigg was also charged with assaulting and resisting Arthur Povey, dock constable, while in the execution of his duty. He pleaded guilty.— Mr. Newman, of the firm of Messrs. Grundy, Kershaw, and Company, appeared on behalf of the Company, and said since the Bridgewater undertaking had been taken by the Ship Canal Company Navigation, the canal had been several time ii blocked by boatmen, who appeared to think that the company would not prosecute. The company, however, were determined to protect their rights and to put an end to this obstruction. It ap- I peared that on the sth October, Heary. Twigg was in charge of a boat named " Jessie " be- longing to Mr. Evans, and of which John Twigg was captain. The boat was being moved from the Francis Dock to the tidal basin, and Henry took the vessel into the lock stern first in such a manner that the helm be- came unshipped. John Twigg then came upon the scene, and both men refused to move the boat either up or down the lock until the helm had been replaced in position. As the helm was very heavy, the dock consta- ble, Arthur Povey, asked the defendants to take the boat where hydraulic machinery could be put into requisition, but they would not do this, and fastened the boat so that traffic was obstructed for an hour. - Eventually a band of men FM brought, and forcibly removed the boat. During this operation the Constable Povey got upon the boat, and John. Twigg seized hold of him slid asked him if he could swim, as he was going to throw him into the water. Povey drew his baton, and said if he pushed him again he would break his arm. Both men were" tipsy."—The defence was that the defend- ants only took their turn through the lock, and that the dock tenter, Thomas Millington, ordered them to go stern first.—Mr. Newman said he did not wish to put the com- pany to the expense of taking the case to the Quarter Sessions as a misdemeanour, nor the defendants to the trouble of going there.—The Bench advised the with- drawal of the summonses for obstruction, and this being , done, John Twigg was fined £1 and costs, Bs. 6d., for the assault.

At the commencement of the proceedings at Widnes Police Court, on Monday, the magistrates present being Messrs. F. H. Gossage and John Brock, Mr. Lewin (mag- istrates' clerk) said he was sorry to inform their wor- ship that one of their brother magistrates was dead. Mr. Evans, of Prescot, it appeared, died very early on Sun- day morning. He used to be in constant attendance at that court before the day for the weekly sessions was changed, and, as their worships very well knew, a more eonsciTtious and energetic magistrate could not possibly be. He would be greatly missed at Prescot.—Mr. GOE- sage said he had always found Mr. Evans to be a most able, judicious, and careful magistrate, and the Bench regretted his death exceedingly.
!LIBERAL MEETING AT FRODSHAM.

On Thursday evening a meeting of Liberals in the Frodsham polling district of the Eddisbury Division was held in Frsham Town Hall The room was. crowded. Mr. Slate' Lewis, of Debby, occupied the chair, and on the platform were Mr. R. Neville, M.P. for Liverpool, /dr. W. Abrams, M.P. for West Limerick; Messrs. J. Jeffs, Rhodes, and IL G. Lina- ker, and T. Handley, W. Handley, T. Clegg, and B. Rniveton, of Runcorn.

The Chairman, in a brief introductory speech, , said they were met to express sympathy with their fellow countrymen in Ireland. and also assembled.' for the purpose of showing their allegiance to that party which was so eloquently and so brillianaly espoused by that grand old man, Mr. Gladstone_ (Applause). Mr. J. Jeffs, in a suitable speech, moved the fol- lowing resolution :—That this meeting strongly pro- tests against the irritating and unjust policy of the Government in trampling upon the rights of our fellow subjects in Ireland assures the Irish people of its sympathy with them in their suffer- ings and struggles • and affirms its conviction that the scheme proposed by Mr. Gladstone for the settle- ment of the Irish question is just, reasonable, and safe." (Applause). Mr H. G. Linaker seconded the resolution, which. was put to the meeting and carried; only two hands were held up to the contrary. Alf Neville, M.P., then delivered a speech, in which he asked who was right and who was wrong at the last genre election with regard to Ireland. Mr Gladstone and the party who acted with him declared that there was ouly one alternative to Home Rule, and that was severe coercion. Tories and Liberal Unionists alike said this was untrue, and was an attempt to mislead the people. No sooner had the Tories got in 'Dower than they brought in a Coercion .Act, and the whole of last session was worse than wasted in passing that precious piece of legislation. The Liberal party were right when they said that Home Rule was the proper remedy hr the ills of Ireland, and that coercion would never prove to be a remedy. (Ap- plause.) Mr. W. Abrahams, M.P., also spoke at considerable length. It was, he said, a matter of history that the Irish party rendered to the Tory party at the General Election in 18&5 all the assistance they possibly could because the Tories had abandoned the policy of coercion, and because the Lord-Lieu- tenant, Lord Carnarvon. had entered into negotia- tions with the leader of the Irish party. The Irish electors did not succeed in returning the Tory party to power; and there came a right about face atroty.be(Afpopulnadus:. tinhathreecTaordryopf aarntyy osuthcehraspowlitiaseaniopt hMadr. pGrleasdesntteo nde ;a nwahlemno almost e fou n d unanimousthedelmrisahnd,pecoopnle- sidered the time had come to give legislative effect Ito their Wishes constitutionally expressed, and the result of that determination was a Home Rule Bill, which would not affect the unity of the Empire, or the supremacy of the Imperial Parliament, or inter- fere with the rights of the minority in Ireland. (Applause.) Mr. B. liniveton said they had a winning cause. Since the General Election there was not a single case where a Gladstonian had become Unionist, but on the other hand there where thousands who had left the ranks of the Unionists and come back to the Gladstonian fold. He moved a vote of thanks to the speakers. (Applause.) Mr. Rhodes seconded the motion, which was carried. Mr. Abrahams replied, and the proceedings con- cluded with a vote of thanks to the Chairman.

' RUNCORN UNION RURAL SANITARY AUTIIORITY.—A. fortnightly meeting M this Authosity was held on Tues- day, at the Workhouse, Dutton. There were present Colonel Ashton (chairman), Revs. J. Lockwood and .1..) W. N. Tanner; Messrs. Mclntyre, Parr, Brandreth, 1 Hadfteld, Stokes,?. Lewis, and H. Percival ; H. Linaker. (clerk), W. H. Llnriker (assistant clerk), Dr. Adams: (medical officer), and Farrinrrton (nuisance inspector). —A communication was read from the Local :Govern- ment Board, in which they enclosed a letter they had received from the Rev. J. H. Wilcockson with reference to the state of the roads at Weston Point. In his letter, Mr. Wilcockson said there had been a great deal of sick- ness in the village, and that he looked forward to the coming winter with dread if something was not done.— In the course of some discussion, it was stated by the clerk that the Highway Board repudiated any responsi- bility in connection with these roads. He added that it was a matter which should be taken up by the rate- payers of Weston Point. —Mr. Brandreth remarked that if the medical officer reported that there was a nuisance injurious to health, that Authority might take action.— The Assistant Clerk : You can make them abate the nuisance.—lt was agreed that the Local Government Board should be informed that the medical officer had been requested to -report as to the sanitary state of the I roads in question.—The Medical Offic6r reported that I there had been an outbreak of measles in the district at Aston and Weston. At Aston about twenty cases had occurred, and at Weston about forty cases. No death had taken place, and the disease appeared to be of a favourable character. The schools .in both townships had been closed on his recommendation. He further re- ported an outbreak of typhoid fever in Weston.—This was the principal business. RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.—A fortnightly meet- ing of this Board was held at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday. There were present Colonel Ashton (chair- man), the Revs. T. Lockwood and J. W. N. Tanner; Messrs. Mclntyre, Parr, Brandreth, Hadfield, Stokes, T. Lewis, H. Percival, Hamilton, Kirkham, Forster, T83401'; H. Linaker (clerk), and W. H.Linaker (assistant clerk).—. Th e Limerick Guardians: A communication was read romj the Dewsbury Board of Guardians in which the Runcorn Board of Guardians were asked to join with them in dis- approving of the action of the authorities in attempting to interfere with the proceedings at a recent meeting of the Limerick Board of Guardians, and in expressing a hope that directions would be given to prevent any similar attempt in future in the United Kingdom of in- terfering with the liberties and privileges of an elected body acting as the represerltatives of the people.—A Member: Where is Dewsbury? Is it in Ireland? (Laugh- ter.)—lt was agreed that the letter should be laid on the table.—The Asylums : On the motion of Mr. Mclntyre, the Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, Messrs. Taylor and Brand- reth and the clerk were deputed to visit the lunatics of the Union at the asylums.-21ft. noughton's Resignation : A letter was read from the collector, Mr.T. Houghton, in which he resigned his appointment as collector for the Union.—The Rev. J. Lockwood said there was not a single case in which they could bring home to the collec- tor any wrong dealing though he had certainly been very careless in the performance of his duties. He recom- mended that the resignation be accepted.—ln answer to a question, the Rev. J. Lockwood said the committee had gone through the whole of the outstanding liabilities with a few exceptions.—Mr. Hadfield said they under- stood that there had been £7OO in arrears, and he wished to know how much of that had been lost. —The Rev. J. Lockwood paid they would be able to supply that infor- mation in another fortnight.—Mr. Hadfield said con- sidering the way the collector had neglected his duties they ought not to let him come there and cooly resignl his position but ought rather to dismiss him.—The Rev. J. Lockwood said that not one-twentieth of the cases had fallen into arrears through the neglect of the collec- t tor. He proposed that the resignation be accepted.— Mr. Aaron seconded this proposal.—Mr. Hadfield pro- posed that the collector be dismissed.—Mr. Brand- reth asked if the . collector had not worked under any committee to which he ought to have reported.—The Rev. J. Lockwood: Brandreth said that had been going on for years, and the committee had not found it out, and he thought a motion of censure ought,to be passed on the •committee. (Hear, hear, and laughter.)—The Rev. J. Lockwood said 1 the Board from the chairman downwards was equally responsible.—Mr. Hadfield then withdrew his proposal, and the resignation was accepted.—This was all the I business of public interest. . . div.head: TREAT TO 'WIDNES SCHOLARS.
div.p: TREAT TO 'WIDNES SCHOLARS.

Twelve months ago Mr: G. H. Bolton, managing director of the Widnes Alkali Company, generously arranged for and defrayed the cost of sending 1,000 scholars to the Liverpool Exhibition, and again this week he has acted in a similar kind-hearted man- ner. On Thursday 800 elder children from the Wid- nes schools, and 200 from the Satkey and Penketh schools, were by Mr. Bolton's desire, and at his ex- pense conveyed to the Manchester Jubilee Exhibi- tion, and no distinction of party or creed was made. The Board schools supplied 300 children, the Catholic schools 300 children, and the National schools and St. Bede's, Ap- pleton, schools 100 each; and the remainder of the chil- I dren were from the Sankey and Penketh schools. Advan- tage was taken of the occasion to send 100 children from Farnworth Church schools, their expenses being defrayed by Mr. C. E. Barlow, of -the Widnes Alkali Company's works. In addition to these numbers 1,400 other children and grown-up persons travelled by the two special trains arranged for and included the choir of Ditton Parish Church, who for, at the expense of Mr. Joseph Long- ton, of Ditchfield , Hall. A greatly reduced fare was charged. The journey was safely accomplished by about eleven o'clack, and the youngsters spent a. most happy time in viewing the wonders exposed to their gaze. Order and control was obtained by placing one teacher in care of ten children, and the affair passed off without a hitch. Ample refreshments were provided by Mr. Bolton. The Wichies contingent arrived home at half-past eight, but the Farnworth aud Hough Green party were delayed on the return journey, and did not arrive at their destination until nearly ten O'clock.

ACCIDENT TO A DonLIN STEAMER.—The London and North-Western Company's steamer Alexandra, which carries cargo and third-class passengers, did not arrive in Dublin on Thursday morning though due shortly After midnight. It was reported soon afterwards at the North Wall that when 13 miles outside Holyhead on Wednesday night a huge sea struck the Alexandra and disabled her. One passenger was killed and several persons badly in- jured. The steamer put back to Holyhead, and the in- jured were taken to the hospital. The other passengers arrived safely in Dublin on Thursday morning by the steamer Banshee.
THE WITCH'S FATE.
A CRITEL PREJUDICE OF OLD TIMES MORE THAN EQUALLED Now.

Not many decades ago in this country the people were excited over witchcraft. Persons suspected were thrown into the water; if not witches they would drown; if they were witches, they would swim ashore, and would be put to death! In any event, they were, doomed! Not many years ago if a person were taken sick with advanced disorder of the kidneys, the physician would pronounce the disease Bright's disease, and when so declared, he regarded his responsibility at an end, for medical authority admitted that the disease was incur- able. When the physician found a patient thus afflicted, he would say, "Oh, a slight attack of the kidneys; will be all right ma little while." He knew to the contrary. But if he could keep his patient on his hands for a few months, he knew he would derive a great revenue from his case, and then, when the disease had progressed to a certain stage, he would state the facts and retire, ex- onerated from all blame. But the error of supposing the disease incurable has , swayed the public mind long after the fact has ceased to I be. But public opinion has been educated to the true' status of the case by those who have discounted the incurability theory, and the public recognises and testi- fies to the fact that Warner's SAP& Cure is a specific for this disease. This has been shown with thousands of testimonials. Upon referring to them in our files we find that £I,OOO reward will be given to anyone who can prove that so far as the manufacturers know they are not genuine, and that hundreds of thousands similar in character could be published if it were necessary. This condition of things is very amusing to the jour- nalist, who looks upon all sides of every question. Proof should be accepted by all, but prejudice fights proof for many years. It seems strange that when a proprietaFy medicine is doing the good that Warner's SAFI§ Cure is, that the physicians do not publicly endorse it. Many of them, we are told, privately prescribe it. A few years ago as stated, when a man had Bright's disease, the doctor boldly announced it, because he thought it relieved him of responsibility. To-day when prominent people are dying (and hun- dreds of thousands of common people die of the same disease), we are told that doctors disguise the fact that it is Bright's disease of the kidneys, and say that they die of paralysis, of apoplexy, of pneumonia, of consumpi. tion, of general debility of rheumatism, of heart dis- ease, of blood poisoning, or some other of the names of the direct effects of kidney disease. They are not the real disease We sometimes wonder if they avoid stating the real cause of disease for fear they will drive the public into patronage of the only scientific proprietary specific for kidney diseases and the thousand and one diseases that originate in inactive kidneys. We do not believe every advertisement we read. Some people perhaps may regard this article as an advertise- ment, and will not believe it, but we are candid enough to say that we believe the parties above-mentioned have stated their case and proved it; and under such circum- stances the public is unwise if it is longer influenced by adverse prejudice.—The Church Review, August 28.

TRAVELLING WITHOUT TicKgr.—Flarriet Louisa Banks, described as a domestic servant, of 28, Angel-street, Manchester, was charged with having been drunk, and with having travelled in a third-class carriage on the London and North-Western Railway, from Manchester to warrinqton, on the previous day, without having paid her fare. It was stated that on the arrival of the 1-2 p.m. train from Manchester at Bank Quay Station, pri- soner was found to be drunk in a carriage, and, as she had no ticket, she was placed under arrest. A soldier was travelling in the same carriage, and prisoner said that he had obtained a ticket for her, but this he denied. She also said that she was sober when she en- tered the train, but the soldier had given her some whis- key. The Bench ordered her to pay- the fare, or go to prison for seven days in default of so doing.
