Runcorn were a man short, but, on the other hand, the home team were with- out the services of T. Larkin, whose place at half back was filled by a younger brother from the second team. The game was pleasantly contested, and both teams played with great spirit and dash. Litherland, however, managed to outstay the visitors. For Runcorn A. Bassendale, at full back, played a fine game, his kicking, against the wind, too, being something to remember. The game at the call of time was—Litherland four tries and five minors to Runcorn A one minor. PARR RANGERS V. ST. ALBAN'S (WARRINGTON.)—These teams met for the first time at Warrington, on Saturday. The visitors set the ball in motion, but it was returned, _
, and Joseph Greensll got possession'and made a good run which resulted in a minor. After this the home team rushed play to the visitors 25, where several scrimmages

took place. The visitors' forwards were, however, t'oo good for the home team, and they rushed the ball to half way, where a scrimmage took place. F. Beach, the visitors' half-back, got hold, and made a pass to Green- all, who made a splendid attempt to, drop at goal, the ball just missing the post. On turning, the Rangers made matters more lively, and the game resulted as fol- lows—St. Albans, one disputed try; Rangers, three minors.

WIDNES V. TOTTINGTON.—Over 2,000 spectators wit- nessed the meeting of these clubs on the Widnes ground on Saturday, and great was the surprise of the Totting- tonians when they were defeated by one goal, one try, and five minors, to five minors. Hitherto this season Tottington had been most successful, having only been beaten by one clubCastleford. On Saturday, however, they were beaten on their merits. They played a smart game, both offensive and defensive; They the brilliant tactics of the home men overcame all opposition, and both forward and behind they had to admit—and they admitted it with the best grace possible—that they had met more than their match, and this even when Widnes were , shorthanded, Kiddie, Morris, and Fogg being absent. Hughes and Gandy, both fine forward players, secured the tries, and Farrell placed the goal. The play was fast and exciting throughout. For the winners, Far- rell, Parkinson, Plumpton, Smith, Hughes, Gandy, and Hardman, and for Tottin,,vton Coop and Worthington played a fine game. Teams—Widnes : S.Bingham, back; Plumpton, Parkinson, and Barker, three-quarter backs; Farrell and Howard, half backs; Smith (captain), Hughes, Woods, Gandy, Barber, J. Bingham, T. Wilkin- son, T. Pennington,- and Hardman, forwards. Totting- ton :,Coop, back, Worthington, Mallelieu, and P. Barlow, three-quarter backs; Fogg and Fletcher, half backs; spencer, Smethurst, Nobb, Walker, Green, Holt, Wilkin- son, and Casey, forwards.

iIINCOILN i:MANNINGHAM.—The first encounter be- tween these organizations took place on the ground of the former on Saturday, about 2,000 spectators ast.sembl- ing. Both teams were minus several of their regular players. Only two thirties were played, on account of the visitors having to return by an early train. The home team won the toss, and Holmes kicked off, Woods returning, but Newton retaliated with a punt into the home 25. Scrimmaging was the order of the day for some time, until good footwork by the Runcornites car- ried hostilities to the centre, where Moxon kicked .to

Woods, and following up well, tackled the latter in his own 25 before he could return. Before the game had proceeded ten minutes Clarkson fell heavily and broke his collar-bone, and the visitors played fourteen men after that period. W9ods, by a strong punt, transferred play into Manningham quarters, where M`Donald got possession and ran finely, but an erratic pass nullified his efforts. The Runcornites now carried the game by a series of short rushes into the visitors' 25, where they pressed Manningham for some time, but the fine tackling of the latter's forwards prevented the home team from scor- ing. After a lot of scrimmaging, time was called with the game in the centre, and a very uninteresting match re- sulted pointless. The home team s,howed their dissatis- faction with the referee's decision on various points of the game. For Runcorn Faulkner played a dashing game, and put in a few capital runs, whilst his tackling was worthy of commendation. The Brothers Hughes, Clarke, and Speakman showed up remarkably well. Teams :—Runcorn T. Woods, back; H. Cawley, H. C. Speakman, and W. Riley, three-quarter-backs; H. Hughes (captain) and H. G. Andrews, half-backs; W. Wright, W. Hughes, J. Clarke. J. Hoffland, G. Gatley, J. Lewis, W. Faulkner, W. H. Beady, and Carr, for- wards. Manningham : W. Robinson, back; H. Noble, J. Newton and F. Robinson, three-quarter-backs; R. Pocock ind W. H. Pickard, half-backs; E. Holmes (captain), A. Clarkson, C. Calvert, W. Gill, H. Moxon, W. Midgley, J. WDonald, If. Pawson„ and T. Milner, forwards.

WARRINGTON v.'BROUGHTON (" A '') TEAMS.) This match was played on the new ground, Wilderspool Causeway, on Saturday, in fine weather, before about 2,500 spectators. Broughton brought a very strong team with them including Deane, and Jordan (Lancashire county), and it was generally thought that Warrington would lose, but this was not the case, as the home team played a grand combined game, beating their opponents at every point. The home captain won the toss, and Deane kicked off for Broughton at 3-30, play resting in Wfrrington quarters, owing to Randalls failing to re- turn. The home forwards went away with a dribble, Deane saving by kicking into touch. Some give and take play ensued, when Whittle secured the ball from a scrimmage and passed to Antrobus, who threw to Evans, this player kicking to Dennett, who sent the ball into touch in the Broughton 25. Dennett next got possession but he was charged off the ball as he was kicking, and Nevins picked up and to the forwards, who dribbled near the line, Deane kicking dead. Antrobus returned the drop-out, and Deane be- ing collared before he could return, play res- ted in Broughton quarters. A good run by Evans brought about a scrimmage near the visitors' lines, vim had again to touch down. Immediately after the drop- out, Antrobus passed to Evans, who made a short run and passed to Daniels, the latter player being pushed into touch by Dennett. Whittle next passed to Evans, who made a long kick, Dennett returning into touch, The Warrington forwards broke away from the line-out, and play raged in the visitors' 25, when Whittle passed to Molyneaux, who ran through his opponents, and when near the line passed to Nevins, who had no difficulty in placing the ball behind the posts, Isherwood kicking a nice goal. Deane kicked off, Evans returning well, and the home scrimmagers improved matters by a good drib- ble. Some fast and exciting play was now witnessed, both lots of backs playing grandly. Good passing be-

tween Whittle, Antrobus, and Evans forced Smith to touch down. Molyneaux charged down the drop-out, and the home forwards worked the ball down to the visitors' goal line, but Robertshaw, Lombard, and Lodge relieved to centre, Evans saving. Isherwood was next con- spicuous by a long kick, Smith returning into touch. An- trobus now passed to Whittle who threw across to Apple- ton, but Jordan intercepted and kicked to centre. From the line out Antrobus put in a nice run and passed to Daniels, who was brought down by Jordon. Hackett and Randalls broke away from the scrimmage and took play to near the visitors line, but Robertshaw, by a beautiful dribble, brought the ball back again, and Ap- pleton having his kick charged down caused play to be located in the home 25. The home forwards, however, soon removed the danger, and from the line out, near the Broughton quarter flag, Nevins passed to Appleton, who dropped at goal, a minor resulting. Dennett dropped out and Antrobus returned, and Nevins gaining pos- session from a kick by one of the visiting backs put in a good run, being tackled near the line. Gregory passed nicely to Dennett, who kicked into touch. Isherwood, Eyes, and Hayes retaliated with a beautiful dribble, and Whittle giving Evans a chance this player dropped at goal, a 'lead ball being registered. Half-time being called, the score stood—Warrington, 1 goal and 4 minor points to Broughton nil. In the second half Warrington still had the upper hand, tries being obtained by Nevins and Daniels, and won a splendid game by 1 goal, 2 tries, and 10 minors to I minor. Teams :—Warrington: Full back, Jolley; three-quarter backs, Daniels, Evans and Appleton; half backs, Whittle (captain) and Antrobus; forwards, Molyneaux Hayes, Craghan, Eyes, Hackett, Nevins, Randalls, Donohue, and Isherwood. Broughton: Full back, A. E. Smith; three-quarter backs, Jordan, Den- nett, and Deane (captain) • half backs, Gregory knd Sumner; forwards Break-riell, Dixon, Lodge, Robert- shaw, Goodby, Ilpsford, Lombard, Race, and Glen- dinning.

div.head: 111 E EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 29, 1887.
div.p: 111 E EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 29, 1887.

The match at Runcorn, on Saturday, presented at least one unique feature. During the hour the occupied not even a single minor point was to show how the battle had gone. Early in the game Clarkson had the misfortune to break his collar bone, and Manning- ham had afterwards to play 14 men. Perhaps this fact explains why they kept the ball so close, and prevented that fast, open game in which Runcorn always shine. Runcorn, however, had very hard lines not to score at least three tries. The presence of Davies and Wain- wright in their usual positions would, no doubt, have made a difference in the result, and we trust these ster- ling players will turn up against "Old Boys " to-day. At the same time the Manningham defence was very strong; and every credit is due to them for saving a defeat.

Widnes were in 'winning form on Saturday, and cleverly amounted for Tottington. The number of spec- tators present was above the average, and their delighti at the fine display of both backs and forwards of the home team was unbounded. Plumpton came out of his shell, and gave a sterling exhibition at centre three quarter, and Farrell and Parkinson played a dashing game. The combination and speed of the forwards was a fine feature, and the honour of scoring the tries be- longs to this division of the team.

div.head: WAIMMGTON V. BROUGHTON.
div.p: WAIMMGTON V. BROUGHTON.

This match was played at Broughton on Saturday, be- fore a fair attendance of spectators. A large number journeyed from Warrington to witness their favourites play, and the day being exceptionally fine a good match was anticipated. They were not disappointed, as the game was stubbornly contested from start to finish, the passing and dribbling being fine, the ball travelling with great rapidity from goal to goal. The home team were indeed lucky to win, as they took the only opportunity that was afforded them, through a piece of poor play on the part of Buxton. The visitors experienced hard lines on several occasions, and the shots at goal by Barnes and Massey, and the mistake made by the last-named, who ran to the line and dropped on the wrong sidq when a try was certain, were very unfortunate. The Broughton team were strengthened by the addition of Ashton, of the Broughton Rangers, whilst Moss,of International renown, also figured in their ranks. The visitors mustered their full strength. Barnes having won the toss, Flowers, as captain of the Broughton team, set the ball in motion, and play was taken to the Broughton territory. From the first scrimmage Rome passed nicely to Flowers, who ran the ball back to centre, Massey bringing him down in grand style. Exchange kicking by Barnes, Buxton, and Kneen settled play at centre, and a movement was star- ted here in which Moss, Evans, and Ashton were promi- nent. the leather going over the line, Massey saving by kicking dead. On the drop out the visitors' forwards followed up well, and prevented a return, and W. Dillon, Ashton, and Fair. Turner took the leather over the Broughton line, Kneen saving. Flowers dropped out, and Buxton returned between quarter-flags. Jolley kicked to the Broughton line, where Evans made his mark, but assisted his side little. Pretty passing by Prince and Mowers relieved the pressure. Speakman stopped a rush of the Broughton forwards in grand style, but they kept up the attack on the Warrington citadel. Flowers got over from some 100 le play, but this was disallowed. The leather was brought back, and from the subsequent scrimmage formed Flowers made his mark from a pass of Warren's, but this availed little. Speakman here passed to Barnes, and the latter trans- ferred to Massey, who replied with a huge punt to the Broughton lines. The home team retaliated to centre field, and Fair. Turner tried hard to get away, but was well held by Arnold. A good kick by Massey again placed the Broughton lines in jeopardy, but Kneen saved his lines from disaster, only a minor resulting. Wormald re-started, and Arnold checked a movement in which Littlewood, Davies, and W. Dillon were conspicuous. Prince, by h timely kick to centre, was well backed up , by a neat dribble by Evans to the Warrington quarter ' flag.; but Povey ' replied by dribbling back to centre. Splendid passing by both teams was loudly applauded, ' and shortly afterwards Barnes was to be seen threading his way through the Broughton ranks, Flowers just hold- ing him in the nick of time. A scrimmage being formed at Quarter flag, Speakman secured possession and passed , to Barnes. who made a splendid bid for goal, the ball 't grazing the posts on the outside' a minor-only resulting. Barnes returned the drop out to Broughton 25, and , Flowers was forced to concede another minor. Flowers _ _ _

restarted. and Barnes again replied to the Broughton lines, and when half time was called it was found that Warrington had scored four minors to Broughton one minor. Frank Turner restarted, and play settled for a time at centre field. A pass by Rome to Prince was spoiled by Jolley, the ball finally rolling in touch in Broughton territory. A good pass was made by Barnes to Massey, who, in trying to score, fell on the wrong side of the line when grounding the ball. The visitors' forwards, by a combined rush, took the leather over, Rome conceding a minor. Kneen dropped out, and the Broughton men took the game Ito the Warrington lines. A free kick by Kneen was returned with interest by Barnes, and a series of scrimmages formed here. Wormald passed neatly to Flowers, and this player taking off at high speed, eluded the opposing backs, and a try seemed inevitable, when Massey racing up just managed to kick the ball dead as both went over the line. Wormald replied to the kick out, and from a scrimmage shortly afterwards formed at centre, Moss made a gdod run to the Warrington centre, but Flowers put in a big punt to the Warrington lines, and the home team forwards following up well com- pletely baffied Buxton' and Rome was thus enabled to score the highest point in the game. Arnold failed at a difficult place. Notwithstanding this reverse the visitors played up with renewed' vigour, and from the recom- mencement of hostilities they kept up a continual siege on the home team lines. Jolley tried hard to get away, but all the visitors' efforts to score a tangible point were fruitless, and when no side was called, Warrington had to retire defeated by one try and two minors to six minors. On the Warrington side Barnes WB:4, indeed, the shin- ing light, and if he continues in the same form as Satur- day last higher laurels are certainly in store for him. Of the remaining three-quarters Massey put in some useful work, while Jolley had little to do. Buxton lost what merit he gained through the misfortune in the second half. The halves have certainly been seen to better ad- vantage. The forwards worked hard, and if special mention ought to be made none are more deserving than W. Dillon, Ashton, and Fair. Turner. On the Broughton side Flowers put in some useful work, whilst Kneen was particularly safe at hack. Of the halves Rome was cer- tainly the pick. The forwards were a strong lot, and neither side could claim an advantge, though in the home team ranks Evans, Ashton, and Smith deserve special mention. The teams were as follows :—Warrington : J. Bux- ton, back; J. Jolley, T. Barnes, and J. T. Massey. three quarters; J. E. Warren and W. Speakman, half backs: Fair. Turner, Frank Turner, Ashton, T. Davies, J. Rigby, W. Dillon, R. Littlewood, W. Povey, and E. Dillon, forwards. Broughton: J. Kneen, back; F. Prince, E. Flowers, and J. F. Arnold, three quarters C, Rome and W. Tolson, half backs • A. E. Evans, F. Wor- maid, P. Lodge, J. Wall, J. Jackson, J. G. Smith, M. Ashworth, J. Ashton, and F. S. Moss, forwards. Um- pires, R. Mudie and E. Gilbert. Referee, A. M. Crook (Free Wanderers). WEST LANCASHIRE AND BORDER TOWNS RUGBY UNION.

A meeting of the committee of this Union was held on Friday evening at the Goat Hotel, Peter's-lane, Liver- pool. The following clubs were represented :—Wigan Rovers, Ince Conservative, Liverpool Hornets, Aspull, Widnes, St. Helen? 4th L.A.V., Widnes St. Mary's, St. 'Helens Recreation, Warrington, Litherland, Tyldesley, Blundellsands, &c. The principal busine.ss of the gather- ing was the draw for the Junior Cup, the first round of which must be completed on or before the sth of Novem- ber. The clubs were drawn in the following order, the first-named in each case having choice of ground Silverwell Hornets v. Low Green. Referee, H. Varley. —lnce Conservative Athletic v. Standish. Referee, J. J. M`Laughlin. Scot-lane v. Biekershaw Old Boys. Referee, C. Lewis.—Goose Green v. Lowe House True Blues. Referee, J. J. Latham.--Chorley v. Highfield. Referee, F. C. Davis. Firs-lane (Leigh) v. Standish North End, Referee, A. M'Laughlin.—Wigan Rovers v. Woodman Rovers. Referee, J. Gregson.—West Leigh v. Platt Bridge. Referee, J. Fowles.—St. Mark's (St. Helens) v. Poolstock.—Liverpool Hornets v. Liverpool South End.—Blundellsands v. New Brighton Olympic. Referee, W. Ireland..St.Cleopas's v. 4th L.A.V. Referee, R. L. Jackson.—Widnes Hornets v. Warrington St. Paul's. Referee, T. Egan, senr.—Bank Quay Free Wanderers v. Widnes St. Mary's. Referee, C. Sims.— Sutton v. Sankey (Warrington.) Referee, S. H. Ken- drick. Widnes Recreation v. Wycliffe. Referee, R. Crompton.—Lymm v. Warrington Hornets. Referee, C. Pownall.—Farnworth v. Runcorn Recreation. Referee, C. R. Adamson.—Widnes True Blues v. Altrincham. Referee, T. Barnes. senr.—Walton, a bye,—lt NM stated that in all probability the Union will play Westmorland at Wigan on November 21st.

div.head: NOTES BY THE WAY.
div.p: NOTES BY THE WAY.

A hitch has arisen in regard to the Runcorn v. Brad- ford fixture. It appears that when Bradford were in the South last season, Guys Hospital were arranging a Northern tour for this winter, and the secretary of the Bradford club gave them a:fixture for November 19th. Forgetting this circumstance, Bradford club agreed with Mr. Langshaw for Runcorn to visit Yorkshire on the same date. Bradford have, however, been released from their awkward dilemma by Runcorn gracefully. giving way; but the encounter between the teams will take place on a Wednesday not yet decided upon..

div.head: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL
div.p: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL

A meeting of this Council was held at the Town Hall on Tuesday evening, for the purpose of wind- ing up the business of the municipal year. The Mayor (Alderman Pickmere) presided, and there were also present Aldermen Harrison, Holmes, Burgess, Davies, Chandley, Sutton, Crostield, and Webster; Councillors Greening, Jolley, Francomb, Barker, Dixem, H. Roberts, Heaton, J. V. Taylor, Wright, Ashton, Fleming, Tinsley, Platt, Marsh, J. Taylor, W. Pierpoint, Greenall, and Belton; Messrs. Brook (town clerk), Whittle (deputy town clerk), and Chorley (borough treasurer). WATCH COMMITTES.-THE PLACES OF EINTHRkAINMENT.

The minutes of the Watch Committee contained the following :—Report of the Borough Surveyor and the Chief Constable, that they had examined all the places of amusement in the Borough, as requested by the COlll- - Resolution: That the report be approved, and that the Town Clerk forward to. the owners of the dif- ferent buildings the several recommendations contained in the report.—The minutes also referred to the annual report of the Chief Constable, which we give in another column.

The MAYOR moved, and Alderman HARRISON seconded. the adoption of the report. The MAYOR remarked that the Chief Constable, in company with the Borough Surveyor, reported on the various places of amusement in the borough, and with a few slight alterations they considered them perfectly safe in case of panic or fire. Councillor FLEMING asked what places of amusement were mentioned in the report. The MAYOR said the Theatre and Public Hall were re- ferred to.
Councillor FLamisu thought they ought also to have a report as to places where concerts and other gatherings were held.

The MAYOR : They are not licensed premises. Councillor FLEnNo asked if it was not possible to deal with them. He was in the League Hall the other night, and he thought it was a very dangerous place, and there were other places in as bad or worse condition. . .
The MAYOR : We can suggest in those cases, but we cannot interfere with them.

Councillor FLiamiNo said there were perhaps some churches in the town which needed looking to. (Laugh- ter.) The MAYOR: The Town Clerk says we cannot. The minutes were then confirmed. FINANCE COMMITTEE.
The Finance Conimittoe recommended that a sum of thirty guineas be paid to the borough auditors for auditing the treasurer's accounts for the year ending 25th March, 1887.

Alderman ;Imams, in moving the confirmation of the minutes, said that at the meeting held on the previous day a vote of thanks was accorded to Councillor Brown for his services during the past year, and they were anxious that that fact should be included in the minutes of the municipal year now expiring. It would be pleasant information to know that Councillor Brown had very much improved in health, and that he was continu- ing his services in auditing the accounts. He could not attend at the offices, but he did the work at home. (Hear, hear.) Councillor GREENING seconded the motion, which was agreed to.

div.head: STREET IMPROVEMENT AND LIGHTING conruirrEE.
div.p: STREET IMPROVEMENT AND LIGHTING conruirrEE.

The Street Improvement Committee recommended that plans of the following buildings be approved :—Eight houses in Knutsford-road, for Mr. E. Jameson; new vestry to Emmanuel Church, Bold-street; and four houses in Lovely-lane, for Mr. John Appleton; and "that the sum of £l5 be paid to Mr. John Wainwright for a small plot of land m front of his premises in Wilders- pool-causeway." It was also resolved that the best thanks of the committee be given to Mr. Councillor Platt for his services as chairman of the committee during the past year. _
Orithe motion of Councilor PLATT, seconded by Coun- cillor GREENING, the thinutes were adopted.
SANITARY COMMITTEE:

This committee recommended that the tender of the Warrington Slate Company Limited, to supply 6,000 blue bricks at 42s 3d per 1,600, be accepted. There was ,also a resolution on the minutes that the committee visit and report upon the Longford and intercepting de- pots at an early date, and another resolution to the effect that the best thanks of the committee be giveri to Mr. Alderman Burgess for his able and valuable services as chairman of the committee during the past year. The return for the quarter ending Ist October, of the medical officer of health was also contained in the minutes. It stated that during the quarter under notice there were reported under the Notification Act, 133 cases of infec- tious disease, as compared with 35 cases in the corres- pozding quarter of 1886, and 726 and 374 in the first and second quarters of the present year. Scarlet fever, which had only been observed in one instance in the previous part of the year, was reported to have attacked 33 persons during the recent quarter. Locally the disease showed the greatest prevalence in the east part of the town, Manchester-road and Battersby-lane sup- plying the largest proportion of cases. Of the 33 cases reported to the Health Department, 30 cases, or 90 per cent, were removed to the hospital." "Calculated on the estimated population of the borough at the middle of this year, the death rate was equal to 18.7 per 1,000, as compared with 21-7 the average rate in the third quarters of the previouS five years. The mean death rate for the same period in the 28 large English town's is 203." On the motion of Alderman Burrows, seconded by Alderman SUTTON, the minutes were passed. . PAVING AND SEWERAGE COMMITTEE.

This committee recommended -as- follows :—That the tender of Messrs. Clare and Ridgway for the supply of 20,000 chequered tiles at 68s 10d per 1,000 be accepted. That the tender of Mr. Thomas Pilkington to supply horses, carts, and drivers at 6s 5d per day, and his ten- der to cart materials from Bank Quay Wharf and other places, according to schedule of distances, be accepted. That the best thanks of the committee be given to Mr. Alderman Davies for his services as chairman of this committee during the past year. The committee are pleasoa to learn that Mr. Councillor Brown is recovering from his long illness, and hope that he will soon be able to resume his position as a member of the committee. Alderman DAVIEg moved and Councillor Wniener seconded the confirmation of the minutes. The MAYOR said he was sure they were all glad to hear that Councillor Brown was improving after his dangerons illness. (Hear, hear.) , The minutes were adopted. THE FREE LIBRARY QUESTION.—PROPOSAL BY THE COMMITTEE. At a meeting of the Museum and Library Committee held on the 14th October, it was resolved that the best thanks of this Conimittee be given to Mr. William Rob- son for his gift of a portrait of his brother, Mr. Thomas Robson, the artist, painted by Crosier. A loan was re- ported of Chinese and Japanese embroidery from Mrs. Charles Holme, Hampstead. It was resolved that Messrs. W. Owen and J. E. Worsley be requested to report as to the best way of disposing for exhibition, or otherwise, of the tiles from St. Austin's Friary; that Messrs. T. G. Ryland.% Joseph Davies, and Robert Pierpoint be appoin- ted a Sub-Committee to consider and report upon the resolutions referred to this Committee from the Council respecting the lending of books without charge, and that they be empowered to call in Messrs. Thomas Morris and Frederick Monks to act on the Sub-Com- mittee. The Committee also reported as to the free library question. In this report they stated that--" It is in the first place desirable that it should be clearly understood that the Acts of Parliament do not require the establishment of a Free Lending Library, and that the establishment of a library at all is only one of the purposes to which the penny rate may be applied within the discretion of the Town Council, to whom the general management, regulation, and control of the institutions are entrusted. There is this condition attached in the Acts, viz., that the admission to such libraries and museums shall be free to the public, which condition has always been fully complied with here. The institutions, all or any of which may be supported by the penny rate, are libraries, museums, and schools of science and art." Having referred to the case of the Wigan library the Committee went on V) say , "With every desire on our part to make the Library absolutely free to borrowers, we are of opinion that the sum produced by the penny rate, which would be the only certain income, is not large enough at present to justify such a course, and that to adopt that course in present circumstances would entail immediate indebted- ness, followed by the necessity of applying to Parliament for powers to levy a higher rate. It has b..n suggested that the payment of the annual or quarterly subscrip- tions is beyond the means of many of the inhabitants. With a view to affording the greatest possible facilities for the use of the Library, we propose as an experiment to lend out books to ratepayers or inhabitants of the municipal borough at a charge of one penny per book under the usual safeguards and arrangements in use at the Free Lending Libraries in other towns. In other

respects the same rules will apply to there borrovrers as to the subscribers of Is. 6d. a quarter, or Ss. a year, or any larger amounts. We further propose that persons not being ratepayers or inhabitants shall pay double the above rates. We hope that at no distant time the income from the penny rate (which has been,' however, station- ary for the last seven years) may so increase that the Lending Library may, with safety and certainty, become absolutely free; but, in the meantime, we trust that the plan proposed will work satisfactorily, and will approach as nearly as possible to the desires expressed at the vari- ous public meetings which have considered the question. —(Signed) T. G. RYLAND% JOSEPH Bevies, F. MoNks, THOMAS MORRIS, ROBERT nERPOINT." It was resolved that the best thanks of the Committee be given to Mr. Beamont for his services as president during the year. Aldenhan WEBSTER, in moving the confirmation of the ' minutes of the above committee, referred to a presenta- tion to the Art Gallery of a portrait of Mr. Thomas Rob- son the donor being Mr. William Robson. It was a peculiar pleasure to him to have to make the announce- ment that night, because it was his great honour to an- nounce to the Council the gift of a large number of por- traits and other works of art which had been painted by Mr. Thomas Robson, the artist. Alluding to the ques- tion of a Free Lending Library, Alderman Webster said that after a very long examination of the question, and the holding of several meetings, the Sub-Committee agreed unanimously to the report which appeared on the agenda paper. The report went into the matter very fully, and showed clearly that it would be impossible with their present income to provide a Free Lending Library. The first paragraph in the report clearly showed what he thought had been altogether misunder- stood by those who had advocated a Free Lending Li- brary. It had been urged over and over again that every ratepayer in the borough had a legal right to have books lent to him to comply with the provisions of the Act of Parliament. The fact was that there was 1, not a single syllable in the Act of Parliament authorising in any shape or way the free lending of books out of any library; and the Attorney-General I said in his few remarks in the House of Commons— which had been dignified by the name of an" opinion" I —that it might be considered quite questionable whether the lending of books at all was legal. However, there was no condition attached to the Acts, witb the excep- tion that the libraries and museums should be free to the public. That was the only condition, and that con- dition had always been observed in Warrington. The admission to the library was free; there had been no charge made and the books were there. The whole matter was fixity gone into in the report, and the Coun- cil would see exactly how the matter stood at present. The committee fully sympathised with the desire that there should be a free lending library—(hear, hear)—and it was quite possible that in the course of a little time, when the income and the rate increased, and so on, that that might become feasible; but at the present time matters were very far from that stage. Their means were limited, and would barely meet all their expendi- ture. They did manage to keep up the institution itself, which, he was proud to say, was one that was generally admitted, by all parties that passed through it, to be one worthy of the borough, as well as a credit to the county itself, and there were very few similar institu- tions that were better managed, or were in a better state of preservation. (Hear, hear.) Alderman Strrrost seconded the proposal that the minutes be adopted. He was very pleased to think that they had that report of the Museum Committee presented to them that night, and also to think that the long-pend- ing question as to the library would be settled for at least some time to come.

Alderman Weasnot said hetshould just like to add that the report had been agreed to unanimously not only by members of the committee, but also by the two gentle- men who were invited by the committee to confer with them—Mr. Morris and Mr. Monks. Alderman Surrox continuing, said he had no doubt everybody in Warrington would be glad when they were in a position to make that a free lending library. It only showei the necessity of everybody making themselves acquainted with what they had to say on a subject of that kind as to the legality or illegality of conducting the library in the way it had been done. It appeared from what had been said and from that report that they had not been acting illegally. He thought it would be better for any one who objected to the library existing as it is, instead of speaking so dictatorially to the com- mittee who had every desire to conduct the library in a proper manner and to the satisfaction and benefit of the town, to go carefully into the question before making attacks on the committee. Ile hoped they should soon have the library made into a free lending library, but he was sure that the arrangement proposed by the com- mittee was likely to be satisfactory to everybody. (Hear, hear.) Councillor W. PIIMPOINT supported the minutes Of the committee, but at the same time he wished to take ex- ception to a sentence that fell from the lips of Alderman Sutton when he said that the gentlemen who had been actively working in the direction of making the library free hadspoken in a dictatorial way to the Museum Com- mittee. It would no doubt be a great deal better if every one of them would examine carefully into a question be- fore they Ventured to speak upon it, and he, as a member of the Museum Committee, who had not taken that active interest in their work that he ought to have done, must say that when he came to examine the accounts of the committee and found that they had commenced their year with a credit balance at the bank and finished it with a debit balance, he thought they had been guilty of doing something no committee ought to be allowed to do in the town of Warrington. (Hear, hear.) He was afraid the same thing applied to Other committees. (Hear, hear.) They would see at the end Of the agenda a motion Which stood in his name with regard to the library, but if that report of the committee was adopted it would do away with the necessity of his moving that resolution. Councillor DIXON said that he was sure that there were many people in Warrington who would not be satisfied until there was a Free Lending Library in the town. They had got it in Widnes and other towns, and he could net see why they should not have it in a town like Warrington. It was necessary that children should be well educated. Those who had to move about in a manu- facturing district knew the importance of having the young people educated, and it would be of great advan- tage if they could have books to read at home. Councillor WRIGHT said it was with peculiar pleasure that he supported the adoption of the minutes and the report. He had always been in favour of a Free Lend- ing Library, providing that the rates of the borough would justify it, but he maintained that they could not afford to add anything to the rates. The rates were al- ready high enough. Why he said that he had peculiar pleasure in supporting the resolution was because it was exactly what he had said before to a particular friend of his. This friend sent inquiries to various people in the town asking them for an expression of their views, and his (Councillor Wright's) expression was that if the working-men of Warrington desired a book they might pay a penny for it in the same manner as the poor people paid a penny for their medicine at the Infirmary. He thought that the committee had come to a very wise Conclusion. Councillor H. ROYIEIITS said that he also was pleased with the manner in which the Museum Committee had met those who were advocating a Free Lending Library. At the same time he thought that had it not been for the agitation, and the pressure that agitation had brought to bear upon the committee, they would not have had evi- dence as early as they had had of a distinct change of tone on behalf of the committee in regard to the pro- posal. He accepted the proposal, because in the report there were two or three sentences which led them to hope for something better. The report showed that the com- mittee had a desire to make the Library absolutely free, and that they hoped that, at no distant time, the income from the penny rate would be sufficient. He looked upon that as almost tantamount to a pledge that the Library Committee would take the earliest opportunity of making the Library free in every sense of the word. He thought that everyone, considering the financial con- ditions, would be quite prepared to accept the report, in the hope that the offer would not be very distant in its accomplishment. Alderman HARRISON said that bp di a mit think that Mr. Roberts was quite correct in saying that the para- graph alluded to in the report, which gave him satisfac- tion, was the outcome of the agitation which had been created in favour of a Free Lending Library. As a mem- ber of the committee, he could assure Mr. Roberts that there had never been anything else but a desire on the part of the committee to comply with the request of the gentlemen who had moved in the matter. Vie commit- tee were also in favour of a Free Lending Library, and the only difficulty that met them was the one of funds. This was not the outcome of the agitation at all, but the voluntary wish and desire of the Museum, Library, and Arts Committee. Perhaps it might to some extent modify the asperity of some of those gentlemen who had ',been so strongly opposed to a charge being made for 'books, when he assured them that out of that fund the Library had been sustained in the acquisition of new books, and that the rates proper in this respect had not been touched upon. If that system was kept up for a few years longer the Library would be enlarged without having been in the slightest degree oppressive to the ratepayers of Warrington. Councillor Bovrox said that he should like it to be known that he had always looked with pleasure upon the manner in which the committee had tried to spend their money. If the committee could see their way, they would do all they could towards making the library a free lending one. Councillor PLATT said that he was very glad that this question appeared to be settled, at all events for the time present. Alderman Harrison had referred to the want of funds. He thought that he could point out one matter, at all events that would help him in that respect. He found from Corporation accounts that the Literary and Philosophical Society had the use of a room, gas, cleaning, and other expenses, for ten shillings per an- num. He thought that it would be much better if the charge was £lO per annum. The society, of which he happened to be a member, were, he thought, not quite paupers. They should not take anything irom the funds of the library, but should rather add to those funds. He thought that this was a matter which might well be looked into by the committee, and it was one that might be done without any offence to the society. He believed that there were other societies that used the room for a very nominal charge, or none at all. The question of

the proper use of that room might help towards making the library free. ' Councillor JOLLNY said that he had spoken to many of the members of the committee, and he had found that they had thedesire to make the library a free lending one if they had the means. His conviction was that the Mugmim Committee deserved thanks fee what they had done, 'and he was sure that they would do a great deal more had they the means to do it with. Alderman Dams said that he thought that the re- marks of one or two gentlemen led them to expect that they would shortly have a free lending library, but he must say that they could hardly expect it yet. He gig:re the gentlemen who, outside the Council, had advocated aninquiry into this matter all the credit for it. At the same time there had been certain questions, especially those of a legal character, in regard to which he thought they had been under a wrong impression. A question had been put to the Attorney-General, who, in his reply, ' said that the Public Library Act of 1855 gave no author- ity for making any distinction between persons who sub- scribe and persons who do not. The question was "What powers does the Library Act of 1855 give ?" and he narrowed his reply to the question put to him. He did not say that it was ultra vires to make any charge at all. This particular Act of Parliament was pass- to deal with public and not lending libraries, libraries such as at the British Museum, the Bodleian Library, and others of that character, and the intention was that the Library should be open for the inhabitants' inspection. There was no authority to lend at all, and if the question had been put to the Attorney-General in that light, as it affected public libraries who lent books out, he could say that they had no power under that Act of Parliament. He wanted it to be well impressed on the public that the Attorney-General did not for a moment impeach the propriety of the Council in conducting the library, to the best interests of the town, in their own way. Clause 21 of the Act gave power to the Corpora- tion, through their committee, to conduct the library in the way they thought best. In the interests of Warring- ton, it was thought desirable that books should be lent out, and that had been done. He thought that they should know something as to how the Museum, Library, and Arts Committee had been conducted, and with what success. He should like to call the attention of the Coun- cil to the buildings, representing in value Some £3,000 or £4,000. The building itself was given to the town free, and costs were subsequently incurred to the extent of about £l,OOO. The promoters banded the institution to the town free of charge and the £3,000 or £4,000 re- presented was only weighted to-day with a debt of about £l,lOO. This had been brought about by the conduct of the men who had managed the institution. At Wigan, a law town than Wamngton to begin with, they had had £24,000 put at their disposal, and yet had to pay £3Bl a year to support the library. Part of that was a voluntary rate of £l4l a year. In Warrington they, had done it for £528 a year, and paid £7B as rent to the sinking fund. This was brought about by donations and subscriptions, and by good management. At present there were subscribers who paid 5s a year, and there were other subscribers ranging up to two guineas. What did they now propose? They said td the people of Warrington, young and fold, "if you want a book, ou can have it for a penny." I They found from experience that books were generally kept out for about a fortnight, so that would be a penny I cost in a fortnight, and if a person during a month or so did not want to read, he would not have to pay a sub- I scription. With regard to outsiders it was proposed that where 5s was now charged they should pay 10s, or, in- stead of paying the penny subscription when they took out books, should pay twopence. Ile thought that was fair, as these people gave nothing to the rates that sup- porteclthe library. They mnst not, he urged, be under the impression that the penny rate was such as to enable them to do more than they were doing, for during the last seven years that rate had hardly increased at all. ,Alderman WEBerns said that Mr. Dixon had remarked that the people would never be satisfied until the library was made into a free lending one. Councillor Dixon would see, if he read the report, that the way was open. All the people had to do was to supply the cash. With regard to the Literary and Philosophical, and other so- cieties, the object of the committee had been to make the institution as publicly useful as possible, and it had been the custom when any kindred institution of that character wanted rooms, to in some cases grant them entirely free, if no expense was thereby incurred, and in cases where expense had been incurred a charge to meet that expense had been made. The MAYOR said that he was very glad that the question was settled. He did not think that the working classes would grumble at tlist charge of a penny per volume, but would be happy to pay it if they wished to read the books.
k The minutes were then put to the meeting and con 7 firmed. .
CEMETERY COMMITTEE.

To this committee the Registrar reported that the in- terments for the" past four weeks were—Adults 27, minors 27, and stillborn and premature 7; and for the corresiSonding period last year—adults 30, minors 47, and stillborn and premature 10. The receipts for the past four i weeks were £49 3s. 2d. and for the corresponding period last year £BB ss. The committee also resolved that thanks be given to Alderman Harrison, the chair- man, and Councillor Brown, the deputy-chairman, for their services during the past year. Approved on, the motion of Alderman HARRISON, seconded by Councillor FLEMING.

-SCHOOL A - •/INCE COMMITTEE. The Inspector had re • • rted to this committee that 62 cases had been inquir •• into by the Board of Guardians, and school fees allowed in 56 eases for 127 children.; 20 cases had been before the magistrates, and fines inflicted in 18 cases, 1 ordered to be whipped, and 1 warrant ordered. 32 cases were brought before the committee and dealt with. The average attendance at the public elementary schools during The month of August was 7,513; last year 7,462, increase 51; and for the month of September 7,834, last year 7,634, increase 200. The com- mittee thanked the chairman, Alderman Webster, for his services.
, The minutes were approved on the motion of Alder- man Wassrza, seconded by Councillor TAYLOR.

TOWN HALL, PARK .AND BATHS COMMITTER. . The HAT'HKEEpER reported that the income from the bathi for the past two weeks was £3 ss, and for the cor- responding period last year £4.7s id. The committee thanked Mr. George Fowler for his gift of a number of small birds ' for the aviary, and Mr. J. Charlton Parr for his gift of a riale black swan for the pond in the gardens. The minutes were confirmed on the proposition of the MAYOR, seconded by Alderman HARRISON.

div.head: es colamiriEß.—THlC AUDIT OF ACCOUNTS.
div.p: es colamiriEß.—THlC AUDIT OF ACCOUNTS.

This Committee recommended that the sum of thirty guineas be voted to the Borough auditors for their ser- vices in auditing the accounts of the gas department. Alderman HoLmss proposed, and Alderman WEBSTER seconded, the confirmation of the minutes. Councillor BOLTON said that he did not think it was right that the Borough auditors should be paid from dif- ferent Committees. The Finance Committee had already voted them thirty guineas. This was making a piece- dent which he did not believe in. The Gas Commilebse had an auditor who had been paid fifteen guineas. He also could not understand why these gentlemen had been so long in auditing the accounts, and why it was necessary to make the further payment recommended. Was this, he wished to know, to be an annual charge? The ac- counts must have been in a deplorable condition if they took a month to audit, as he was told Was the case. If this was to be an annual charge he would move a reso- lution that the money be not paid. Councillor W. PIERPOINT said that he hoped, as one means towards freeing the library, the Gas Committee would consider whether they could not let the Museum Committee have the gas and coke free, or at least that they would not charge them any more than the largest consumers were charged. Councillor H. ROBERTS said he should like, to know if it was intended to continue the services of ordinary auditors in addition to the borough auditors and how it was that, before paying for services rendered, they had not got the report of the borough auditors on this impor- tant question?

Alderman HOLMES said that it was according to the will of the Council that the borough auditors had audited these accounts. With reference to the payment recom- mended it did not at all cover the fee that the auditors were really entitled to, but the committee had concluded to make that payment, and the auditors had concluded to accept it. A resolution of the Council required that the accounts should be audited, and if the Council wished it otherwise it would be all right. They had not adopted any resolution regarding the fifteen guineas, but the im- pression was that they should not continue that par- ment. Speaking for himself, he thought it would be an advantage to do so. The auditors had said generally that the accounts were correct, and made a suggestion with regard to the keeping of some pat of the accounts. Councillor H. ROBERTS said he preferred the borough auditors to a private auditor, and dkl.not think the pay- ment too much. The MAYOR thought that, in a large concern like the gas works it was advisable to have an independent audi- tor, who occasionally checked the accounts. He was about to put the motion that the minutes be con- firmed, when Councillor BOLTON desired leave to move a resolution. The MAYOR said that Alderman Holmes had made his reply. Councillor Bolton could not now put a resohi. tion.

Councillor Purr: We all took it that Mr. Holmes was not replying, but simply giving an explanation. Councillor BOLTON then left the Council Chamber, re- marking: "I shall leave you to it; I shall walk out of the room."
Alderman HennisoN said he did not think Councillor Bolton had been quite fairly used, though he did not think that was intentional.
Councillor DIXON mentioned that he had consented to second a resolution that Councillor Bolton had intended to move.
tlderrnan HOLMES said that he had merely followed the course of procedure, and did not wish to be discour- teous to Councillor Bolton. _

The MAYOII said he thought Councillor Bolton had been rather hasty in leaving the room. Alderman DAVIES : Perhaps it will do if the Gas Com- mittee will report whether or not it is advisable to have two audits.

John Richard Pickmere, Esq., Alderman of this 80r04.7: for the able and satisfactory manner in which he IP' discharged the responsible duties devolving upon him as Mayor and chief magistrate of this borough during thig his fifth year of office, and for the unvarying conitesi' kindness, and impartiality displayed by 'm when Pr" siding over the deliberations of the Council and in no intercourse with its members."

The resolution was seconded by Alderman Waasiry and supported by Aldermen Caosrump, Bunosss, CHANDLEY, and Sorrow, who spoke in terms of appvecia; tion of the Mayor's services, after which it was carrieu With applause. The Mayon briefly replied, and the proceedings nated.
MAYORAL PRESENTATION AT WARRINGTON.

An interesting ceremony took place in the Conn" cil Chamber of the Town Hall on Monday afternoon* when the Mayor (Alderman Pickmere) was presen" ted with a gold chronometer, and the Mayoress with a handsome diamond pendant and spray. The two presents cost about .£l7O, and the fund with which they were purchased was subscribed to bl nearly two hundred ladies and gentlemen, who de- sired to in that manner express their appreciation of the very fitting way in which Mr. and Mrs. Pick- mere have carried out the Mayoral duties during the memorable Jubilee year. The vestibule of the Town Hall had for the occasion been decorated vrith Iplants, and the windows of the Council Chamber, were draped with lace curtains. A large number cn ladies and gentlemen were present by invitation, the member for the borough, Sir Gilbert Greenall. and Lady Greenall, Mrs. Quekett, Mr. and Mrs. Bea' mont, and a numb& of Aldermen and Councillors of the borough being amongst those who had met to witness the ceremony. Mr. George Riley, before the proceedings commenced, and as the room being gradually filled by the visitors, played several, selections on the piano, and as the Mayor and Mayoress entered the room he played "Auld Lang Syne." The presentation was made by Alderman Holmes, chairman a the Presentation Committee, and one of the oldest members of the Council, who said that the duty he had undertaken was a pleasant one, for if there was one pleasure more than another, it was to recognise when, they could good actions on the part of their fellow townsmen. Some months ago they were in a considerable difficulty in the Corporation, as they were practically without a Mayor, and had to consider who was the most suit- able to fill that important post. He believed it was the unanimous wish of the inhabitants of Warring- ton that they should ask Alderman Pickmere to re- sume the duties which he had' so well filled years before. (Applause.) After several interviews it, that gentleman. he consented to accept that office, and he (Alderman Holmes) remembered one 'ex_pres; sion he made use of—" If I do accept the °Moe will take care that the people of Warrington shall know that they have a Mayor amongst them." (AP- plause.) That had been verified by subsequent circumstances, and Alderman Pickmere had shown that they had a Mayor in Warrington. (Applause.) Immediately after the appointment it was neces- sary that some steps should be taken to celebrate the 50th anniversary of her Majesty's reign, and th!, first thing done was to call together a number 01 gentlemen to mitke arrangements for a Jubilee &le' bration in the town; and he thought that the n3BIY ner in which that celebration was carried out re- fleeted very great credit on the Mayor as well ss upon Mrs Pickmere, who gathered roundhera ininro bet of ladies to do the work generally assignen ladies under such circumstances. Her share of work was done in a verycreditable manner,,anu to the satisfaction of the inhabitants of Varna& i ton. (Applause.) The result was that they thong': they ought to do something more than a''d cora to them a simple vote ,of thanks, Li% that it was right to ask for subscriPtlw• to a testimonial in recognition of their servlce-4, Alderman Holmes then presented the pendant ar„ spray to the Mayoress, and the chronometer to of Mayor. In a few words of reply, Mrs. PICIDISUP said that it had always been a pleasant duty to haedr to aid the Mayor in carrying out anything tila..!le come within her capacity during his term or That would, she added, ever be a memorable unc, sion to her; but she should not need to have tho"; bright jewels before her to remember the 111811„ kindnesses of the people of Warrington. A refog was also made by his WORSHIP, who, in returneoa sincere thanks for the handsome gifts' rent,a„iy that he and the Mayoress had been most ue,,;ad touched by the proceedings of that afternoon,ota. the kind feeling that had prompted the prele the tion. He was pleased that they had allow'eu., that Mayoress to select the objects, and he took 1' It to the presentation was more an konour to her t,III/with himself. She was particularly well pleasentbiags the selection, and, although a great maul jwere suggested to her, at the end she plene self. There was an old saying that "Cenci sow woman against her will, she'll be of th ease, opinion still." (Laughter.) ft was 80 in t.,,b1 Wag as his wife told him that as his old wirhaae ‘l!' nearly done, she was determined he should cheri„, new one. (Laughter.) She would alwaY° ll her gift with affection, and when the Oive_r d the good should take them hence, the jewels Men as watch would be handed down to their clii f the a memento of the kindness and generositY also people of Warrington. A vote of thanks w_7oosi- passed to the Mayor and Mayoress, on the Pla the tion of Mr. Beamont and Alderman Holmes, n"Coaa- treasurer and secretary of the Presentation_ vie mittee were thanked for their services uuthen motion of the Mayor. Refreshments welltiotis partaken of, and Mr. Riley gave further 80' of music.

FRIGHTFUL RAILWAY COLLISION AT FILYMOUTH.—.A serious railway accident occurred at Plymouth on Tues- das on the arrival of the two o'clock train from Exeter. The train was standing at the ticket platform, waiting to be pushed into the Great Western Station, when the engine which was to drive it in dashed into the rearmost carriage, crushing and smashing it. These was much consterna- tion among the passengers, who were immediately seen jumping from the carriages on either side; but in the hind compartments several persons were found lying about more or less unconscious, and bleeding from cuts and wounds on various parts of their bodies. , They were at once removed to the waiting-room, and here they were attended by Dr. Fox. There was no one killed, and it is hoped that no one has been fatallyi njured. It is sup- posed that the driver forgot or found it impossible to ap- py the brake. , SINGULAR BOATING FATALITY—On Saturday afternoon, a small boat was proceeding from Pharay Island to Eday Island, Orkneys, a distance of about two miles, with four men on board and an ox, when the :ox put one of its feet through the bottom. The little craft began to fill rapidly, and in a hurried struggle to turn the beast out the boat capsized. Two of the men, James and Robert Allen, saved themselves by holding to the boat until assistance arrived, but the other two sank, and their bodies have not been recovered. I have, somehow, become possessed, 'latterly, with a growing conviction that there is not going to be one honest trade or business left. I can hardly, even now, think of one where dishonest practices are not resorted to in order to make a sub- sistence, or perhaps something more. A great deal has been said, and written, and done about, and with but- terine, but lam of opinion that we have a great many other compounds foisted upon us that do us far more harm than purified fats. Were Ito say that there are hundreds of articles of food and clothing that have been I subjected to the wily arts of the adulterator, I should not exaggerate, and I think I should be nearer the mark if I were to say that it is almost, if not quite, impossible to find a single article that is adulteratable that has not been improved. And this has grown so upon us, and with us, that we have almost ceased to regard it as dis- honesty. It has, in fact, come to be an important part of a business education to know how to sell articles of inferior quality, with perhaps an improved shine on them, or kink on them, off better than one's neighbours. We are departing from that high standard of morality that regulated the conduct of the Quaker mercer who I directed and instructed all his assistants that they were ; to be strictly honest with his customers, and not to do I anything that could not be supported by some paabage from Scripture. But even the ethics of the honestly- disposed Quaker Scripturally supported though they were, were not sUfficient to restrain the zeal of at least , one of.his assistants: This one was a verdant youth

from the country, who, as may be expected, was pretty well soaked with theology; the parson and schoolmaster of the village having'seen to that. Therefore, when John received his instructions from his master, he felt that he was the right man in the right place. So well was he grounded in Scriptural knowledge that his master began to set him up as an example of probity and straightforwardness in his business dealings. John had an opportunity of proving that he was well up in Scriptural quotations, and of supporting his every- day actions thereby. A lady came into the shop one morning to buy a sealskin jacket. She was not one of your ordinary customers who believe every- thing or everybody. No, she was one of those who know that a Lig price price must be paid for an article or it cannot be good. John had shown her every quality of jacket that was in the shop, and his being an establishment where small profits and quick returns were believed in, he had quoted fifteen pounds as his top price. The lady wanted one better, and John was at his wits'-end to accommodate her, for he was sure that if he sold a jacket of that value, his day's takings would beat any of the other assistants. John bethought him of another parcel of jackets at twenty-five pounds each, and he fetched one for the lady to look at. It was just the thing, and John effected the sale. Passing the money on to his master, who attended to the cash him- self, John resumed his work. At the dinner table on that day the subject of the sealskin jacket was broached, and John had to give an explanation which was not altogether satisfactory to the old man, who reproached him in rather severe terms for practising such dishonesty with a customer who had so implicitly trusted to his truthfulness in his descriptions of the articles he had to offer her. So angry was he that he told John' who seemed lost for an excuse for his con- duct, that if he could not quote a passage from the Scriptures that was applicable to his case by tea-time, he should have to dispense with his services. . At tea-time John was given an opportunity of vindi- cating his unusual conduct, by the old Quaker saving, "Well, John, has thee been able to call to thy mind a quotation that will support thy conduct of this morning ?" "Yes, sir," said John. "Well, I should like to hear it, because I do not think I could find one myself. Does it apply to the case, John ?"

"It does, sir," said John. "Then let me hear what it is." "Well, sir, it is a passage which is very well known, and I think you will know it when I give it you. ,It is this She was a stranger, and I took her in." The old Quaker looked very grave, and he tried to explain to John that he misunderstood the meaning of the passage, but he did not return the lady the extra tett pounds that John had overcharged her. Now, though tradespeople resort to such means to gull the public, there is no doubt that they have a good deal to put up with, and many a time get a little change from a certain class of that same public. But I will give Boswell's ideas on the subject, as expressed to me last week in a conversation I had with him.

Ther is a good decal o' adulteration un a good decal o' trickery practised wi' a good deeal o' things, un unless o' fairly understand a thing when yo'r buyin' id, yo'r iable to be ta'en in. But, yo' know, if fooak wodn'd buy adulterated articles, nobry would sell urn; sooa, yo' see, id like cuts booath ways. Aw've no deawt ther's a good decal o' rubbish sowd ; but, at t' same time, ther's a good decal o' rubbish gooas a-buyin' id. Tradesmen dom'd allus hey id ther own way; they ged set on a bit sometimes. Yo' know. ther's so mony fooak gooin' abeawt cheeatin' other fooak tell it's a varra difficult thing for some tradesmen to mek booatli ends meet. It's wed l known to business fooak generally as there's a certain class goin' abeawt fro' one nebberhood to another, un fro' one teawn to another, geddin' howd o' oas they con, un payin' for nowt; un as soon as a nebberhood or teawn geds too hot for um they do a slope, un tradesmen soon find eawt as ther nod woth lookin' after. This class o' fooak robs yo' o' yo'r profit. Neaw, yo'd varra likely think as fooak as gooas in for them sooart o' tricks would be t' lowest un mooast ignorant as yo' could find, but if yo' think ony such thing yo' never med a bigger mistake i' yo'r life; for i'atead o' thad, it's varra often them at: is gifted wi' V gab un is wed l edicated as does t' mooast on id, un suc- ceeds t' best. Done yo' see? Yo'r desaved wi' ther looks un ther oily, tongues. Aw'll gi' yo' an instance heaw aw wer once tekken in misel, un heaw aw wer led up to id. Of coourse, yo' know as a tooathry year sin aw used to hey a shop a bit heigher up t' street, un as aw sowd sewing machines. Well, id sometimes happened as aw'd to let a sewing machine gooa eawt on tick, wi' th' understanding as id would be paid for on a certain day, or within a certain time. - - •
t' shop one mornin' when a fine-lookin', well-dressed, gentlemanly chap 000 m in un said, "Good morning, Mr. Hopton." "Good mornin' " aw sed.

, He sed. "I am in the education line, Mr. Hopton, and I coach youths in various branches o' education, in order to qualify them to pass examinations that are necessary to their obtaining degrees in their pro- fessions."
Aw sed, "Just sooa!" un aw wondered if he intended me to be coached up, sooa as aw could pass for a doctor, or a lawyer, or happen a parson or summat o' thad sooart. _ __ • _ .

He sed, "Well, Mr. Hopton, as you are no doubt aware, it is necessary that anyone who has any- thing to sell must advertise himself, or people will never know it." " Ther's no deawt o' thad," aw sed, un aw still won- derd wodever t' fella could be drivin' at. "That being so," he sed," I want you to do me the favour of putting this bill in your window," un he pood a little bit of a bill eawt of his pockut un handed id to me. Aw lookt this bill o'er, un aw fun as his name wer Simcock, un as he lived at side o' St. Alban's Chapel. Aw thowt to misel as he'd done a decal o' talkin' o'er a varra little job as wornd at o necessary. But it's some fooaks' way,• yo' know. If thad chap hod walked into my shop un hed sed, Will yo' put this bill in your window, please?' aw should he put id in just t' same. Aw sed, "Oh, yes, aw'll do thad for yo'," un tekkin' a pin ea.wt o' ml waistcoat, aw pinned id to t' window frame. He sed, "Oh, thank you. Mr. Hopton, ever so much." Aw. sed, " Yo'r quite welcome to ony good as aw con do yo' this way." He stood tatkire to me ever so long, un he towd roo as he hedn'd bin i' teawn mony months, but so far he'd done varra weal in his business. He wer quite chatty un plain-spokken, un he seemed to try to mek lussel as agreeable as he could; un aw like formed a good opinion on him. (To be Concluded in our Next.)

THE WARRINGTON LIBRARY. Slr,—After all, the Town Council have failed to rise to the occasion. The result of their deliberations is very discouraging to the opponents of a hateful double tax, but I trust this matter will never be allowed to drop until the Library is free indeed. So we are to pay id. a book, "just like they do for a bottle of medicine at the Infirmary." The very idea of ? Comparing honest, hardworking, self-respecting men, who wish to put everything on a legal footing, to the dirty, intemperate, improvident people who have to resort to charitable medicine and scrape together four , farthings before they can be trusted with a bottle. Just think of it. The thought makes:my blood boil, and the more so as I meditate upon the arguments used at the ' Council meeting. To my mind, things have been allowed to go terribly awry with respect to the Library, with- out knowing it, and we have received a sudden awaken- ing. If the penny rate in other towns is devoted to, and found quite sufficient for, the purposes for which it was intended, why is it not so used in Warrington? Again, if the committee are so cocksure the Libraries Act never contemplated the lending of books, why in the world do they not act up to their convictions and cease lending altogether? What is the good of half-heartedly doing a thing? Why not place everybody upon the same footing? The position is simple enough. The Act either does or does not authorise the lending of books, and I should like to know which it does. If it does so authorise them, it is on certain specific conditions, and those conditions I desire to see carried out. I pay my penny rate to support a free library, and yet if I go for a book I am to pay another penny for what I have already paid for! This I regard as an iniquitous proceeding, and it shall receive no countenance from me. The committee are evidently in an illegal and unstable position and the sooner they are made to see it the bet- ter. The whole matter has been approached and con- sidered with prejudiced minds, and I regret the commit- tee could not see their way to accept the undertaking that was given to defray any loss that resulted from an experiment in the way of a really free library. We are terribly behind the times in this benighted Conservative 'town, but I trust the rising generation will provide men of broader, more liberal, more sympathetic, and more enterprising minds than those who at present "have do- minion over us," and that they will see to it that over and above everything also, among all classes, there will be what does not at present exist, viz :—perfect EQUALITY.

MR. MONKS AND THE PUBLIC LIBRARY. Sir,—l cannot help thinking sometimes that those who actively or passively oppose the freeing of the library do themselves an injustice when they profess that they are not able to see the force of certain arguments that are used by the advocates of a free library: I fancy that this is not due to any weakness in the intellectual parts a these gentlemen. but rather that it is an exemplifica- tion of the old saying that there are none so blind as those who don't wish to see. Mr. F. Monks, as we all know, is not opposed to a free library, but he is a gen- tleman who has been at great pains to restrain the en- thusiasm for the freeing of the institution which every- body believes he is possessed of. Mr. Monks says he cannot at all find where the injustice of the present mode of conducting the library comes in, because every one has the same privelege of taking books by paying a subscription, while no one can take a book without paying a subscription. Now, sir, it may be that in Mr. Monk's mind the quality of justice is a very refined and meta- physical thing, but if you will allow me, fthink I may, by using what I consider is an apposite illustration, show wherein the present mode of conducting the library is grossly unjust and unfair according to ordinary ideas of 3ustice and fairplay. Let us suppose, then, that the master of a certain school decides that it will be for the benefit of his scholars if each of them contribute a sum of money to be spent in the purchase of toys or other things which give pleasure to children. Having obtained the contributions the master expends them as stated, places the toys and other things on a shelf or ledge at a uniform height from the ground, and then tells the scholars they all have an equal right and an equal chance of getting a toy because all they need do is to reach one down from the shelf. But how would it be were the shelf placed at such a height from the ground that, while the taller scholars could reach the toys with ease, and while some others who were not quite so tall could get at them with a little exertion, there was still a considerable number of the younger and shorter scholars who could not get a share of the things they so much desired to have by any amount of effort. Would Mr. Monks deny for a moment that such a method of distri- buting the toys was grossly unfair and unjust? And if the master of the school were to argue that there was no injustice because each of the scholars had the same op- portunity allowed him, would not Mr. Monks say that such an argument was an insult to men who were sup- posed to have the power of reasoning? Yet, sir, I mountain that this case is exactly analagous to the case of the public library. In order to keep up this library there is a contribution of money taken every year from the pockets of the ratepayers and after this contribution is taken and spent, there is a barrier against the use of the books set up in the shape of a subscription. To the well-to-do the payment of this subscription is nothing; it does not deprive them of a single luxury. To another class the payment of the subscription means that they must deprive themselves of some necessary or luxury, or lessen the funds which men who are endowed with the faculty of looking " before and after" wish to lay up against old age or misfortune. To a third class, as all experience proves, the imposition of a subscription is an absolutetlebarment of the use of books. In the case of the third class, poverty as inevitably and as necessarily deprives them of them of the use of things which many of them desire to have as would shortness of stature in the case I have just used as an illustration. In the case of the library as in that of the illustration the deprivation is due to circumstances over which as a rule the victims have little or /b 0 control. And yet we have gentlemen like Mr. Monks who come forward and say that they see no injustice in an arrangement which when looked, at as it ought to be looked at, is of the very essence of injustice. —I am, sir,
