CALIFORNIA AND ENGLISH WOMEN. am kid returned from a visit to California,l that garden of the Lord, where the climate is so delight- ful that it is a treat simply to live and breathe in it. I went in mid-winter (January) and found dot I could sit out of doors all day, amid the most lovely surroundings of flowers, fruit and scenery—roses, heliotrope, fuchsias, geraniums, and the orange groves fragrant on every hand. I never imagined anything so lovely. The con- ditions of life seem perfect. But I found that, while lovely homes abound, the scarcity of household help lays a burden on the housewife, who is obliged to resort to Chinamen, with all the disadvantages of language and habits. I have always felt a deep mterest in the position of women in my own country, and knowing how hard it is for an educated woman to earn a competence in this country, I at once saw that here was a splendid opening if only they were sensible enough to take hold of it. There are thousands of homes in California where an educated, sensible woman would be treated as a trusted friend and equal, if she was prepared to be a real help, for in that country labour stands on golden feet, and is honourable; while idleness is a disgrace. Ladies, even the wives of millionaires, are doing their own work rather than employ, the Chinaman. They would wel- come any number of sensible women skilled in house- work—such as farmers' daughters and the kind that go out as mothers' helps and nursery governesses at home; but let it be understood that no one need go out with an idea of teaching, for education of the best kind is absolutely free. A knowledge of cooking is important, and will command the highest wages—£36 a year is the lowest salary ever paid in Southern California, and £4O, £5O, and even more would gladly be given to the right kind of help—but let not the useless, frivolous woman

Lovers of verse, and versifiers will be delighted with the current issue of the Canterbury Poets. It is a vol- ume of "Ballades and Rondeaus, chants royal, sestinas, villanelles, &c., selected with chapter on the various forms by Gleeson White." It is hardly necessary to say that the present issue, from the very nature of it, in- cludes some of the choicest, and at the same time, quaintest verse ever published. It is a storehouse of good things. Here, by way of extract, is a charming triolet by Mr. Austin Dobson : In the School of Coquettes ' Madame Rose is a scholar :- 0, they fish with all nets, In the School of Coquettes! When her broach she forgets, 'l'is to show her new collar; In the School of Coquettes Madame Rose is a scholar.

It should be added that Mr. White's introductory chapter is really a most valuable treatise on the various forms of verse in the volume. In the "Great Writers" series, also published by Mr. Walter Scott, we have the "Life of John Keats, "by William Michael Rossetti. This story of the poet's life is admirably told, for Mr. Rossetti is an eminent hand in work of this kind, and possesses a critical judgment of the first quality. He disposes effectually, and, it is to be hoped, for all time of the story that Keats was killed by the reviewers, or as Byron puts it, was "snuf- fed out by an article." Like Byron himself, Keats was incapable of being crushed in this way, and wrote some of his best poetry after the brutal attacks which were made upon his first volume of poems. Keats died of consumption—a disease which also carried off one of his brothers. When it is remembered that he passed off the scene before he was twenty-six, it is a matter of won- der that he left so much verse which is perfect of its kind. He looked, as he once said, "upon fine phrases as a lover," and he has left many fine phrases which the world will not willingly let die—for as he himself said—" A thing of beauty is a joy for ever." Keats died in Rome, and it is pleasant to remember in connection with his place of burial in Rome, that on a wall near his grave there is a medallion portrait of the poet executed and presented by the late Warrington Wood. The tenth series of Health Lectures delivered in Man- chester is issued in book form, price Is., by Mr. John Heywood. There are eight lectures and they deal for the most part with the causes of disease and their pre- vention. The first lecture is by,Dr. Ransome and is on "Some causes of preventible disease." The titles of the other lectures are "Occupation in relation to disease," "Temperament in relation to disease," "Climate in the treatment of disease," "The relation of age to disease?" the influence of education on health," "Heredity in relation to disease," and "Diet in relation to disease." "The Manchester Quarterly, an illustrated journal of Literature and Art" is published by Mr. TOhn Heywood for the Manchester Literary Club. The current issue may be called the Wordsworth number, for it contains no less than three papers on the great poet, namely, "Recent Work on Wordsworth" by J. H. Nodal • I "Wordsworth in London," by W. E. A. Oxon; and "Wordsworth on Beggars" by John Mortimer. Other contents are" Reminiscences of a trip to the East," by William Artingstall (with illustrations) ; "Lake Le- man and English Literature." by C. T. Tallent-Bateman, and a sonnet "Death, the liberator," by J. B. Oldham. The following is from Mr. Artingstall's article and refers to the dogs of Constantinople We cannot leave the subject of roads without mention- ing „the dogs. They are übiquitous, you may sometimes count 30 or even 40 in a small street; they live on the garbage that is thrown out; they are the masters of the roadway. If they lie downto sleep in a little patch of sunshine, the men walk round them or step over them. Rarely will you see one ill-treated ; it is breeding time, and there are numerous litters of puppies, the shop- keepers bringing out old boxes, Izc., for them to breed in ; they never leave the street in which they are born ; if a strange dog ventures over the boundary line, there I is an immediate gathering of the clans, and he is roughly 1 expelled. There are patricians and beggars amongst the dogs ; one that happens to be born in a street where: bakers, provision dealers, &c., abound, is fat and well fed, has a comfortable, well-to-do appearance • in the next street, devoted to hardware and cobblers, he is thin, starved, and miserable—an accident of birth; promotion by merit is unknown amongst them. Cassell's Magazine for October contains, amongst other good things, "More about Mr. Smith," "Some Quaker Customs," "A Healthy Nursery," "Great Storms," "Letters from the Planets," Sic. Mr. F. E. Weatherly contributes'. a charming song "The Little Kerchief," and "The Gatherer" has a large collection. The illustration of the story "AU Souls' Night" is an unusually fine and highly finished piece of work.—The October number of the "Quiver" concludes a volume, and there is an announcement of "a new and perma- nently enlarged series." It will be on the old linos, of course, and there is every promise of this highly popular magazine for Sunday and general reading becoming still more popular.—" Little Folks" has a very pretty coloured frontispiece—" Puss to Tea." The opening story—" Adventures of Careless Ned "—is capital both in text and illustration. It will make the children laugh; it is so natural. "The Boy Hunters of Kentucky" has now reached chapter twelve, and the boy readers of England are hoping it will "go on for ever." Then there are papers (illustrated) for very little folk especially adapted for those who can ,read a little, but not much. The Magazine of Art for October concludes the last volume, and a splendid volume it makes. Nothing can exceed the beauty and finish of the fine series of full page etchings which are now given from month to month. The etching for the October number is iff the painting of "The madness of Hugo Van Der Goes" by Emile Wanters. There are six other illustrations of other works of this great artist, with a biographical sketch by Mr. M. H. Speilmann. An article on Flint
ALDERMAN HARRISON AND DALLAM FORGE WORKMEN.

At the Borough Court yesterday morning, Mr. P. Davies, solicitor, addressing Alderman Harrison, the presiding magistrate, said that his worship would recollect a case recently heard at the court, in which his client was brought up for an assault upon his wife. It was mentioned by him (Mr. Davies) that he had no witnesses to call, but would ask Mr. Hunt to speak to the character of the defendant. Mr. Hunt then gave evidence as to his character, which was a very excellent one. He (Mr. Davies) remarked that defendant had worked for fifteen years at Dallam Forge. His worship on that occa- sion made a remark, which had been reported, and it seemed that the employes of Dallam Forge took great offence at that remark. A letter subsequently appeared in the papers, which, had he not been away at the time, he should have replied to. He wished now to say that he did not quite agree with Alderman Harrison's statement that he used as an argument three successive times thatbecause a man had worked at Dallam Forge for that period he could not possibly be guilty of such an aggrava- ted assault. He (Mr. Davies) denied having said so, or having used such a foolish argument. What he said was that he left the case entirely in the hands of their worship, but should not be doing his duty unless he called Mr. Hunt, and in passing he mentioned that defendant bad worked at the Dal- lam Forge for fifteen years. He never argued that ' defendant could not, therefore, be guilty of an as- sault. His worship Most certainly must have ;nis- i understood him.—Alderman Harrison said that the letter was a private one, written to Mr. Bleckly, and at the time it was written be had not the slightest idea that it would be published afterwards, or he should have qualified one observation that he made with reference to Mr. Davies. But he was still under the impression that Mr. Davies did twice repeat the argument thatin consequence of this man having I worked fifteen years at the Dallam Forge, he there- fore could not be such a man as had been described by the wife. He was still firmly of that opinion.— Mr. Davies said that the wife alleged that the de- fendant had never worked a month together for he did not know how long, and he (Mr. Davies) then remarked that he could not be the man described. —Mr. White (magistrates' clerk) remarked that Mr. Davies urged it as an argument that defendant must have been- a man of good character, or he would not have been employed fifteen years at the forge.—Alderman Harrison : That is all that I said. After a few further remarks the subject dropped.

DEATH OF A SITSPECTED DYNAMITEE.—An iuquest was held on Wednesday at the Southwark Coroner's Court touching the death of a man named Brown, or Joseph Cohen, who is supposed to have been an American dyna- mitard. Deceased had been heard to speak a having been in America, and the last two of the few persons who came to see him in his lodgings appeared to be I Americans. One of these men, who was in court, was identified by another witness, and gave evidence. He said that about two months ago he met, and went over the House of Commons with, a man named Melville, whom the police now stated was the London agent of the Clan-na-Gael. The police also said that the "tall, fair man" who conducted the witness and Melville over the House was Mr. Joseph Nolan, M.P. After hearing further and medical evidence, the jury returned a verdict of "Death from natural causes."

--- CLAIM FOR PROFESSIONAL ATTENDANCE.—On Thursday afternoon, at the County Court at War- rington, his Honour Judge Ffoulkes gave his deci- sion in a case in which Dr. Handyside, of Earles- town, sued a man named Thomas Clubb, a miner, of Newton, for the sum of £lO 135., said to be due in respect to medical attendance by plaintiff and his assistant on the wife and daughter of the defen- dant. Mr. P. Davies • again appeared for the plain- tiff, and Mr. Rideal defended. Particulars of the case were given in our last issue. His Honour said that he must uphold the opinion he formed at the last sitting of the court, and give judgment for .C. 5 6s. 6d., being the amount due for the personal at- tendance of -Dr. Handyside. What was charged for the attendance of Dr. Handyside's assistant, who at the time was not fully qualified, was disallowed in consequence of that fact.

div.p: think of going. I may say that I consider housework easier , there than at home. No fires are needed even in winter, ' except for cooking; every man cleans his own shoes and sees the kitchen stove supplied with wood: coal is not needed. The climate is so beautiful that the houses keep clean with less work. They are lovely fairy homes, with I one or two verandahs round, covered with vines or climbing exotics. Nearly all the houses are painted white, and beautifully contrast with the surrounding trees. As I was in California in a public capacity, I was able to form committees of influential citizens, mostly ladies, in a few large towns, who were most anxious to help in this truly philanthropic work. They are prepared to re- ceive, and care for until they find places, any number of ladies whom I shall send, only stipulating that they shall be total abstainers, and bring a guarantee from me that they have credentials of character and ability to under- take the duties of a house. I wrote one letter from California similar to this for a London paper, and eleven ladies have already arrived in consequence, and are do- ing well. One, a school teacher, but who had done her own housework, went to Los Angeles with her brother, stayed at a boarding house, and the lady, learning that she was willing to take a situation, offered her the care of the bedrooms at a salary of £4a month. Before the month was up she said, • You are worth £6," and gave it her. I saw the young lady hefore leaving, and it was a treat to see her delight and gratitude, and she said she could not have imagined such a beautiful climate and country, and she has sent for her mother and sisters. The cost of passage for a number would be £2O for- (lntermediate) on ocean steamer and excursion, com- fortable carriages, with every comfort and sleeping ac- commodation, free. I came home by this route of rail- road, and found it most enjoyable. From Liverpool to New York takes from seven to ten days, the railroad journey from New York to Los Angeles six or seven days. I do not advise anyone to go to San Francisco; it is the place where all nationalities congregate, and wages are lower; but at Los Angeles, Passadena, and Riverside, wages are as I have stated. lam preparing a lecture on Californian life, which I hope to deliver shortly. I may add that clothing is dearer than at home, except that, manufactured in America; provisions are cheaper, and there is a lavish abundance on the tables. The same clothing can be worn all the year round—it should be light woollen or print. There is no excessive heat and no intense cold. Vegetation goes on all the year round, and many trees will grow ten feet in a year. The earth fairly laughs with verdure and beauty • even the wild flowers are glorious—the 1 fields being ablaze with gold and purple. The climate of California is as much superior to the rest of the States as the climate of the States is superior to ours. My life is a very busy one, but if I have not made everything plain, I will answer concise questions, only asking that a stamped addressed envelope be enclosed.— Yours, &c., MRS. MARGARETE PARKER, Founder of the British Women's Temperance Association. The Home Lea, Penketh, Warrington, October 24th, 1887.

div.head: N W BOOKS, &c-
div.p: N W BOOKS, &c-

In the Camelot Series for October, Mr. Walter Scott publishes the prose writings of Henrich Heine. They are edited with a critical and biographical introduction by Mr. Havelock Ellis, who does full justice to this mar- vellous German writer. Heine was a genius of the highest order—a fact which stands revealed as much in his prose as in his verse. The following is a passage no better than a hundred others from the " Reisbilder ":

"It will be my last song; the stars will gaze on me as in the nights of my youth, the loving moonlight will once more kiss my cheeks, the spirit chorus of nightin- gales long dead will sound from afar, my sleep-drunken eyes will close, my soul will echo with the notes of my harp; I shall smell the flowers of Brenta. A tree will shadow my grave. I would gladly have it a palm, but that tree will not grow in the North. It will be a linden, and on summer evenings lovers will sit there and caress; the green-finch, who rocks himself on the branches, will be listening silently, and my linden will rustle tenderly over the heads of the happy ones, who will be so happy that they will have no time to read what is written on the white tombstone. But when later the lover has lost his love, then he will come again to the well-known lin- den, and sigh, and weep, and gaze long and oft upon the stone, and read the inscription He loved the flowers of Brenta."

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 29, 1887.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 29, 1887.

Knapping, by Mr. H. F. Wilo'fl, is profusely illustrated from drawings by Mr. L. Speed, while no less than thirty-two examples are given of "new coins for old" by Mr. L. F. Day. "The Americans at the Salon" leads to illustrations of some very fine pictures; "En Octobre "is in every way charming. "No. 46 Meck- lenburgh Square" (with six illustrations) affords a peep at the art treasures of Mr. Sala. There is an unusually powerful engraving of Tanner's "Ulysses taunting Poly- phemus," and the customary "chronicle of art." "The The Lady's World, published by Messrs. Cassell, has now completed the first year of its existence as a magazine of fashion and society, and its success has been so great that it has been determined to enlarge it; and, widening its area, to issue it under the title of "The Woman's World." It is announced that Mr. Oscar Wilde, who will be the editor, "will deal with many of those questions in the discussion of which he has already taken a prominent part in public." A large number of ladies have already promised their co-operation, and there is every prospect of the new series entering on a career of great usefulness. The third part of the new serial "The Sea—its stirring story of adventure, peril, and heroism," is profusely and beautifully illuslrated. An account is given of the loss of the Kent and the Birkenhead, and, in contrast to the splendid discipline observed in these cases, the story is told of the loss of the French vessel the Medusa. There is, too, a description of the siege of Gibraltar, with several striking illustrations. "Familiar Wild Flowers," first series, is concluded with part 20. The two coloured plates are of the fox- glove and burdock, accompanied by the usual descrip, tion of the plants. Part 17 of the Life and Times of Queen Victoria" (illustrated) covers the important period of 1868-7-8, when we have the reform agitation, and Mr. Disraeli and Mr. Gladstone Prime Ministers in succession. Part 21 of Cassell's Illustrated Shake- spore includes nearly the whole of "The Winter's Tale," with the customary fine full page plates. The Encyclo- pcedic Dictionary part 45) carries the reader from words beginning with "Ii" to le." As an instance of the fullness of the work, we may point out that a page of three columns is occupied in describing and illustrating the various meanings of the word "lay." We have, to give two instances, "Lay apart all filthiness" from James 1., 21; and from Macaulay, I will lay on for Tusculum, And lay thou on for Rome.

div.head: HART CASE.
div.p: THE HART CASE.

At Warrington County Court, on Thursday, before his Honour Judge Ffoulkes, the case was mentioned of Hart v. Thornton. It is an action brought by the plaintiff for the recovery of some papers alleged to be in the possession of the defendant.—On his Honour taking his seat Mr. Wharton. barrister, Manchester, who represents the p'aintiffs, said that the case was fixed for that day, b tit was thought that it would be impossible to reat. n it, and it had been suggested that the hearing should be taken next Monday. A summons for perjury upon certain answers to interrogatories had been taken out in connec- tion with the case, and it had been decided that the I hearing of this summons before the magistrates should Ibe taken next Thursday. He thought that possibly as this would be a question of oath against oath—or rather of about ten oaths against one—his Hon- our would prefer that the question should be settled by the magistrates before His Honour dealt with it.— Mr. Mulliolland, barrister, Liverpool, who appeared for the defendant, offered most strenuous opposition to Mr. Wharton's application. The case, he said, was a very serious one indeed for one party or the other. This was a case that had occupied the attention of the su- perior courts. Some persons in Warrington, it appeared, imagined that Mr. Thornton had possession of some papers, and had threatened Mr. Thorntofi, for which they had been brought before the magistrates. They were let off with a caution, and they commenced civil proceedings, claiming the return of some papers which they said were valuable to them. His friend's client had delivered interrogatories to the defendant, which Mr. Thornton had answered to the best of his knowledge and belief. The plaintiff had now actually involved the aid of the Criminal Court in order to drag him (Mr. Thornton) into a court where his mouth was closed, and to bring witnesses against him on a charge of perjury. This, he alleged, had been done with the deliberate object of prejudicing the fair trial of the action now pending before his Hon- our. The case had been fixed for Monday next, when, in the ordinary course of business, the defendant would have an opportunity of saying on oath whether or not the statements made against him were true. Therefore, he asked his Honour not to accede to the application.—His' Honour : I cannot force.any party to fix any particular day.—Mr. Wharton said that it would be a sufficient reply to Mr. Mulholland's remarks to mention that the whole of his witnesses were present, waiting for the case to be tried, and he was willing, if it could be done, to proceed with it that day.—After further conversation, it was agreed to hold a special sitting of the court to-day (Saturday), when the hearing of the action will be pro- ceeded with.

IWARRINGTON. • pEARS' ST. PAUL'S CHURCH, WARRINGTON.—OR Sunday the annual day school sermons were preached in pEARS' this church, in the morning by the vicar, the Rev. S. Wilkinson, and in .he evening by the Rev. G. D. Wray. There were good congregations. 10IEARS' Sr. JOHN'S PRESBYTERIAN Urnme.a.—On Sun- day the Sunday school anniversary sermons were I preached in this church by the Rev. John Huey, pEARs, .11. A.. 13. D., of Manchester. The services were well attended, particularly that of the evening, and pEARS, collections were taken onbehalf of the schools. BAZAAR AT HILL CLIFFE.—On Thursday after- noon a bazaar for the purpose of raising funds to -DEARS' erect a new Baptist school was opened in the school- I room, at Hill Cliffe, by Mr. Thomas Baxter, of Ash- ton, Chester. The weather was unfavourable, but PEARS' I I there was a good attendance. The stalls were i -a- well stocked with a varied assortment of goods. IpE Adts, WARRINGTON GRAMMAR SCHOOL—The Oliver' ' Heywood Classical Scholarship of £5O per annum I for two years, at Owens College, has been gained by TIEARS' ' Mr. A. Stanley Kidd. who has been the head boy of the Grammar Grammar School for the past twelve months. , The scholarship was awarded, after an open corn- 1011114EARS' petition, held at the Owens College, on the 10th and -1- illth of thepresent month. ! IN MEMORIAM.—A tablet is, it is stated, to be pEAns' i placed in Warrington Parish Church by the officers of the 3rd Battalion South Lancashire Regiment in -1-,EARs, memory of Lieutenant H. F. Eckersley, 2nd Bat- talion Prince Albert's Regiment, who was killed in action at Kyettka, Burmah, on February 5, 1886. pEARS' Lieutenant Eckersley was the youngest son of Mr, N. Eckersley, of Standish Hall, Hindley, sometime M.P. for Wigan., , plums, LECTURE AT PADGATE.—OR Thursday evening Mr. R. R. T. Burnett, F.G.S., vice-president of the Man- chester Geological. Society, gave a lecture, entitled ' "Geologic life; is it evolution ?" in the Wesleyan! school-room, at Padgate, under the auspices of the, Padgate Wesleyan Mutual Improvement Society. The chair was occupied by Mr. W. H. J. Jenkins. Owing, probably, to the severity of the weather, there was not a large attendance. At the conclu- sion a, vote of thanks was passed to Mr. Burnett for his lecture, on the proposition of Mr. Bennett. LECTURE ON CHIVALRY.—On Monday evening, at a meeting of the Holy Trinity Literary Society, Mr. Sydney Taylor, 8.A., read a paper on "Chiv- alry." The chair was occupied by the president (the Rev. E. C. E. Carleton.) Having traced the rise of the order of chivalry and described its cere- monies and constitution, Mr. Taylor summed up the benefits which had accrued from chivalry—the in- troduction of the "humanities of war," and its en- nobling and refining influence on society.—A dis- cussion took place on the paper, and Mr. Taylor was awarded a cordial vote of thanks. "SOME Somer. SPEeTnits."—lt will be seen from our advertising columns that a lecture on " Some I social spectres" will be given by the Rev. W.L. Watkinson, in Bold-street Wesleyan Schoolroom, on Wednesday next. Mr. Watkinson is a distin- guished Wesleyan preacher, and was selected to give the Fernley lecture upon "The influence of scepticism upon character" at the conference geld in London in 1886 The lecture to be given in War- rington is said to be of a very racy and humorous character, and will no doubt be found to be deeply interming, especially when delivered in Mr. Wat- kinson's inimitable style. COCICHEDOE MISSION MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT CLASS.—The usual .weekly meeting of this society was held on Monday night, when a paper was read by Mr. Munro on "Astronomy." The subject was well handled by the essayist, who dwelt at con- , siderable length on the planets, &c. Several illus- trations were given on the black board showing the nature of eclipses, and the chart of the various orbits of the planets, in their relative position round the sun. After the reading of the paper, Messrs. Haigh, Wadsworth, Farrar, Blease, Ather- ton, Oldham, and the president spoke upon the sub- , ject, and asked several questions. 1 i , SALE OF PnopEnrY.—On Wednesday, at the Lion Hotel. Wartington, Mr. T. Sutton, auctioneer, offered , for sale, pursuant to an order of the Court of Chan- I eery, a small freehold farm of over four acres of land, with dwelling-house, outbuildings, &c., situate in Latchford, and in the occupation of Mr. James! Fryer. This farm, it may be mentioned, formed part of the Harrison estate, in connection with I which there has been so much litigation. Bidding commenced at £5OO, and was continued till the amount offered reached £626, at which sum the I property waS disposed of to Mr. J. C. Parr, of Grap- penhall. Messrs. W. D. Jeans and Co. were the solicitors for the vendors. ARMY BLUCHERS, 6s 6d per pair, splendid value, at Haynes',' 42, and 44, Horsemarket-street.—Advt. WESLEYAN MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY.-- ' On Wednesday evening the members of this society held a meeting, when a discourse on Home Rule was listened to with much interest. The essayist was Mr. T. C. London, and the meeting was presided over by the Rev. W. Brookes. Touching upon the gravity of the subject. Mr. London proceeded to note that Mr. Gladstone's scheme was the only one that had been propounded, and, although his bills were dead, yet their spirit still lived. Mr. London's remedy was the settlement of the Land Question and Local Government, as opposed to an Irish Parliament at Dublin. A debate followed, in which Messrs. But- ler, Horton, C. Plinston, Whatmough, and Hay- ward opposed, while W. J. Dunn supported the essayist. HousEßßEAkiNG.—James Towey, a rag gatherer, was charged at the Borough Court, on Monday, with having broken into the house of Percy Wilson, of Wilderspool•road, on the Friday previous, and stolen sixteen bottles, a skirt, and other articles, to the value of ss. in all. During the day Constable Hollingsworth met the prisoner in Bank-street, carrying a bag. The officer examined the bag, and then, being suspicious that something was wrong, took it and the defendant to the police station, 1 , where a message was afterwards received from Mr. I Wilson that his premises had been broken into and 1 various articles taken. Subsequently the things I found in prisoner's bag were identified as those that had been stolen, and it was found that prisoner had been seen in Mr. Wilson's yard during Friday fore- noon. The Bench sent prisoner to gaol for three months with hard labour. ST. PAUL'S MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY.— On Monday, the session of this society was opened by a conversazione, a large number of members and friends being present. The proceedings were com- menced by the Vicar, who gave a short address as to the objects of the society; after which an inter- esting musical performance was gone through. songs being given by Misses Horton, Sykes, Locker. and Williams, and Mr. Sherlock. Mr. Parry and his sister also gave some duets on the piano and violin. After the concert tea was served, and altogether a most enjoyable evening was spent. One feature of the evening's entertainment was the beautiful dis- play of microscopic specimens exhibited by Messrs. L. Greening, J. Chorley, F. Monks, and J. Dutton. Mr. Knowles, jun., also favoured the audience with some capital recitations, and all acknowledged that the greatest credit was due to the indefatigable secretary (Mr. Knowles), assisted by an energetic sub-committee. Alr. G. Riley accompanied with his usual ability. CONSERVATIVE WARD MEETING.—On Monday evening the annual meeting of the Conservatives of the South-West Ward was held in the Assembly. room of the Conservative-Club, for the election of a committee and delegate's to the Council of the As- sociation for the current year. The chair was oc- cupied by Mr. Robert Pierpoint.—The Chairman said that having been appointed chairman of the whole of the Association, it would be better for him to place his resignation of chair- man of this ward in the hands or the meeting. Ile thanked all the members of the ward for the courtesy and kindness they had al- ways shown towards him, as well as for the help ' they had always been willing to give him.—Coun- cilor Wright expressed his regret that they were about to lose Mr. Pierpoint's services, and preposed the appointment of Alderman Sutton as chairman of the ward.—The motion was seconded by Mr. John Tilley, supported by the Chairman, and heartily agreed to.—ln returning thanks, Alderman Sutton said they had had a hard fight on many occasions to win, as their majority had only been one, two, or three.—Messrs. S. E. Johnson and W. W. Westwell wer6 appointed vice-chairmen, and Councillor J. E. Wright was re-elected hon. secretary, on the motion of the Chairman, seconded by Councillor Francomb. RE-OPENING, FRIDAY NEXT, SMART AND Co.'s educational establishment for ladies and gentlemen, conducted by Mr. Fred Smart. Gentlemen are taught a fine, bold, business hand, and ladies a beautiful flowing style. Terms for the complete mune, one guinea. Book-keeping by double entry; thoroughly taught, that is, all the details of journalising, posting, balanc- ing, preparing balance sheets, profit and loss account, Itc., and to keep a set of books in strict accordance with a wen-regulated counting-house. Our certificate for proficiency is given to each pupil. Arithmetic taught upon the most approved prin- ciples, including the shortest method of mental calculation. Open on Fridays only, from three until nine o'clock at night, at the Co-operative Hall, Sankey-street, Warrington.—Note, no classes, each pupil taught separately. Lessons, one hour each subject. The lessons date from the week the pupil com- mences. Prospectuses may be had at any time at the -Co- operative Hall, or will be forwarded to any address. Parents i andintending pupils are invited to eall.—iidet.

div.head: OUR FINANCIAL LETTER.
div.p: OUR FINANCIAL LETTER.

[FROM OUR OWN CORRESPONDENT.] 23, Old Broad-street, E.C. Another fortnightly settlement on the Stock Exchange has come round, and with it a far healthier feeling than prevailed at the last settlement. What is more, prices actually showed an upward tendency on the making up day, when every influence is brought to bear to send them down. It would, in the present state of things, be exacting too much to look for anything like a prolonged "boom," as the public do not come to the support of the market. Confidence is wanted, and until that is estab- lished there is no good in looking for anything like con- tinuity. There are several investments at the present time which are deserving of attention on the part of inves- tors. As a solid investment the Anglo-Argentine Tram- way Company is worth notice. The service of this com- pany is in Buenos Ayres, and the growth of the city, both in population and wealth, has been so rapid, that house property is dearer than in London. The result IS that the tramway company has been very prosperous, and thelast dividend paid was 12 per cent'. Since then the company has ac- quired the Boca line of trams, which have showed an in- crease of 20 per cent, on the traffic returns. The £lO shares are about to undergo re-construction, and be made £5 shares. The market value of these £5 shares, when this has been accomplished, will not be less than

The recent action of two outside brokers, heard in the Mayor's Court the other day, is an illustration how necessary it is for the public to know what they are doing. In this case the Stock Exchange granted a special quotation to certain shares of a company, and refused it to others. Meantime the outside brokers deal with those having no quotation, and, as far as the public are con- cerned are worthless as negotiable securities, 'therefore the difficulty arises in being sure that what you may be buying from an "outside " broker is recognised in the Stock Exchange. which, in this instance, was not. The prospectus of a company styling itself Condy's White Lead Company, Limited, has been issued with a capital of £200,000. The company is promoted by the London Founders Association, of which Mr. H. S. Fos- ter, a member of the London School Board, is the mana- ging director. The directorate is not a very strong one, although two M.P.'s figure there. One of these 13 Dr. Macdonald, who has figured in the two previous com- panies promoted by Mr. Foster's company, viz., the abortive North British Fresh Fish Supply and the Green- wich Ferry Company.

div.head: MUNICIPAL ELECTIONS.
div.p: THE MUNICIPAL ELECTIONS.

The time within which the nominations for seats on the Town Council could be made expired on Monday afternoon, so that the whole of the candidates are how before the public. It will be seen from the complete list that we give below that in only one ward—the South- East—are the nominations in excess of the vacancies to be filled. For the South-East Ward, in addition to Mr. R. W. Marsh, the retiring councillor, who seeks re-elec. tion, and Mr. N. B. Percival, the nominee of the Rate- payers' Association, Mr. S. Barlow and Mr. W. Diggle were nominated, but it will be seen that Mr. Diggle has been disqualified owing to the invalidity of his nomina- tion paper. The only contest of the election, therefore, will take the form of a three-cornered duel between Mr. Marsh, Mr. Barlow, and Mr. Percival. The addresses of these three candidates will be seen in our advertising columns. In the other wards, the candidates have, of course, already been declared elected, and in the South- East Ward the issue will be determined on Tuesday next by the ratepayers at the ballot boxes. The follow- ing is a list of the

OBJECTIONS TO NOMINATION PAPERS. On Tuesday afternoon the Mayor attended at the Town Hall, "to hear and decide objections to nomination papers." Mr. 11. J. Longton, as the agent of Mr. N. B. Per- cival, objected to to nomination of Mr. S. Barlow. Mr. Longton urged that the address was not sufficiently full to enable a letter posted in London to find Mr. Barlow. That was usually the criterion taken as regards these ad- dresses. There might be many "Folly's" in other towns. The Mayor: There may be many follies. (Laughter.)— Mr. Longton said Mr. Barlow might have lived at The Folly, Folly-lane, Widnes.—The Mayor: The nomination paper is headed "The Borough of Warrington," and -it is also dated "The 24th October, 1887, Town Clerk's Office, Warrington." Don't you think that is quite suffi- cient Longton said that those words meant that that was an election of councillors for Warrington.—The Mayor: I think we all know that Mr. Barlow resides in Warrington. If a stranger came to the town, and saw the words The Folly, Folly-lane," and saw the words on the nomination paper "The Town Clerk's Office, Warrington," he would say, "This is a man trying to get municipal honours in the Borough of Warrington."—After 130M0 discussion, The Deputy Town Clerk said the only question involved was one of identity • and it was for him (the Mayor) to decide whether that was a sufficient description to enable him to identify the candidate. To the town clerk's mind it was quite sufficient, and it was not necessary to insert the word "Warrington."—The Mayor: We must over-rule your objection,Mr. Longton.—The second objec- tion was that the nomination paper was signed" Alfred Downes," whereas on the burgess list he appeared as " Alfred Downs."—This objection was also over-ruled, and the nomination paper of Mr. Barlow was held to be good. The nomination of Mr. Diggle was objected to by Mr. Holbrook, of Newton-le-Willows, agent of Mr. R. W. Marsh, on the following grounds, viz. :-Ist, that the heading of the nomination paper was improperly filled up, " Town Councillor "being inserted where it ought to be" two councillors ." 2nd, the address of the candi- date insufficiently stated," 19, Wellington-street," being inserted, whereas it ought to be " 19, Wellington-street, Warrington ;" 3rd, the polling district of proposer and seconder was not entered, the word " powlling " being used erroneously; 4th, the nomination paper did not contain the signature of any burgesses either as pro- poser or seconder, or as assentmg ; sth, the num- bers of the burgesses were not stated as on the list, 499 E not being in the list at all, and 4,972 not being the number of "Barlow Robert ;" 6th, The name Taylor Henry. No. 499 E., was altogether in- correct; the correct name of the person whose signa- ture it was supposed to be being Henry Timothy Taylor, who was also so described on the list. 7th. The notice of assent by the burgesses was incorrectly dated 24/10/87 day of Oct. 188 , being the fraction of a day in the year 188 , and, therefore, much too early a date for this election.—The Mayor allowed the objection for the reasons stated in paragraphs filo and six, and Mr. Diggle was, therefore, disqualified. As several inquiries have been made as to the quali- fication of a town cocillor, it may be stated that the only qualification no required is that the person nominated should be on the burgess list forthe borough. The property qualification was abolished in 184.

div.p: FATAL EXPLOSION AT NEWCASTLE. The Ann Pit of the Walker Colliery, near Newcastle-on- Tyne, took fire on Monday night. It was at fist stated that 27 lives had been lost. There were 30 men work- ing in the Brockley seam and three were brought out alive, but seriously injured. Five dead bodies were then recovered, and it was feared that the other 22 were dead. A telegram on Tuesday morning, however, announced, that the explosion and consequent fire had resulted in the loss of six lives only. There were 110 men in the mine, of whom 22 were in the Brockwell seam, 200 fathoms deep; ten men and three boys were in the south district, and nine men in the east district, under John Pickett, who,had instructions to fire shots if neces- sary. About half-past eight p.m the men in the south district became aware, by the interruption of the cur' rents, that an explosion had occurred, and proceeded bY a circuitous way, to the east district, where they came upon the bodies of six of the nine men working tb_iere' and found three seriously injured. They endeathvule ap_' to remove the latter, but were driven away bi had proaching choke damp. Meanwhile, an explosion been nlor- observed from the head of the shaft, and an e2C-und ing party descended, and after great difficulty, fo The and brought the three injured men to the surface. men in'the south district and all others in the mine safely brought up. There were signs of a shot Inhge been fired. All the men were found close together,.i ajass lamp used was the Davy lamp, with tin case anr,.„,la • front. To THE BURGESSES OF THE SOUTH-EAST 1. WARD. LADIES A/VD GrfTLEMEN,—liaving been duly nominated as a Candidate for the Representation of your Ward in the Coun- cil, I willingly offer you my services. My course of action shall be thoroughly Independent, having not the slightest regard to any clique or party which may dominate in the Council or elsewhere. My sole desire and earnest exertion shall be devoted to les- sen the wasteful and absurd expenditure that is going on, and thus relieve the pockets of our of erburdened ratepayers. • lam a very large ratepayer myself, and I feel no longer willing to submit to the rates remaining at such a high figure. They must come down, "by hook or by crook," to ss. in the 2. Instead of being one of the lowest, we are, unfortunately, one of the highest rated boroughs in the kingdom, and it is, therefore, no wonder we are making so little progress. I cast the blame not upon any single member of the Coun- cil ; the whole body (including Aldermen) are responsible. What is the remedy Apply at once a strict, searching inquiry into the "why and wherefore" of every depart- ment of corporate work and expenditure. I undertake to say that if a proper check was given in this direction, you might at least save, to begin ,with, £l,OOO per annum, and if elected as your representative I will endeavour to ac- complish it. I will not now go into details, but I may have an oppor- tunity of addressing you on various matters during the contest. MARE.—I am thoroughly disgusted with the canvassing business. \ I shall go in for the" purity ticket," and employ neither canvassers nor agents. I rely simply upon the intelli- gence and judgment of my fellow-ratepayers to record their votes as they may deem advisable, and if elected I will fear- lessly do my duty. lam, Yours faithfully. SAMUEL BARLOW. "The Polley," Warrington, Octobly 25th, 1887.

r THE BURGESSES OF THE SOUTH-EAST WARD. ELECTION OF TOWN COUNCILLORS, IST NOVEMBER, 1887. LADIES AND GENTLEMEN,—My term of office as One Of your representatives in the Town Council will expire on the First of November next, and in response to the invitation of a large number of Electors, I have again consented tO seek re-election. I need scarcely tell you that I have been unani- mously adopted by the Conservative Association as the Candi- date for this Ward. In again seeking your suffrage, I feel I may do so with the fullest confidence, being convinced that my actions and votes in the Town Council have always been such as to :meet with your approval. Should you do me the honour to re-elect me, I shall, without reference to person or party, always do my utmost to keep the expenditure down to the lowest possible point, consistent with tSsThealth and prosperity of the borough. I promise that my special attention will be given to the re- moval and prevention of any grievance that may oppress the Ratepayers of the Ward. TO THE BURGESSES OF THE SOUTH-EAST WARD. Lentss A/CD GE/CTLEMEN.—liavIng been nominated and assented to by a body of influential gentlemen of this Ward for the vacancy in the Town Council, as my three nominations papers confirm, I come forward for such position. lam also the Sole Candidate of the Ratepayers' Association, which is established to regulate matters on these occasions, to keep down rates, to select suitable candidates, competent to repre- sent voters in the Town Council, to act in an unbiassed and non-political manner, and to study the Interests of the Rate- payers in the expenditure of their money; also to support measures advantageous to the interest of the Borough. The Committee of the Association deeply deplore and strongly condemn that, at the eleventh hour, Mr. Samuel Barlow should come forward as a Candidate in face of the Associa- tion to which he belongs, and upset its arrangements. I recognise that a candidate for municipal honours takes up a responsible position, and it would be well if our worthy Aldermen had to undergo the same ordeal; but we must leave that to future legislation. If you elect me, my policy will be to support measures of reform such as the foundation of a Free Lending Library, in order to enable the working classes to meet the educational re- quirements of the times. I shall also strive to prevent unne- cessary outlay of money on the Intercepting Depots, and to counteract the disagreeable and injurious smells which we have to contend with, and which I think can be done by a pro- cess of scientific skill, as in pure air. As to the Water Question, I am favourable to the purchase of the Waterworks by the Corporation, if accomplished on the principle of the Gas Works, and if it can be purchased at a fair price, as an investment under our control. I consider that. Cheap gas and water are most essential to the prosperity of the town. My attention will be given to the paving of the streets in the interests of. proPerty owners and tenants combined. As regards the wall and grounds of the Town Hall, I will use my discretion not to lavish money away foolishly upon it to increase your rates. If any practical scheme can be brought forward for better Bath accommodation with wash-houses, it will be studied by me. I shall oppose 7 improper sanitary reforms; for instance. urinals erected in unsuitable places, which create a nuisance to the residents near and to the general public. I will also give my attention to the Sewerage Department. Now, as the town is much extended and the population in- creased, it is contemplated by Government to have the Borough Boundaries revised, which will lead to the equaliza- tion of the respective Wards, and as the Ship Canal is passing through the Borough, adequate dock accommodation will be required. The River Committee will want strength and sound judgment to support them in this grand scheme, and to see that the river is not so polluted as it has been. This I promise to watch very carefully for the town's interest. Now, Ladies and Gentlemen and Fellow Working-men, hav- ing laid before you a few Items for municipal work, I would rt.spectfully ask your consideration to them before you vote, and If you favour me with your patronage and confidence I will do my utmost to perform my duties to your satisfaction. If I am returned to the Town Council it will only be going again once more to my old seat, which, after seven years' service I vacated at the time Dr. Hackie entered the Council, and from which he now retires. I appeal to the masses as well as the classes to do me the honour of recording their votes for me as ' your independent Ratepayers' Candidate, and, living and hav- ing my place of business in your Ward, I dare pledge myself that your interests will be well understood and carefully atten- ded to by me. I am,' Ladies and Gentlemen, Yours faithfully, \ NATHAN BROWN PERCIVAL., Peel Place, 27, Church-street, Warrington, October 27th, 1887.

The basis of the settlement of the Bolton ironyorkers' strike shows that the men resume work immediately. The "Freeman's Journal says the sister of the lad Casey, who was shot at MitcheLstown, died on Thursday through grief, which undermined a robust con- stitution. FATAL RAILWAY ACCIDENT.—Mr. Alfred Summers, brother of the member for Huddersfield, was killed on the railway at Stalybridgs Station, on Friday morning, by a Stockport train. His head was terribly injured. THE STRIKE IN THE NAIL TRADE.—R Is stated that up- wards of 15,000 operatives have how been out on strike eight weeks for an advance in wages. The greatest des- titution exists in Staffordshire and Worcestershire. 4 MR. GLADSTONE'S RETURN TO HAWARDEN. Mr. Gladstone left Studley Royal on Friday morning on his return to Hawarden, and was accorded a warm wel- come at Ripon, where, however, he did not speak. Harrogate was reached at 10-20, and the station was crowded with people, who cheered heartily on recognis- ing Mr. Gladstone. At Leeds, Batley, Dewsbury, Mirfield, and Hudders- field, Mr. Gladstone had a most enthusiastic welcome from the large crowds which had asseilibled to greet that eminent statesman, who smilingly bowed his acknow- ledgments, but maintained silence. The day proved remarkably fine. Mr. Gladstone reached Warrington shortly after half- past one. He made a brief stay, but there were only a few persons on the platform. There was a large number at Chester.
